12.2.b Some practical Integrals

 Measuring lengths, areas, and volumes
Let’s focus on a special case of measurement where we measure like a carpenter, that is, we look at the starting point and the ending points and we assume everything in between is part of the length. This means we only need to know how to measure intervals ((a,b)= {xa<x<b}). The standard Lebesgue interval measure for this is
\[\displaystyle m\Big((a,b)\Big) := b-a\]%255CBig)%2520%253A%253D%2520b-a?scale=1)
If we level up to area then we measure rectangles which have corners ((x_1,x_2), (c,b), (c,d),(a,d)), we write this as ((x_1,x_2)(y_1, y_2))
(m((x_1,x_2)(y_1,y_2)) = (x_2-x_1) (y_2-y_1) = m((x_1,x_2))m( (y_1,y_2)))


 * Quick Check

To measure volumes we use which of these. - A product of three intervals: \[m\Big((x_1,x_2)\times (y_1,y_2)\times (z_1,z_2)\Big)=m\Big((x_1,x_2)\Big) \cdot m\Big((y_1,y_2)\Big)\cdot m\Big((z_1,z_2)\Big)\]%255Ctimes%2520(y_1%252Cy_2)%255Ctimes%2520(z_1%252Cz_2)%255CBig)%253Dm%255CBig((x_1%252Cx_2)%255CBig)%2520%255Ccdot%2520m%255CBig((y_1%252Cy_2)%255CBig)%255Ccdot%2520m%255CBig((z_1%252Cz_2)%255CBig)?scale=1) *


Correct: but there is a better answer. - Area of the base times the height: \[m\Big((x_1,x_2)\times (y_1,y_2)\times (z_1,z_2)\Big)=m\Big((x_1,x_2)\times (y_1,y_2)\Big) \cdot m\Big((z_1,z_2)\Big)\]%255Ctimes%2520(y_1%252Cy_2)%255Ctimes%2520(z_1%252Cz_2)%255CBig)%253Dm%255CBig((x_1%252Cx_2)%255Ctimes%2520(y_1%252Cy_2)%255CBig)%2520%255Ccdot%2520m%255CBig((z_1%252Cz_2)%255CBig)?scale=1) *
Correct: but there is a better answer. - Any one of the above. *
Correct: this is the best answer. If we look at how length x width x height or area of base x height each work out they all expand eventually into a product of all interval sides.



 *Newton-Leibniz’s Interval measurement Theorem.
For the Lebesgue integral measure \[m\Big((a,b)\Big)=b-a\]%255CBig)%253Db-a?scale=1) and Lebesgue measurable function \[f:(a,b)\to [-\infty,\infty]\]%255Cto%2520%255B-%255Cinfty%252C%255Cinfty%255D?scale=1) then for \[a<x_1<x_2<b\]
\[\displaystyle F(x_2)-F(x_1) = \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\, dm\]-F(x_1)%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm?scale=1) where \[\displaystyle F(x) := \int_{(a,x)} f\, dm\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm?scale=1).
Said in the more classical interval notation this means
\[\displaystyle F(x)\bigg|_{x_1}^{x_2}=F(x_2)-F(x_1) = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(t) \, dt\]%255Cbigg%257C_%257Bx_1%257D%255E%257Bx_2%257D%253DF(x_2)-F(x_1)%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257Bx_1%257D%255E%257Bx_2%257D%2520f(t)%2520%255C%252C%2520dt?scale=1) wherever \[\displaystyle F(x) := \int f(t)\, dt\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%255Cint%2520f(t)%255C%252C%2520dt?scale=1), equivalently \[\displaystyle \frac{dF}{dx}=f(x)\]?scale=1).


 Proof Lebesgue \[\vdash\] Newton-Leibniz**
We want to learn about ({(x_1,x_2)} f, dm) in terms of (F(x)={(a,x)} f, dm). So we can start with
\[\begin{aligned}
F(x_2) & = \int_{(a,x_2)} f\, dm  & \text{ break into disjoint intervals}\\
& = \int_{(a,x_1)\sqcup (x_1,x_1)\sqcup (x_1,x_2)} f\,d m & \text{measure on disjoint intervals}\\
& = \int_{(a,x_1)}f\, dm + \int_{[x_1,x_1]} f\,dm + \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\,d m & \text{notice }\begin{array}{c}m([x_1,x_1])=0\\ F(x_1)=\int_{(a,x_1)} fdm\end{array}\\
& = F(x_1) + 0 + \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\,d m.
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520break%2520into%2520disjoint%2520intervals%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%255Csqcup%2520(x_1%252Cx_1)%255Csqcup%2520(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bmeasure%2520on%2520disjoint%2520intervals%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%257Df%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B%255Bx_1%252Cx_1%255D%257D%2520f%255C%252Cdm%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bnotice%2520%257D%255Cbegin%257Barray%257D%257Bc%257Dm(%255Bx_1%252Cx_1%255D)%253D0%255C%255C%2520F(x_1)%253D%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%257D%2520fdm%255Cend%257Barray%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520F(x_1)%2520%252B%25200%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m.%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Now we just solve for the term we want to know about
\[\displaystyle \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\, dm = F(x_2)-F(x_1)\]%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%253D%2520F(x_2)-F(x_1)?scale=1).


 * Newton-Leibniz’ Can Fail for non-interval measures: Counting \[\not\vDash\] Newton-Leibniz
Now let’s change measures just to demonstrate that this claim is very much about the condition of the interval measure. We need only create a model (example) where the claim fails, so this is a \[\vDash\] situation. Let us use the function (f(x)=x) and choose (a=0<x_1=1<x_2<2).
\[\begin{aligned}
\int_{(1,2)} x\, d\mu & = 0 & \text{ because }\mu\Big((1,2)\Big)=0\\
F(2) - F(1) & = \int_{(0,2)} x\, d\mu  - \int_{(0,1)}x \, d\mu \\
& = \int_{[1,1]} x\,d\mu  & \text{because }\mu((0,1))=0=\mu((1,2)), \text{ and} \mu([1,1])=1\\
& = 1
\end{aligned}\]%257D%2520x%255C%252C%2520d%255Cmu%2520%2526%2520%253D%25200%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520because%2520%257D%255Cmu%255CBig((1%252C2)%255CBig)%253D0%255C%255C%250AF(2)%2520-%2520F(1)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(0%252C2)%257D%2520x%255C%252C%2520d%255Cmu%2520%2520-%2520%255Cint_%257B(0%252C1)%257Dx%2520%255C%252C%2520d%255Cmu%2520%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B%255B1%252C1%255D%257D%2520x%255C%252Cd%255Cmu%2520%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bbecause%2520%257D%255Cmu((0%252C1))%253D0%253D%255Cmu((1%252C2))%252C%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520and%257D%2520%255Cmu(%255B1%252C1%255D)%253D1%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%25201%2520%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
So \[\displaystyle \int_{(1,2)} x\,d\mu =0\neq x\bigg|_{1}^{2}=2-1=1\]%257D%2520x%255C%252Cd%255Cmu%2520%253D0%255Cneq%2520x%255Cbigg%257C_%257B1%257D%255E%257B2%257D%253D2-1%253D1?scale=1). What went wrong? Nothing. We simply used a measure where (([x_1,x_2])) and so a measurement that vanished for intervals no longer vanishes.
Always make sure you are using an interval measure when applying the Newton-Leibniz Theorem.

 Probability Measures
Measures in probability are specialized to have a total measure of 1 on the entire sample space (). The measure on the space is usually called a “probability measure” and we here are denoting it by () though you may see it as (P) or () elsewhere. The measurable functions (X:) in probability are called “random variables” and denoted often as simply (X). They are not variables at all, they are functions, but the term is meant to retain the character of some the original writings on probability.

* 12.2.b Combing Integral and Derivative thinking
 The power of measurement is strongest when we can go forward with integrals and backwards with derivatives.

 Video
y=(y*x)/x and therefore Calculus

 A bit of history and context
Historically derivatives were defined as the slope of tangents to a curve or instantaneous rates of change. These concepts are not immediately logical—how do you define a unique tangent to a graph without already having the slope, i.e. it makes for a circular definition. An instant in time is also not a precise concept. But its ability to solve questions made Newton (1660’s) a hero of science. Between the 1800-1900’s Cauchy, Weirestrass, and Riemann each contributed ideas to make the concept precise. Still issued persisted not least of which was the difficulty in stacking integrals measurements. While geometry suggested we can remeasure as many times as we like, the formulas of the Cauchy-Riemann method had gaps and oddities that did not match the graphical intuition.
To solve these problem Lebesgue’s integral (1900) threw the subject on its head. Instead of beginning with the concept of smaller and smaller approximations, Lebesgue classified what a measurement under the basic concept that: the whole is the sum of its parts. Once created integrals stand out as accumulation of measurements under any grouping into parts – be those small approximations or large chunks. The concept now being sound later authors such as Radon-Nikodym (1915) explored how to convert the calculus of the previous generation into this formalism. This new integral has proved compelling flexible and useful so it has dominated the sciences. For data sciences and probability it is the main tool. Icon Progress Bar (browser only)

 For interval measures the derivative is the slope of the tangent line to accumulation curve.

 Example 1: The Interval Derivative of position is velocity.
In a high-school physics class you likely measured position (x(t)) at a time (t) starting from time 0. So the distance accumulates over the interval (E=[0,t)). The problem is that we can travel at different velocities (positive or negative speeds). The times we travel faster we go further.



Slope of a line segment as the ratio of rise over run


So to approximate total distance over the time interval (E) will can get a good approximation by adding up small units in time to capture moments we travel a fixed velocities. That is we have an integral. An integral of what? Well by the definition of the derivative it is an integral of the derivative of position.

 Example 2: Interval Derivative of weight is density.
Now an example from a physical measurement: the weight (w) of an object. We can divide the weight up amongst the volume using the customary Lebesgue measure (m). For example we can take a core sample of mud at the bottom of a lake and calculate its weight as an integral (or a numerical approximation of the integral). Now if we measure the weight at different heights of the cylinder then we get varied weights. The weight changes based on the density of the mud. A more dense mud will weigh more. So a suitable interpretation for the derivative of weight per volume is density.


 What is a tangent line?
Sometimes we over-learn the lesson of tangents to a circle. After all the exposure tho the word tangent in mathematics is usually made along side sine, cosine and the unit circle so the confusion is understandable. But if we look to the word “tangent” in the conversional meaning we are describing a topic that begin as related but in retrospect may have diverged. So the key is that at some point the two topic did appear the same. In this same way a tangent to a curve is a line that for some period approximates the shape of the graph.

Tangents may not exist.
Tangent lines, if they exist, are unique.
Tangents may touch the graph in many places and may even approximate the graph in more than one place.



 The Derivative as Change of Measure
Now the Newton-Leibniz theorem and its geometric conceptualization of the derivative as rate of change has been enormously valuable but there are roles for derivatives where “rate of change” is less compelling as an explanation. Take for instance measurements of chaotic data like earth quakes, stock markets, or network traffic. Below we picture the seismology of the Cabo de Gata earthquake 2025. We see the behavior is quite erratic with sharp changes in direction that make it impossible to place a straight line as local approximation. That is this curve has few discernible tangents.



Seismograph of Terremoto Cabo de Gata 2025, Almju, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons


The absence of discernible tangents here does not mean we should not attempt to use this as a measure compared to another. It simply means we should not compare it to an interval measure. In fact one the most important measures to compare with is the simple concentration measure (_c). The graph above indicates the first noticeable motion in the graph as the P-wave – the primary wave indicating the start of the tremor. The next measure S-wave is secondary /shear wave. The distance in time between these markers can be used to predict the distance from sensor to the origin of wave. Another common integral is an interval measure but shifted to the domain of frequencies through a process known as Fourier transforms. So in short the interval measure and its associated Riemann integral and slope of tangents interpretation is not directly useful for these data but other integrals and derivatives are essential.
Try to think of derivatives as formulas to change measures and not simply as slopes. While the slope perspective is important in many historical applications it is not in the end the only interpretation and many modern data centered goals are better understood as comparing measures, not tangents of graphs.

 A bit of history
Historically derivatives were defined as the slope of tangents to a curve or instantaneous rates of change. These concepts are not immediately logical—how do you define a unique tangent to a graph without already having the slope, i.e. it makes for a circular definition. An instant in time is also not a precise concept. But its ability to solve questions made Newton (1660’s) a hero of science. Between the 1800-1900’s Cauchy, Weirestrass, and Riemann each contributed ideas to make the concept precise. Still issued persisted not least of which was the difficulty in stacking integrals measurements. While geometry suggested we can remeasure as many times as we like, the formulas of the Cauchy-Riemann method had gaps and oddities that did not match the graphical intuition.
To solve these problem Lebesgue’s integral (1900) threw the subject on its head. Instead of beginning with the concept of smaller and smaller approximations, Lebesgue classified what a measurement under the basic concept that: the whole is the sum of its parts. Once created integrals stand out as accumulation of measurements under any grouping into parts – be those small approximations or large chunks. The concept now being sound later authors such as Radon-Nikodym (1915) explored how to convert the calculus of the previous generation into this formalism.
Thes are admittedly the most recent to the list but they are extraordinarily more diverse making the concept of measurement match so many more applications that it quickly clarified the field. Here derivatives are ways to change measure, and have no need to be grounded in concepts of slopes of tangents. Its explosive use in modern probability, finance, machine learning, and data science make it the right match for the computationally minded amongst us. Even so, if your primary aims are engineering, mechanics, or classical physics then the narrower picture created by Newton and Leibniz will be enough. Just be mindful not to draw upon the wrong formulas as the answers can be quit different.



 Mean Value Theorem for Interval measurements
A common re-telling the Newton-Leibniz theorem is to multiply both sides by (1/x=1/(x_2-x_1) because this has a description in terms of concepts like speed and rates of change and averages. In this form it is known as the “Mean Value Theorem” (mean is a synonym to “average”).

 Interpreting the Mean Value Theorem in Applications
You enter the highway at 8:00 am and drive for 1 hour and exit 70 miles away. Your average speed is therefore 70 miles per hour. If the speed limit is 65 miles per hour then the traffic toll system has enough evidence to charge you with speeding. This despite having not seen you actually speed at any instant in time. Why? Well the average rate of change was 70 mph and by the Mean Value Theorem there must be some point (c) where your speed (x’(t)) (the derivative of your position (x(t)) at time (t)).
This is an example of a theoretical claim. The problem with enforcing this is that perhaps your state laws require evidence in the form of a specific photograph of an instance of speeding. That is, a computational logic might be required to enforce the law. On the other hand even that could be called into question with many practical logical concerns, such as the accuracy of the data collected. Always remember to return to the simpler lessons of logic before drawing conclusion as to the validity of some purely theoretical claim.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing

math156 Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
Why do we have calculus? Well y=(y*x)/x is a pithy answer but it comes close to getting to the point. Integral structures, where the whole is the sum of its parts, are modeled well by multiplication, simply because multiplication distributes over addition. Differentiable structures, where rates of change become stable in finitely many measurements, are modeled well by division, simply because slopes of lines are fractions. Finally multiplication and division are inverses of each other so it is possible to fashion an entire theory of calculation–a “calculus”– around this observation: integrals and derivatives are inverses to each other.

 *Objectives

Recognize the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus in single variable form, both ways
Interpret the meaning of integral
Interpret the meaning of differential
Explain in general why knowledge of differential informs you of integrals and vice versa

\[\displaystyle F(x_2)-F(x_1) = \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\, dm\]-F(x_1)%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm?scale=1) where \[\displaystyle F(x) := \int_{(a,x)} f\, dm\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm?scale=1).

We want to learn about ({(x_1,x_2)} f, dm) in terms of (F(x)={(a,x)} f, dm). So we can start with
\[\begin{aligned}
F(x_2) & = \int_{(a,x_2)} f\, dm  & \text{ break into disjoint intervals}\\
& = \int_{(a,x_1)\sqcup (x_1,x_1)\sqcup (x_1,x_2)} f\,d m & \text{measure on disjoint intervals}\\
& = \int_{(a,x_1)}f\, dm + \int_{[x_1,x_1]} f\,dm + \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\,d m & \text{notice }\begin{array}{c}m([x_1,x_1])=0\\ F(x_1)=\int_{(a,x_1)} fdm\end{array}\\
& = F(x_1) + 0 + \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\,d m.
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520break%2520into%2520disjoint%2520intervals%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%255Csqcup%2520(x_1%252Cx_1)%255Csqcup%2520(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bmeasure%2520on%2520disjoint%2520intervals%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%257Df%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B%255Bx_1%252Cx_1%255D%257D%2520f%255C%252Cdm%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bnotice%2520%257D%255Cbegin%257Barray%257D%257Bc%257Dm(%255Bx_1%252Cx_1%255D)%253D0%255C%255C%2520F(x_1)%253D%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%257D%2520fdm%255Cend%257Barray%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520F(x_1)%2520%252B%25200%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m.%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)

\[\displaystyle \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\, dm = F(x_2)-F(x_1)\]%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%253D%2520F(x_2)-F(x_1)?scale=1).



Now let’s change measures just to demonstrate that this claim is very much about the condition of the interval measure. We need only create a model (example) where the claim fails, so this is a \[\vDash\] situation. Let us use the function (f(x)=x) and choose (a=0<x_1=1<x_2<2).
\[\begin{aligned}
\int_{(1,2)} x\, d\mu & = 0 & \text{ because }\mu\Big((1,2)\Big)=0\\
F(2) - F(1) & = \int_{(0,2)} x\, d\mu  - \int_{(0,1)}x \, d\mu \\
& = \int_{[1,1]} x\,d\mu  & \text{because }\mu((0,1))=0=\mu((1,2)), \text{ and} \mu([1,1])=1\\
& = 1

Suppose that () is a measure which is absolutely continuous on \[[a,b]\] with respect the Lebesgue interval measure \[m([a,b])=b-a\]%253Db-a?scale=1). Define \[F:[a,b]\to [-\infty,\infty]\] by \[\displaystyle F(x)=\int_{[a,x]} d\nu\]%253D%255Cint_%257B%255Ba%252Cx%255D%257D%2520d%255Cnu?scale=1). Then the slope of the tangent line to (F) is defined as
\[\begin{aligned}
F'(x) & := \lim_{\begin{array}{c} x_1\leq x\leq x_2\\ \Delta x\to 0\end{array}} \frac{\Delta F}{\Delta x}
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253A%253D%2520%255Clim_%257B%255Cbegin%257Barray%257D%257Bc%257D%2520x_1%255Cleq%2520x%255Cleq%2520x_2%255C%255C%2520%255CDelta%2520x%255Cto%25200%255Cend%257Barray%257D%257D%2520%255Cfrac%257B%255CDelta%2520F%257D%257B%255CDelta%2520x%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Furthermore, this is equal to the Radon-Nikodym derivative, that is,
\[\displaystyle F' = \frac{d\nu}{dm}.\]



Because of the internal measure we have the Newton-Leibniz theorem and we start from there and multiply both sides by (1/x).
\[\begin{aligned}
\frac{F(x_2)-F(x_1)}{x_2-x_1} & = \frac{1}{x_2-x_1}\int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(t) dt = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{f(t) dt}{x_2-x_1}
\end{aligned}\]-F(x_1)%257D%257Bx_2-x_1%257D%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257Bx_2-x_1%257D%255Cint_%257Bx_1%257D%255E%257Bx_2%257D%2520f(t)%2520dt%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257Bx_1%257D%255E%257Bx_2%257D%2520%255Cfrac%257Bf(t)%2520dt%257D%257Bx_2-x_1%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Now we add the limit to this formula which means to assume margin for error \[\varepsilon \gt 0\]. Shrink the interval ([x_1,x_2]) until the area \[\min\{f(c) | x_1\leq c \leq x_2\}\cdot (x_2-x_1)\]%2520%257C%2520x_1%255Cleq%2520c%2520%255Cleq%2520x_2%255C%257D%255Ccdot%2520(x_2-x_1)?scale=1) is within the margin of error of the actual measure \[\displaystyle \int_{x_1}^{x_2}f(t)dt\]dt?scale=1). The following diagram illustrates how this can occur, just shrink to one box.



Curve with rectangle boxes approximating the area under the curve.


So we can replace the integral
\[\begin{aligned}
F'(x) & \overset{definition}{=} \lim_{\begin{array}{c} x_1\leq x\leq x_2\\ \Delta x\to 0\end{array}}\frac{F(x_2)-F(x_1)}{x_2-x_1}
= \lim_{\begin{array}{c} x_1\leq x\leq x_2\\ \Delta x\to 0\end{array}}\int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{f(t) dt}{x_2-x_1} \\
& \overset{approx.}{=} \lim_{\begin{array}{c}x_1\leq x\leq x_2,\\ \Delta x\to 0\end{array}}\left( \frac{1}{x_2-x_1} \min\{f(c)\mid x_1\leq c\leq x_2\} \cdot (x_2-x_1)\right)\\
& = \lim_{\begin{array}{c}x_1\leq x\leq x_2,\\ \Delta x\to 0\end{array}} \min\{f(c)\mid x_1\leq c\leq x_2\} \\
& =  f(x)

Historically derivatives were defined as the slope of tangents to a curve or instantaneous rates of change. These concepts are not immediately logical—how do you define a unique tangent to a graph without already having the slope, i.e. it makes for a circular definition. An instant in time is also not a precise concept. But its ability to solve questions made Newton (1660’s) a hero of science. Between the 1800-1900’s Cauchy, Weirestrass, and Riemann each contributed ideas to make the concept precise.
Lebesgue’s integral (1900) and the Radon-Nikodym derivatives (1915) are admittedly the most recent to the list but they are extraordinarily more diverse making the concept of measurement match so many more applications that it quickly clarified the field. Here derivatives are ways to change measure, and have no need to be grounded in concepts of slopes of tangents. Its explosive use in modern probability, finance, machine learning, and data science make it the right match for the computationally minded amongst us. Even so, if your primary aims are engineering, mechanics, or classical physics then the narrower picture created by Newton and Leibniz will be enough. Just be mindful not to draw upon the wrong formulas as the answers can be quit different.




A common re-telling the Newton-Leibniz theorem is to multiply both sides by (1/x=1/(x_2-x_1) because this has a description in terms of concepts like speed and rates of change and averages. In this form it is known as the “Mean Value Theorem” (mean is a synonym to “average”).



For a measurable function \[f:[a,b]\to [-\infty,\infty]\] let \[\displaystyle F(x) := \int_{[a,x]} f\, dm=\int_a^x f(t)dt\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B%255Ba%252Cx%255D%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm%253D%255Cint_a%255Ex%2520f(t)dt?scale=1) then for (a=0<x_1=1<x_2<2)
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Global rate of change}
& = \frac{\Delta F}{\Delta x} =  \frac{F(x_2)-F(x_1)}{x_2-x_1} \\
& \overset{{\small \text{discovery}}}{=} \int_{x_1}^{x_2} \frac{f(t)}{\Delta x}\,dt\\
& = \text{Accumulated rate of instant change}
\end{aligned}\]-F(x_1)%257D%257Bx_2-x_1%257D%2520%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%255Coverset%257B%257B%255Csmall%2520%255Ctext%257Bdiscovery%257D%257D%257D%257B%253D%257D%2520%255Cint_%257Bx_1%257D%255E%257Bx_2%257D%2520%255Cfrac%257Bf(t)%257D%257B%255CDelta%2520x%257D%255C%252Cdt%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BAccumulated%2520rate%2520of%2520instant%2520change%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Said another way, there is a point (x_1cx_2) such that
\[\displaystyle F'(c) = \frac{\Delta F}{\Delta x}\]%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B%255CDelta%2520F%257D%257B%255CDelta%2520x%257D?scale=1).


You enter the highway at 8:00 am and drive for 1 hour and exit 70 miles away. Your average speed is therefore 70 miles per hour. If the speed limit is 65 miles per hour then the traffic toll system has enough evidence to charge you with speeding. This despite having not seen you actually speed at any instant in time. Why? Well the average rate of change was 70 mph and by the Mean Value Theorem there must be some point (c) where your speed (x’(t)) (the derivative of your position (x(t)) at time (t)).
This is an example of a theoretical claim. The problem with enforcing this is that perhaps your state laws require evidence in the form of a specific photograph of an instance of speeding. That is, a computational logic might be required to enforce the law. On the other hand even that could be called into question with many practical logical concerns, such as the accuracy of the data collected. Always remember to return to the simpler lessons of logic before drawing conclusion as to the validity of some purely theoretical claim.

For the Lebesgue integral measure \[m\Big([a,b]\Big)=b-a\]%253Db-a?scale=1) and Lebesgue measurable function \[f:[a,b]\to [-\infty,\infty]\] then for \[a\leq x_1 \leq x_2 \leq b\]
\[\displaystyle F(x_2)-F(x_1) = \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\, dm\]-F(x_1)%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm?scale=1) where \[\displaystyle F(x) := \int_{(a,x)} f\, dm\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm?scale=1).
Said in the more classical interval notation this means
\[\displaystyle F(x)\bigg|_{x_1}^{x_2}=F(x_2)-F(x_1) = \int_{x_1}^{x_2} f(t) \, dt\]%255Cbigg%257C_%257Bx_1%257D%255E%257Bx_2%257D%253DF(x_2)-F(x_1)%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257Bx_1%257D%255E%257Bx_2%257D%2520f(t)%2520%255C%252C%2520dt?scale=1) wherever \[\displaystyle F(x) := \int f(t)\, dt\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%255Cint%2520f(t)%255C%252C%2520dt?scale=1), equivalently \[\displaystyle \frac{dF}{dx}=f(x)\]?scale=1).



We want to learn about ({(x_1,x_2)} f, dm) in terms of (F(x)={(a,x)} f, dm). So we can start with
\[\begin{aligned}
F(x_2) & = \int_{(a,x_2)} f\, dm  & \text{ break into disjoint intervals}\\
& = \int_{(a,x_1)\sqcup (x_1,x_1)\sqcup (x_1,x_2)} f\,d m & \text{measure on disjoint intervals}\\
& = \int_{(a,x_1)}f\, dm + \int_{[x_1,x_1]} f\,dm + \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\,d m & \text{notice }\begin{array}{c}m([x_1,x_1])=0\\ F(x_1)=\int_{(a,x_1)} fdm\end{array}\\
& = F(x_1) + 0 + \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\,d m.
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520break%2520into%2520disjoint%2520intervals%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%255Csqcup%2520(x_1%252Cx_1)%255Csqcup%2520(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bmeasure%2520on%2520disjoint%2520intervals%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%257Df%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B%255Bx_1%252Cx_1%255D%257D%2520f%255C%252Cdm%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bnotice%2520%257D%255Cbegin%257Barray%257D%257Bc%257Dm(%255Bx_1%252Cx_1%255D)%253D0%255C%255C%2520F(x_1)%253D%255Cint_%257B(a%252Cx_1)%257D%2520fdm%255Cend%257Barray%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520F(x_1)%2520%252B%25200%2520%252B%2520%255Cint_%257B(x_1%252Cx_2)%257D%2520f%255C%252Cd%2520m.%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Now we just solve for the term we want to know about
\[\displaystyle \int_{(x_1,x_2)} f\, dm = F(x_2)-F(x_1)\]%257D%2520f%255C%252C%2520dm%2520%253D%2520F(x_2)-F(x_1)?scale=1).



Now let’s change measures just to demonstrate that this claim is very much about the condition of the interval measure. We need only create a model (example) where the claim fails, so this is a \[\vDash\] situation. Let us use the function (f(x)=x) and choose (a=0<x_1=1<x_2<2).
\[\begin{aligned}
\int_{(1,2)} x\, d\mu & = 0 & \text{ because }\mu\Big((1,2)\Big)=0\\

& = \int_{[1,1]} x\,d\mu  & \text{because }\mu((0,1))=0=\mu((1,2)), \text{ and} \mu([1,1])=1\\
& = 1
\end{aligned}\]%257D%2520x%255C%252C%2520d%255Cmu%2520%2526%2520%253D%25200%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520because%2520%257D%255Cmu%255CBig((1%252C2)%255CBig)%253D0%255C%255C%250AF(2)%2520-%2520F(1)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B(0%252C2)%257D%2520x%255C%252C%2520d%255Cmu%2520%2520-%2520%255Cint_%257B(0%252C1)%257Dx%2520%255C%252C%2520d%255Cmu%2520%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cint_%257B%255B1%252C1%255D%257D%2520x%255C%252Cd%255Cmu%2520%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257Bbecause%2520%257D%255Cmu((0%252C1))%253D0%253D%255Cmu((1%252C2))%252C%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520and%257D%2520%255Cmu(%255B1%252C1%255D)%253D1%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%25201%2520%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)

* 12.2 “Area” & “Slope” Working together
 Many measurements you will encounter are accumulations of smaller measurements. If we learn to compute those measurements the rest is data collection and physical scanners.

 Simple functions
Suppose we know how to measure disjoint subsets (A_1,, A_n). Then we can measure them together because the whole is the sum of its parts:
((A_1A_n) = (A_1)++(A_n))
Now what if we discover along the way that we would like to create a new measure by simply re-weighting each individual term.

 Example: course grading
Let us suppose () represents all graded assessments in a course, each graded as a percentage. To hold on to a specific example here is a possible grade list for our fictitious student.
StudentHomework 1Lab 1Homework 2Lab 2Exam 1 Homework 3Lab 3Exam 2Raw Average \[\displaystyle \frac{\mu(A)}{8}\]%257D%257B8%257D?scale=1)Weighted Average \[\displaystyle \frac{\nu(A)}{8}\]%257D%257B8%257D?scale=1)
Ralphie T. Buffalo****75%80%72%0%74%81%85%83%69%
Cam T. Ram 92% 85%75%82%87%88%95%91%87%
The score for a subset (A) is to add up all the scores in (A) and divide them by the total number of scores, i.e. an average :
\[\displaystyle \mu(A)=\sum_{a\in A} a\]%253D%255Csum_%257Ba%255Cin%2520A%257D%2520a?scale=1)
(We included a column for the measure ((Ralphie)) in row 2 and ((Cam)) in row 3.)
Revisiting the grades. Now suppose we decide it would be better to weight scores based on categories. For example homeworks (H) should count for 40% of the grade, labs (L) for 30%, and exams (E) for 30%. math156 Integrals
There are functions we create from measuring things, and the rest of our data is a calculation with those measurements. So it matters to single out the methods that measurements can be combined to calculate accurate and approximate values of the things we can’t easily measure. When a problem space satisfies the “Integral Law”—the whole is the sum of its parts—that’s when we can safely apply the integral. Part I of several things to say on this.

 *Objectives

Identify the integral law
Relate areas to areas of rectangles
Read the integral notation.



 *Lectures
YouTube video player
Much of today’s integrals are done by computer and done by methods few mathematicians even understand. Even show, there are 3 inch thick textbooks and competitions about the “doing” of integral calculus which continue to be taught as a right of passage to becoming a mathematician. None of those methods are used in modern software and what is used is so easy to access as a package and so fine tuned I consider it more important to know how to choose and use one than to know how it works. The primary lessons are the following.

 When to use an integral
Use an integral whenever you want to measure an overall quantity. Words like “area” and “volume” are good clues. Don’t be shy about it. It doesn’t have to be a math sounding problem. Think of “Sales Volume”. The thing that you want to measure should have a boundary that is easy to describe, the e.g. we know the current daily sales numbers and how many days we have been selling. Then an estimate for the sales is the current daily sales times the number of days. An even better estimate is to use the average daily sales. The actual integral is to add up all the sales of each day. That is an integral. It is also perfectly obvious to a business person and doesn’t seem like you need calculus. But this is only the first step. This is the step to get you aware there is an integral at work in an ordinary project. Over the course of this unit we will start to fill in what knowledge of an integral can do for problem solving and reasoning logically. Here are some questions we might ask and can answer with the calculus.

If I know the average daily sales and I multiply it by the number of days selling is that the same or close to the sum of all the sales?
What if some days I loose product (unsold, spoiled, etc). Can I simply call this “negative area”?
What do I need to predict future sales volume?



 Reading an integral properly
Remember the integral sign is a fancy “S” ∫and usually it is given by a command like “int” or “Integral”. Integrals are then given subscripts or superscripts based on the boundary. The boundary can be some crazy shape called a “domain” DD and we would write
(_D)
If the domain is a straight line segment we just write the end points a and b, so (_a^b). Next we write what we want to sum, and this is an area formula. Let me say this carefully, it is an area formula not a specific area. The formula must adjust to make finer and finer approximations, usually by making smaller and smaller rectangles of height (f(x)) times a width dxdx. But every now and then you need something other than rectangles so you might find a formula like (f(r)dr) where (r) is a radius or (f(x)d) where () is a much more general measure. These are not things you will need to fiddle with you will simply need to be able to read and understand what people are doing and what you are asking a computer to do. All together the integral formulas will look like this.
(_a^b f(x) dx) or (_D f(r) dr) or (_D f(x) d)

* The value of a stock shifts so erratically that we need to simplify the data. See is averaged over time. Plot its highs and lows. These are features. And extracting features is the name of the game in data. And calculus owns that market. So when you see our icon * of an erratic data set. You will think about taming that wave through features.

 Main Object: Features
Given a set (), a feature is a function (f:). If we have two features we might plot them as a pair ((x(),y())) as a point the xy-plane; one point for each datum (). [We saw features several times in this course, most recently in our Handwritten Digit’s lab.]. If we have 3 features we can make a list of 3, a point in 3-dimensional space, and so on. In a future course on Linear Algebra you can explore the significance of multiple features. In this module we will explore just one.

Define and recognize features and linear features.
Model integrals as linear features.
Apply the Mean Value Theorem.
Apply the knowledge that all linear features are integrals for some measure (Riesz Representation Theorem.)

Part 1 All Features are Integrals (Riesz Representation Theorem)
Given a set (), a feature is a function (f:), i.e.: a decimal number or (). Now that can be almost anything which seems unlikely to yield any great insights. Yet, if we play around with some examples we might discover that choosing decimal numbers as the outcome puts some powerful tools within our reach.

 Integrals as Features
Suppose () is a data set which is also set of measurable events (E). If we have a signed measure () on () then we immediately have a feature on (), that is,



LaTeX: :


Now there are some great places to start. You might think of the distance measure (x=x_1-x_0) or maybe one the probability measures we encountered (uniform or Gaussian). [Recall the meaning of measurement form here]. But 2 or 3 features is often not enough and some of those measures might be wholly unrelated to the meaning of the data. So we want more options.

 Creating new features from integrals
Suppose we take a function (f:) that we can integrate (e.g. a continuous functions). Then we can define a new measure



LaTeX: (E) := _{E} f, d


This new measure, that is,



LaTeX: :


So we also get a new feature! And all we needed was to put some function inside our integral. (Notice the pun, the greek letter for n is “nu” pronounced “new” and it’s the letter of our new measure). Don’t act too surprised. Let’s slow down and look at an example.


 The weighted average and Expectation
Suppose our data is a list of decimal numbers (a_1,, a_n). We can take the average, which will put a number to the data, i.e. the average is a feature.



LaTeX:

In computation, information can often be minimized to a number. You might want to argue we should consider lists of numbers too, but as we are looking into the building blocks, the smallest we should go is extracting a single number as our information. The industry has given this asset the name “feature”.

 Definition of Features
A feature on a set  of data is a function  (or in computational syntax def feature( x : Data ) : Float), which assigns a decimal number or an infinity to every point.
In practice and computation we may need to get by with an approximation known as a partial feature which is a function that attempts to assign such a value but may on some inputs be undefined, i.e. , equivalently def feature( x : Data ) : Float?. (Recall  is away to assign an output of nothing to a failed evaluation.)


 Integrals as Features
Perhaps the most common feature in a collection of numbers is that average. However context is important to understand what “average” we intend. We can see the impact by looking 40 years of oil prices.

If the list is not finite we can take an integral as a number instead. *Week 12 Measurement Overview
“Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so.” -Galileo Galilei

 What is a measure?
Rulers work because what we measure is distributed amongst parts. You can measure a long segment, then move the ruler and measure a remaining short part. Add the two quantities and that is the measure. The whole is the sum of its parts. The same intuition applies to things like area and volume of course. But far more important in today’s sciences is the ability to measure this way with things like probability, distributed computing, population studies, and other data. All we need a better concept than a ruler. But a ruler is the perfect icon for the idea of measurement. So whenever you see a ruler * let it be a reminder to think of this rule:
Measurement distributes when the whole is the sum of its parts.
The #Calculus Summary


 Key Definitions**

Measure () Assigning number ((A)) to various subsets (A) such that ((A_1A_2)=(A_1)+(A_2)+), that is, the whole is the sum of its parts.
Difference (x) The number of steps to get from (x_0) to (x_1) in that that direction. Negative differences mean (x_1) comes before (x_0). Commonly (x=x_1-x_0)
Distance / Metric (d(x_0,x_1)) The number of steps between (x_0) and (x_1) in any direction. Always a non-negative value, often the absolute value of a difference such as (d(x,y)=|x_1-x_0|=|x_0-x_1|).
Potential (M) A measurement of an object (M) distributed amongst the measurements of its boundary (M). For example in a rectangle (M) (M= yx=(y_1-y_0)(x_1-x_0))
Area / Volume The absolute value of a potentials.



 Objectives

Recognize situations with distributed data and assign it measurements.
Define and calculate instantaneous rates of change and potential.
Develop the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

text:
*12.1.a
** Measurements
 In a ruler the whole is the sum of its parts… or is it? Sometimes illusions deserve attention.

 *An illusion with a Lesson
There is an illusion so convincing it has earned its own Wikipedia article. It takes a triangle, cuts it into polygons, and rearranges them. Yet once re-arranged, the parts no longer cover the original area! These diagrams of curtesy of Original: CC-BY Krauss. 



The missing area puzzle.


Does the surprise you? While this is an illusion (explained below) the reason it works as a brain teaser is that we are conditioned to understand area does not get lost amongst the parts. Our mind hunts for an explanation. This should not be possible, we believe.


 Explanation of the puzzle
The main clue to offer to the illusion is to point out that the first triangle is not actually a triangle, but a pentagon. So the lower triangle has slightly different angles than the upper one. So put together they do not make one large triangle but a polygon. You can detect this better if we exaggerate the difference in angle.



Missing square puzzle


So what appears as a hypotenuse of a large triangle is in fact dented, and thus looses a small amount of area which our eyes fail to detect. When we rearrange the parts we do not see the an area disappear. In fact the opposite. By rearranging the parts we gather the missing area form the dent into one place where its far more noticeable. Area, as we think of it, truly is the sum of its parts.


 *Integral measurements: The details and Examples
So as seen in the video the world around us has dozens of natural way to glue data together. Whether that be a sum like (x+y) or a disjoint union (XY), addition of resistance, pressure, sales prices and so much more. These quite often behave in just the way the need for the whole to be the sum of its parts. And it introduces an opportunity to use common stories of length and area as metaphors for the often complicated seeming calculations we find ourselves doing. So for the next three parts we explore this technology. We begin by formally declare what is a measurement.
Recall that subsets (E) are a membership test (: ), denoted (xE), which decide if when elements are in the subset. The nuance of which logical context we are in changes what counts as a decision, e.g. classical we have 2 options true of false and so we often write (2) instead of () but in a computer Prop will be the data and in practice Prop may have some intermediates cases like missing evidence or contradictory evidence for membership. The type of all subsets of () is denoted (^{}).


 Measures & Measurable sets
Let () be a set of data. A (positive)measure on () is function defined on various subsets called “measurable subsets” with the quality

Whole is the sum of its parts. Given a possibly unending list of measurable subsets (X_1,X_2,) then the union is measurable. In fact, if they are pairwise disjoint (no two have a point in common) then their measure is precisely




LaTeX: (X_1 X_2) = (X_1) + (X_2)+



The measuring of nothing is 0. The empty subset ({}=) should be measurable with measure (()=0).
Complements are measurable. If a subset (X) is measurable then so is its complement (-X={X}).

If we want to think of () in function terms then

The domain is the power set  (or simply  in classical mathematics).
The codomain is .

We may write  or in software something akin to def measure( as : Collection[A] ) : Float? the precise collection may be something like List, Array, Set, Tree, HashTable etc. and the name of the function will typically depicts its role, e.g. length, weight, word_count, etc.


 *Example Measurements


 Example 1**: Lebesgue’s Interval Distance measurement .
The most common measurement by far is to consider a line interval  from a point  to a point . This actually has many flavors including:
![LaTeX: \begin{aligned} (x_0,x_1) & = { xx_0xx_1} & (x_0,x_1] & = { xx_0xx_1}\ x_0,x_1) & = { xx_0xx_1} & [x_0,x_1] & = { xx_0xx_1} \end{aligned}
Whether you include the final point at the end of an interval doesn’t mean much to the length of the interval, after all a point has negligible thickness in most context. So to each of these intervals we assign a single measurement which is so important that instead of () it gets its own special name (m) and is called the Lebesgue measure.
Each of the above intervals we assign “Lebesgue Measure”: 
[Strictly speaking by convention intervals should have (x_0x_1) so that the difference is never negative and the absolute value is unnecessary, but because we want to emphasize the measure is positive we have added it for extra clarity.]
Now this is not yet a measure until we allow for multiple disjoint intervals 
General Unsigned Distance “Lebesgue Measure”: 
So to measure the shaded regions below we first measure the disjoint parts, , , and add them together to get .



Number line with blue shading between -3 and -1.5 and red shading between 1 and 2.



As a weird quirk in history, the sets that can be measured as intervals are called “Borel sets” and they are “Lebesgue measurable”. Both these mathematicians made great contributions to the details of measurement. But if we are honest, this measurement was known to stone masons and carpenters and perhaps even some species of dogs long before their involvement. So while the honor is appropriate don’t let the names let you think it is complicated idea.


 Example 2**: Lebesgue’s Area Measure 
The concept of distance generalizes to area, and then volumes. Obviously the measure of a rectangle is width times height.



2-D measure of a rectangle and an oval.


If we expect a measure then the total shaded area is the sum of the disjoint shaded areas, i.e. our square (I_1) in blue on the left and our ellipse (I_2) on the right. We will call this the Lebesque measure as well, only now in 2-D. So what is this measure? The shaded rectangle is partitioned into 9 blue sub-squares. So the whole being the sum of its parts, we should declare that measure to be 9.
.
This is part of general strategy we can combine two measures () and () as a product.



LaTeX: ()( IJ) = (I)(J)


Now the ellipse posses a problem. So far we have only considered rectangles as having area. But this is not a rectangle. Yet we do get some clear clues about the way to make an approximation of the area. We can count rectangles that approximate the ellipse. That number here is at least 4 and at most 8. We could get a better estimate by looking at a finer grid and eventually looking for a limit.

Warning: When don’t we have a measure? Suppose instead of area we looked at the picture above and asked to measure “how tall is the shaded region?”

Option 1. Suppose we understand this sentence as asking how many boxes high is enough to fit both pictures, and we can count the blue box as 3 high and the ellipse as 2. So 3 is enough. If we did this we would be answering the question correctly but also demonstrating we do not have a measure. That is the whole has measure 3, and the parts have measures 3 and 2 but (3+2). If we really wanted to include this as a measure then we would need to revisit the idea that the two shapes are disjoint. While they are disjoint in the xy-plane they are not disjoint in the y direction alone. And so in that sense this is not a violation of measurement rules, just a misunderstanding about the meaning of disjoint for this case. An “illusion” as we have been warned about already.
Option 2. An alternative reading of this question is to ask if we stack up the shapes how tall would they be? Here we would in fact add 3 to 2 to get 5. This would be a measure as the whole would be the sum of the parts.

It is crucially important to be precise in our language of measurement. Many times a miscommunication or imprecise phrasing can lead to errors in measurement.


 Example 3:** Counting Measure 
Given (E), the number of integers in (E) is the counting measure. As formula:
[ (E) := |E| ]
Notice this often does take different values on intervals
\[
\begin{aligned}
\zeta\Big((0,1)\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n<1\}| = |\varnothing| = 0 \\
\zeta\Big([0,1)\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n<1\}| = |\{0\}| = 1 \\
\zeta\Big((0,1]\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n\leq 1\}| = |\{1\}| = 1 \\
\zeta\Big([0,1]\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n\leq 1\}| = |\{0,1\}| = 2
\end{aligned}
\]
Some common places to encounter a counting measure like this include:

Counting the number of steps in a loop, e.g. for i in [a...b] Use .
Counting the number of steps in a loop, e.g. for i in [a...b] step 2 Use .
You need to count steps of two nested loops, use .



 Example 4:** Kolmogorov’s Probability Measures , a coin flip example
Suppose you have a coin with Heads H and tails T. The simplest thing to measure is the probability of the two individual outcomes. Here space (={H,T}) and the measure is the uniform measure: . That is:



LaTeX:


Now the more interesting probability is to continue coin flips and see what patterns emerge.


 First flip is heads
.The first flip is heads: ({EE_1=H}). This covers half the options and its measure is 1/2.



Probability tree of coin flips with the branches that start with heads highlighted.




 First flip is tails, second heads
The first flip is tails and second flip is heads: ({EE_1=T, E_2=H}). This covers 1/4 of the options and its measure is 1/4.



Probability tree of coin flips with the branches that start with tails and then heads highlighted.




 Every even flip is tails
Every even flip is tails: (C={EE_{2n}=T}).



Probability of coin flips with branches highlighted if every even flip is tails.


As flips continue the ones that survive are spread out and do not form a customary length. So the right measure here has to come from our understanding of probability laws instead. We can talk of this measure by considering the limit of the proportion, which decreases by 2 every time we reach an even flip (because only half of those are T). In fact, while somewhat boring to do by hand, a computer can just move the symbols around according to the formal rules to get the same answer.
.


 Disjoint events
Disjoint events in probability add their probabilities. This the same rule as measures. The following illustration with coin flips demonstrates this.



Coin flips with two independent events. The blue start with heads, the red begin tails-heads.


We can turn this measurement over to computers.

(A={EE_1=H}) is the set of coin flips where the first flip lands H.
(B={EE_1=T E_{2}=H}) is the set of coin flips where the first flip is T and the second flip lands H.

Notice (AB={}) (because the first flip cannot be both heads and tails). So these two are disjoint.



LaTeX:




 Overlapping events
Non-disjoint sets measures are not directly defined. But probabilities are not just any measure, and these have a solution directly.



Overlapping events cannot be measured as their sum because they are not disjoint.


This would be a good place to pause and notice the essential role of disjoint unions. Suppose we used (C={EE_2=T}) instead of (B). Now
(AC ={EE_1=H, E_2=T})
So now (A) and (C) are not disjoint, and this affects our probability measure



LaTeX:


So be careful to check on the disjoint condition when using measures and if measures alone are not enough information, look at your context to see something else will help.


 Example 5**: Gaussian’s Probability Measure 
Recall the second distribution for probability was useful when data had a target value but would wobble off target with some predictable variation. This was known as Gaussian distribution. See more here Probability unit. The Gaussian Measure applies to decimal numbers (x) and measures them on the “Bell curve” by the following formula.



LaTeX: (X) = e{-()2}


where () is the average value “center of the bell curve” (not a measure!) and () is the standard deviation (how wide the bell is). Below we plot the curve for a bell with deviation () and mean ().



A bell curve centered at mean 0 with deviation 1.


For most people it is not important that you memorize this formula, but notice it is qualitatively different from both the distance and uniform measures.


 *Calculations & Implications
Suppose that () is a positive measure. Then all of the following are true.

Bigger subsets get bigger measures: If  and both are measurable then .
If you steadily approximate a measure from below you will reach the measure. If  are all measurable then .

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
*Week 12 Measurement Overview
“Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so.” -Galileo Galilei

 What is a measure?
Rulers work because what we measure is distributed amongst parts. You can measure a long segment, then move the ruler and measure a remaining short part. Add the two quantities and that is the measure. The whole is the sum of its parts. The same intuition applies to things like area and volume of course. But far more important in today’s sciences is the ability to measure this way with things like probability, distributed computing, population studies, and other data. All we need a better concept than a ruler. But a ruler is the perfect icon for the idea of measurement. So whenever you see a ruler * let it be a reminder to think of this rule:
Measurement distributes when the whole is the sum of its parts.
The #Calculus Summary


 Key Definitions**

Measure () Assigning number ((A)) to various subsets (A) such that ((A_1A_2)=(A_1)+(A_2)+), that is, the whole is the sum of its parts.
Difference (x) The number of steps to get from (x_0) to (x_1) in that that direction. Negative differences mean (x_1) comes before (x_0). Commonly (x=x_1-x_0)
Distance / Metric (d(x_0,x_1)) The number of steps between (x_0) and (x_1) in any direction. Always a non-negative value, often the absolute value of a difference such as (d(x,y)=|x_1-x_0|=|x_0-x_1|).
Potential (M) A measurement of an object (M) distributed amongst the measurements of its boundary (M). For example in a rectangle (M) (M= yx=(y_1-y_0)(x_1-x_0))
Area / Volume The absolute value of a potentials.



 Objectives

Recognize situations with distributed data and assign it measurements.
Define and calculate instantaneous rates of change and potential.
Develop the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

* 12.2.b Changing Measure: The Derivative
 Changing and comparing measurements are the ways we draw explanations. For example we might ask how to time on the one hand and distance on the other. To connect them we need speed: distance per time. We could have weight and volume, which we transform using density. If we put this to an equation we have a measure () that needs to be converted to () and the transformation will be a new function () which we call “the derivative”.

 Derivatives
If  is a measurable and  is measurable then
 is a new measure.
This is what we use for example when we wait our averages or make a probability conditional and many other familiar measurements. In fact the converse is also true.


 Radon-Nikodym Theorem
Given two measures  and , if each time  then also ; then there exists a unique measurable function (f) such that for every measurable set (E)

When each time  then also , we say that “ is absolutely continuous with respect to  and write this as .
The unique function (f) is called the (Radon-Nikodym) derivative of  with respect to  and denote it

Collectively:  implies that . In high-school textbooks this is known as the “Fundamental Theorem of Calculus”.



 Absolute continuity for Distance and Time measures.
Let us consider two measure: position (x) and time (. In a mechanical system whenever time stands still we cannot change position. So measuring time as 0 means position is also zero; so:
Distance () Time
Now if reverse the consideration, it is entirely possible that we stay in one place for a while. So zero distance measure does not force zero time measure. So in general time is not absolutely continuous with respect to distance.


 Absolute Continuity against the interval measure.
Suppose want to compare a measurement () of intervals of the real number line against the interval measure (m([a,b])=b-a). Under these conditions we can squeeze intervals (a<x_1<c<x_2<b) and shrink the interval (X=(x_1,x_2)) around the point (c). Since (m([c,c])=c-c=0) has measure 0, this process has a clear consequence:



LaTeX: m( {x<c<y} (x,y) )={xy} (y-x)=0


So the measurements (m) will have to have their values on these shrinking intervals shrink as well
.
So as in important special case, suppose (f:[a,b]) with the following property for all (acb)
(_{xc} f(x)=f(c)). We say (f) is continuous on ([a,b]).
Then setting (([a,x]) := _{a}^x f(t) dt) we get this property. The condition of continuous on a closed interval has been likened by many to drawing the graph of (f) without lifting your pencil. That is, when you are headed towards a point, you reach it.
This gives you access to a powerful intuition for creating absolutely continuous measures for the interval measure: the are integrals of graphs drawn without lifting the pencil.”


 Integrals and Derivatives with the Interval measure m([a,b])=b-a
Let’s take a close look at the derivative of the interval measure as this is the most historic and geometrically motivated of all the derivative measurements.


 * Newton-Leibniz’s Interval measurement Theorem.

Now let’s change measures just to demonstrate that this claim is very much about the condition of the interval measure. We need only create a model (example) where the claim fails, so this is a  situation. Let us use the function (f(x)=x) and choose (a=0<x_1=1<x_2<2).

*Always make sure you are using an interval measure when applying the Newton-Leibniz Theorem.


 Interval Derivatives as “slopes of tangent lines”


 For interval measures the derivative is the slope of the tangent line to accumulation curve.
Suppose that () is a measure which is absolutely continuous on  with respect the Lebesgue interval measure . Define  by . Then the slope of the tangent line to (F) is defined as

Furthermore, this is equal to the Radon-Nikodym derivative, that is,

Other accepted notation is ,  and . And while we have called (m) the “interval measure” its proper name is the Lebesgue measure. Consult your context and audience for the notation that fits best. And while we use


 Proof Interval Measure  The derivative is the “instant” rate of change.
Because of the internal measure we have the Newton-Leibniz theorem and we start from there and multiply both sides by (1/x).

Now we add the limit to this formula which means to assume margin for error . Shrink the interval ([x_1,x_2]) until the area  is within the margin of error of the actual measure . The following diagram illustrates how this can occur, just shrink to one box.



Curve with rectangle boxes approximating the area under the curve.


So we can replace the integral



LaTeX:




 Example 1: The Interval Derivative of position is velocity.
In a high-school physics class you likely measured position (x(t)) at a time (t) starting from time 0. So the distance accumulates over the interval (E=[0,t)). The problem is that we can travel at different velocities (positive or negative speeds). The times we travel faster we go further.



Slope of a line segment as the ratio of rise over run


So to approximate total distance over the time interval (E) will can get a good approximation by adding up small units in time to capture moments we travel a fixed velocities. That is we have an integral. An integral of what? Well by the definition of the derivative it is an integral of the derivative of position.
.
Now the velocity is the physical concept we need to compute this same individual summands. So the derivative must be equal to the velocity.. The purpose of (dt) is to divide up the measurements in small enough intervals that we can get measurement precise enough to measure within the margin of error.


 Example 2: Interval Derivative of weight is density.
Now an example from a physical measurement: the weight (w) of an object. We can divide the weight up amongst the volume using the customary Lebesgue measure (m). For example we can take a core sample of mud at the bottom of a lake and calculate its weight as an integral (or a numerical approximation of the integral). The core sample a cylinder C with a known radius and height.



LaTeX: w(C) = _C , dm


Now if we measure the weight at different heights of the cylinder then we get varied weights. The weight changes based on the density of the mud. A more dense mud will weigh more. So a suitable interpretation for the derivative of weight per volume is density.


 What is a tangent line?
Sometimes we over-learn the lesson of tangents to a circle. After all the exposure tho the word tangent in mathematics is usually made along side sine, cosine and the unit circle so the confusion is understandable. But if we look to the word “tangent” in the conversional meaning we are describing a topic that begin as related but in retrospect may have diverged. So the key is that at some point the two topic did appear the same. In this same way a tangent to a curve is a line that for some period approximates the shape of the graph.

Tangents may not exist.
Tangent lines, if they exist, are unique.
Tangents may touch the graph in many places and may even approximate the graph in more than one place.



 The Derivative as Change of Measure
Now the Newton-Leibniz theorem and its geometric conceptualization of the derivative as rate of change has been enormously valuable but there are roles for derivatives where “rate of change” is less compelling as an explanation. Take for instance measurements of chaotic data like earth quakes, stock markets, or network traffic. Below we picture the seismology of the Cabo de Gata earthquake 2025. We see the behavior is quite erratic with sharp changes in direction that make it impossible to place a straight line as local approximation. That is this curve has few discernible tangents.



Seismograph of Terremoto Cabo de Gata 2025, Almju, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons


The absence of discernible tangents here does not mean we should not attempt to use this as a measure compared to another. It simply means we should not compare it to an interval measure. In fact one the most important measures to compare with is the simple concentration measure (_c). The graph above indicates the first noticeable motion in the graph as the P-wave – the primary wave indicating the start of the tremor. The next measure S-wave is secondary /shear wave. The distance in time between these markers can be used to predict the distance from sensor to the origin of wave. Another common integral is an interval measure but shifted to the domain of frequencies through a process known as Fourier transforms. So in short the interval measure and its associated Riemann integral and slope of tangents interpretation is not directly useful for these data but other integrals and derivatives are essential.
Try to think of derivatives as formulas to change measures and not simply as slopes. While the slope perspective is important in many historical applications it is not in the end the only interpretation and many modern data centered goals are better understood as comparing measures, not tangents of graphs.

 A bit of history
Historically derivatives were defined as the slope of tangents to a curve or instantaneous rates of change. These concepts are not immediately logical—how do you define a unique tangent to a graph without already having the slope, i.e. it makes for a circular definition. An instant in time is also not a precise concept. But its ability to solve questions made Newton (1660’s) a hero of science. Between the 1800-1900’s Cauchy, Weirestrass, and Riemann each contributed ideas to make the concept precise. Still issued persisted not least of which was the difficulty in stacking integrals measurements. While geometry suggested we can remeasure as many times as we like, the formulas of the Cauchy-Riemann method had gaps and oddities that did not match the graphical intuition.
To solve these problem Lebesgue’s integral (1900) threw the subject on its head. Instead of beginning with the concept of smaller and smaller approximations, Lebesgue classified what a measurement under the basic concept that: the whole is the sum of its parts. Once created integrals stand out as accumulation of measurements under any grouping into parts – be those small approximations or large chunks. The concept now being sound later authors such as Radon-Nikodym (1915) explored how to convert the calculus of the previous generation into this formalism.
Thes are admittedly the most recent to the list but they are extraordinarily more diverse making the concept of measurement match so many more applications that it quickly clarified the field. Here derivatives are ways to change measure, and have no need to be grounded in concepts of slopes of tangents. Its explosive use in modern probability, finance, machine learning, and data science make it the right match for the computationally minded amongst us. Even so, if your primary aims are engineering, mechanics, or classical physics then the narrower picture created by Newton and Leibniz will be enough. Just be mindful not to draw upon the wrong formulas as the answers can be quit different.



 Mean Value Theorem for Interval measurements
A common re-telling the Newton-Leibniz theorem is to multiply both sides by (1/x=1/(x_2-x_1) because this has a description in terms of concepts like speed and rates of change and averages. In this form it is known as the “Mean Value Theorem” (mean is a synonym to “average”).


 Mean Value Theorem
For a measurable function  let  then for (a=0<x_1=1<x_2<2)



LaTeX:


Said another way, there is a point (x_1cx_2) such that
.

 Interpreting the Mean Value Theorem in Applications
You enter the highway at 8:00 am and drive for 1 hour and exit 70 miles away. Your average speed is therefore 70 miles per hour. If the speed limit is 65 miles per hour then the traffic toll system has enough evidence to charge you with speeding. This despite having not seen you actually speed at any instant in time. Why? Well the average rate of change was 70 mph and by the Mean Value Theorem there must be some point (c) where your speed (x’(t)) (the derivative of your position (x(t)) at time (t)).
This is an example of a theoretical claim. The problem with enforcing this is that perhaps your state laws require evidence in the form of a specific photograph of an instance of speeding. That is, a computational logic might be required to enforce the law. On the other hand even that could be called into question with many practical logical concerns, such as the accuracy of the data collected. Always remember to return to the simpler lessons of logic before drawing conclusion as to the validity of some purely theoretical claim.

*12.1.a
** Measurements
 In a ruler the whole is the sum of its parts… or is it? Sometimes illusions deserve attention.

 *An illusion with a Lesson
There is an illusion so convincing it has earned its own Wikipedia article. It takes a triangle, cuts it into polygons, and rearranges them. Yet once re-arranged, the parts no longer cover the original area! These diagrams of curtesy of Original: CC-BY Krauss. 



The missing area puzzle.


Does the surprise you? While this is an illusion (explained below) the reason it works as a brain teaser is that we are conditioned to understand area does not get lost amongst the parts. Our mind hunts for an explanation. This should not be possible, we believe.


 Explanation of the puzzle
The main clue to offer to the illusion is to point out that the first triangle is not actually a triangle, but a pentagon. So the lower triangle has slightly different angles than the upper one. So put together they do not make one large triangle but a polygon. You can detect this better if we exaggerate the difference in angle.



Missing square puzzle


So what appears as a hypotenuse of a large triangle is in fact dented, and thus looses a small amount of area which our eyes fail to detect. When we rearrange the parts we do not see the an area disappear. In fact the opposite. By rearranging the parts we gather the missing area form the dent into one place where its far more noticeable. Area, as we think of it, truly is the sum of its parts.


 *Integral measurements: The details and Examples
So as seen in the video the world around us has dozens of natural way to glue data together. Whether that be a sum like (x+y) or a disjoint union (XY), addition of resistance, pressure, sales prices and so much more. These quite often behave in just the way the need for the whole to be the sum of its parts. And it introduces an opportunity to use common stories of length and area as metaphors for the often complicated seeming calculations we find ourselves doing. So for the next three parts we explore this technology. We begin by formally declare what is a measurement.
Recall that subsets (E) are a membership test (: ), denoted (xE), which decide if when elements are in the subset. The nuance of which logical context we are in changes what counts as a decision, e.g. classical we have 2 options true of false and so we often write (2) instead of () but in a computer Prop will be the data and in practice Prop may have some intermediates cases like missing evidence or contradictory evidence for membership. The type of all subsets of () is denoted (^{}).


 Measures & Measurable sets
Let () be a set of data. A (positive)measure on () is function defined on various subsets called “measurable subsets” with the quality

Whole is the sum of its parts. Given a possibly unending list of measurable subsets (X_1,X_2,) then the union is measurable. In fact, if they are pairwise disjoint (no two have a point in common) then their measure is precisely




LaTeX: (X_1 X_2) = (X_1) + (X_2)+



The measuring of nothing is 0. The empty subset ({}=) should be measurable with measure (()=0).
Complements are measurable. If a subset (X) is measurable then so is its complement (-X={X}).

If we want to think of () in function terms then

The domain is the power set  (or simply  in classical mathematics).
The codomain is .

We may write  or in software something akin to def measure( as : Collection[A] ) : Float? the precise collection may be something like List, Array, Set, Tree, HashTable etc. and the name of the function will typically depicts its role, e.g. length, weight, word_count, etc.


 *Example Measurements


 Example 1**: Lebesgue’s Interval Distance measurement .
The most common measurement by far is to consider a line interval  from a point  to a point . This actually has many flavors including:
![LaTeX: \begin{aligned} (x_0,x_1) & = { xx_0xx_1} & (x_0,x_1] & = { xx_0xx_1}\ x_0,x_1) & = { xx_0xx_1} & [x_0,x_1] & = { xx_0xx_1} \end{aligned}
Whether you include the final point at the end of an interval doesn’t mean much to the length of the interval, after all a point has negligible thickness in most context. So to each of these intervals we assign a single measurement which is so important that instead of () it gets its own special name (m) and is called the Lebesgue measure.
Each of the above intervals we assign “Lebesgue Measure”: 
[Strictly speaking by convention intervals should have (x_0x_1) so that the difference is never negative and the absolute value is unnecessary, but because we want to emphasize the measure is positive we have added it for extra clarity.]
Now this is not yet a measure until we allow for multiple disjoint intervals 
General Unsigned Distance “Lebesgue Measure”: 
So to measure the shaded regions below we first measure the disjoint parts, , , and add them together to get .



Number line with blue shading between -3 and -1.5 and red shading between 1 and 2.



As a weird quirk in history, the sets that can be measured as intervals are called “Borel sets” and they are “Lebesgue measurable”. Both these mathematicians made great contributions to the details of measurement. But if we are honest, this measurement was known to stone masons and carpenters and perhaps even some species of dogs long before their involvement. So while the honor is appropriate don’t let the names let you think it is complicated idea.


 Example 2**: Lebesgue’s Area Measure 
The concept of distance generalizes to area, and then volumes. Obviously the measure of a rectangle is width times height.



2-D measure of a rectangle and an oval.


If we expect a measure then the total shaded area is the sum of the disjoint shaded areas, i.e. our square (I_1) in blue on the left and our ellipse (I_2) on the right. We will call this the Lebesque measure as well, only now in 2-D. So what is this measure? The shaded rectangle is partitioned into 9 blue sub-squares. So the whole being the sum of its parts, we should declare that measure to be 9.
.
This is part of general strategy we can combine two measures () and () as a product.



LaTeX: ()( IJ) = (I)(J)


Now the ellipse posses a problem. So far we have only considered rectangles as having area. But this is not a rectangle. Yet we do get some clear clues about the way to make an approximation of the area. We can count rectangles that approximate the ellipse. That number here is at least 4 and at most 8. We could get a better estimate by looking at a finer grid and eventually looking for a limit.

Warning: When don’t we have a measure? Suppose instead of area we looked at the picture above and asked to measure “how tall is the shaded region?”

Option 1. Suppose we understand this sentence as asking how many boxes high is enough to fit both pictures, and we can count the blue box as 3 high and the ellipse as 2. So 3 is enough. If we did this we would be answering the question correctly but also demonstrating we do not have a measure. That is the whole has measure 3, and the parts have measures 3 and 2 but (3+2). If we really wanted to include this as a measure then we would need to revisit the idea that the two shapes are disjoint. While they are disjoint in the xy-plane they are not disjoint in the y direction alone. And so in that sense this is not a violation of measurement rules, just a misunderstanding about the meaning of disjoint for this case. An “illusion” as we have been warned about already.
Option 2. An alternative reading of this question is to ask if we stack up the shapes how tall would they be? Here we would in fact add 3 to 2 to get 5. This would be a measure as the whole would be the sum of the parts.

It is crucially important to be precise in our language of measurement. Many times a miscommunication or imprecise phrasing can lead to errors in measurement.


 Example 3:** Counting Measure 
Given (E), the number of integers in (E) is the counting measure. As formula:
[ (E) := |E| ]
Notice this often does take different values on intervals
\[
\begin{aligned}
\zeta\Big((0,1)\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n<1\}| = |\varnothing| = 0 \\
\zeta\Big([0,1)\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n<1\}| = |\{0\}| = 1 \\
\zeta\Big((0,1]\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n\leq 1\}| = |\{1\}| = 1 \\
\zeta\Big([0,1]\Big) &= |\{n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n\leq 1\}| = |\{0,1\}| = 2
\end{aligned}
\]

Counting the number of steps in a loop, e.g. for i in [a...b] Use .

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
*Week 12 Measurement Overview
“Measure what is measurable, and make measurable what is not so.” -Galileo Galilei

 What is a measure?
Rulers work because what we measure is distributed amongst parts. You can measure a long segment, then move the ruler and measure a remaining short part. Add the two quantities and that is the measure. The whole is the sum of its parts. The same intuition applies to things like area and volume of course. But far more important in today’s sciences is the ability to measure this way with things like probability, distributed computing, population studies, and other data. All we need a better concept than a ruler. But a ruler is the perfect icon for the idea of measurement. So whenever you see a ruler * let it be a reminder to think of this rule:
Measurement distributes when the whole is the sum of its parts.
The #Calculus Summary


 Key Definitions**

Measure () Assigning number ((A)) to various subsets (A) such that ((A_1A_2)=(A_1)+(A_2)+), that is, the whole is the sum of its parts.
Difference (x) The number of steps to get from (x_0) to (x_1) in that that direction. Negative differences mean (x_1) comes before (x_0). Commonly (x=x_1-x_0)
Distance / Metric (d(x_0,x_1)) The number of steps between (x_0) and (x_1) in any direction. Always a non-negative value, often the absolute value of a difference such as (d(x,y)=|x_1-x_0|=|x_0-x_1|).
Potential (M) A measurement of an object (M) distributed amongst the measurements of its boundary (M). For example in a rectangle (M) (M= yx=(y_1-y_0)(x_1-x_0))
Area / Volume The absolute value of a potentials.



 Objectives

Recognize situations with distributed data and assign it measurements.
Define and calculate instantaneous rates of change and potential.
Develop the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
