title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Week 9 Overview (5 mins) Overview
The last of the inductive logics we will pursue are gathered under two general names:

Abductive Reasoning: deciding what is plausible.
Probabilistic Reasoning: assigning a measurement to outcomes.


 Abductive Reasoning
Abductive reasoning is most commonly practiced in investigations, for example, it is plausible given the evidence that so-and-so happened. This can be applied everywhere from in law practices, to medicine, and to scientific experiments. Stated logically, it is the process of guessing the missing context that would validate the claims. That is, given evidence (E), some established theory (T), make some hypothetical assumptions (H) such that



LaTeX: T, H E


Notice in contrast when we had deductive reasoning we had all the elements to the left of the turnstile () and wanted to conclude the values on the right. So if deduction is like calculating, e.g. (2+3=?), then abduction. is a way solving for an unknown, e.g. (2+x=5), what is (x)?

 What’s with the name?
Abduct is a word most of us hear in negative stations, someone is taken away against their will, or a person of authority leaves their post unattended. The philosophy Charles Peirce coined the term for logical purposes possibly influenced by how it sounds in comparison to induction and deduction and because it meaning “to lead away” could be understood as how learning what is plausible is often a fight not to be mislead. It is a settled term today in any case.
As a general remark, some logicians treat abduction as separate from induction form a third in the list of deduction, induction, abduction. Our own definition of induction is to reason beyond the evidence and therefore include abduction. Whether we treat abduction as a subset of induction or as a separate style of reasoning is not too consequential. Just be aware that authors differ on this topic.



 Probabilistic Reasoning
Probability assigns a number to events as a way of (hopefully) quantifying why events happen the way the see them happen. If we flip a coin we expect a heads as often as a tail. We therefore do not find it unfair to choose which team begins a match with the ball based on a coin toss. But if instead choose the starting team by flipping a pencil to see if lands on the side or on the tip, suddenly we would think it unfair to one of the teams because in our experience it is astronomically unlikely that a pencil will ever land on anything but its side. Probability seeks to put a number to that experience so that we can easily explain why coin flip events are so different from pencil flip events.

 Is it rational?
Mathematicians are drawn mostly to the probabilistic side of reasoning because it puts numbers in our hands and with that a great many mathematical tools become available. Even so, when pressed to explain the justifications of putting numbers to events we are often forced to confront a form of abductive reasoning as justification. In our final unit we will preview two the dueling philosophies of probability (frequentist and Bayesian). The existences of an open debate is a sign of the youth of probability as a subject. Many of its main tools were invented in the past century and its logical footing is shifting as well. It is an exciting time to join the subject.



 Objectives

Recognize and describe differences between Abductive & Probabilistic Logic
Observe and discuss distribution, uniform distribution versus Gaussian Distribution
Compute with conditional probability.
Analyze Monte Carlo and Las Vegas Algorihtms

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Week 7
Day 1 Relations and Orders
We saw with deduction that one of the ways to build a new data type is to modify what we mean by “equals”. In programs we override equality. But you are likely familiar with other ways we relate data. For example, some numbers are large, others are small, that means (xy). Likewise some expressions in reasoning benefit from organization.

 General Relations
To turn data like 541 or a PDF into a value we can judge we need to create a relation. Here are some samples relations.

P(541) = “541 is positive”. Something we can judge, and we judge it is true.
P(541) = “541 is even.” Something we can also judge, but this time we judge it is false.
Q(MyCV.pdf) = “MyCV.pdf has page numbers.” Something we can judge. Is it true? We’d have to read the file to find out.


 Propositions
A Proposition is a sentence we can claim and judge. The outcome depends on our mode. Recall from Week 1 we have three forms of propositions

() for Theory is generally True () and False ()
() for Computation is generally True () and False () but must be supported by evidence so it may not come to an end if the evidence never comes.
() for Practice is generally True (), False () along with a host of gray are, perhaps Maybe, or Unknown, or Likely, Unlikely, etc. We will here simplify and just allow a single third value +.



 Relations
So what is a Relation? First choose the appropriate proposition category (Theory, Computation, or Practice). Then a Relation is a function form lists of types (X_1, X_2,, X_n) into (). That is
(P:X_1X_n)

P(x) = “x is positive”. This is not something we can judge yet, but as soon as we replace the variable by a value we will be able to judge it. In fact this sort of claim is simply true of false, Theory proposition applies.. So this is a function from data into propositions but it only makes sense when given decimal numbers (). It is a Relation (P:{,})
P(x,y) = “x +y =0”. This is a either true or false, so we can judge this once given decimal numbers of x and y so this is a relation (P:{,})
Q(x) = “x has page numbers”. Here x is a file, so File is our input type. However, the concept of “has page number” is clear for documents but it means nothing for images, videos and so many other documents. This suggests a practical proposition of Prop={true, false, undefined}. This is a relation (Q: -> {}). In common software syntax this might be def hasPageNumbers(x : File) : Option[Boolean]. The Option wrapper allows us to give back a value of True/False when it makes sense, or nothing when the input file is not a document.



 General Relation Vocabulary

Valence or Arity is the number of inputs to a relation. E.g. P(x), Q(x) are valence 1, also called unary. P(x,y) is binary, valence 2.
Homogeneous: a relation (R:X_1X_n) where for each (i,j), (X_i=X_j). In this case we often write (R:X^n).
Heterogenous: a relation that may not be homogeneous. In general a homogeneous relation is also heterogenous but not the other way around.

Mathematical Conventions
Mathematics tends to study relations (R:X_1X_n) more fully than other subjects and much of mathematics is in the Theory camp of reasoning. Because of this most of mathematics sees relations as just true and false. When this is the case then it is enough to know just the values which are true.
({(x_1,, x_n)X_1X_n R(x_1,, x_n) })
Because of this, much of mathematics will define relations not by a function but by a subset, that is, mathematics will often write
(RX_1X_n)
Even if this is bit short cited on the part of mathematicians not to consider the nuance of relations in computation and in practice, it is still a notation used broadly and you can introduce that notation meaning in fact (R:X_1X_n). Just add that clarity to your discussion in text.



 Binary Homogeneous Relations
Amongst the most used relations are binary homogeneous relations
(R:XX)
In this case we generally prefer an infix notation. Example, instead of (R(x,y)) we choose some symbol, maybe = or < or == etc. and write things like
(x=y), (x<y), x==y, x!=y, (xy)
Since we need to keep talking about many binary homogeneous relations we will continue to use R as a generic name
(xRy)

 Reflexive law
A binary homogeneous relation (R:X^2) is called reflexive if
(x.(xRx))

In number equality is reflexive (x=x), less than is not reflexive (5<5) is false, but less-than or equal is reflexive (xx)
In programming if one data type B extends another A it means every method for A is a method for B as well, though B may have further methods. Under this definition A has all the methods that A has so A extends A. However, in writing a program you may not be allowed to write A extends A as that leads the programming language to get confused with circular reasoning. This is a difference in definitions, so even experts can disagree on this one with good reason.
A daughter inherits traits from her father, but a daughter does not inherit traits from herself. So inheritence is not generally reflexive.

Reflexive Closure
In some situations it is convenient to assume a relation is reflexive even if it is not. Think of promoting (x<y) into (xy). This literally means
(xy := (x=x) (x<y))
We can do this to absolutely any binary homogeneous relation (R:X^2)
(xy := (x=x) (x<y))
The resulting relation (R^=) is called the reflexive closure. The notation we usually use is to add part of the equal sign to the original symbol. Here are some examples

(< )
()

In other situations we want to remove reflexivity. We can do this as well.
(xy := (xx) (xy))
The notation similarly strikes out the equal portion.


 Transitive Law
So what makes something an order? While humans make the rules, and thus can change them, by far the most popular definitions agree on one rule, the transitive law.
( (a < b )(b< c) (a< c))


 Symmetric and Anti-symmetric laws
Two further relations laws are commonly encountered.

Symmetric: (xRy yR x)
Anti-symmetric: (xRy yRx x=y)

As we have seen there is a notion of “closure” for each of these. We simply force a relation to be symmetric. However, the closure for anti-symmetric is more sublte because it is forced to change the notion of equality. So this creates what we early called a partition.



 Special Relations
Now mostly because of the popular use there are a bunch of combinations of these four rules that get names and you might be expected to know them in your future so we lets give them here.

 Equivalence relation
Definition. A homogeneous binary relation (R:X^2) is called an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, transitive, and symmetric.
Equivalence relations usually uses language like this
(x=y), (xy), (xy), x==y, x.equals(y), equals(x,y)
You may also here the words “congruent” or “equivalent” or “isomorphic” as synonyms to equivalence relations. As always, it is ok to ask someone to explain their terms if you are not sure what they mean. And if you use a term, be able to explain it yourself.


 Order relations
Definition. A homogeneous binary relation (R:X^2) is called an order relation if it is transitive. It is furthermore

A pre order if it is transitive and reflexive
A partial order if it is transitive, reflexive, and anti-symmetric.
A total order if it is transitive, reflexive, anti-symmetric, and for every (x,yX), (xRy) or (yRx).

There are many traditional order languages but some common ones include
(x< y), (xy), (xy), (xy)
One of the reasons that transitive is so hard to avoid is that in almost all logics, entailment itself is transitive:



LaTeX:


So once we get going with propositions it is often hard to avoid the transitive condition.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Week 8 Day 2 Using Default Logic
Let’s dig in to the logic of defaults. The setting we want to consider is when we make our reasonable assumptions about expected deductions but acknowledge that some of our assumptions could be overridden if new information is brought to light. The point is to outline in a disciplined way the process of modifying our assumptions. The method we will outline does to work in all situations however. We will limit our exploration to scenarios that meet the following criteria:

We have a clear authority to decide on rules. This might be a design specification, a client, or requirements of governance & laws.
We can spend the time/resources to explore the optimal configurations. Often setting up a default logic plan takes some upfront work.
The complexity of the solution does not interfere with desired implementation. You can think of the opposite: suppose the instructions are so complicated that you spend more time using the new instructions than getting actual work done.

Now if your situation meets these criteria then the following tool is for you!

 Defeasible Logic & Default Reasoning
Defeasible Logics are non-monotonic logics where we explicitly signal what judgments can be made invalid by later evidence, rather than assuming that all judgments would collapse under later judgments.
Example. Each of the following is valid in a manner that does not become invalid by the addition of future evidence.

If my battery is dead then I cannot make a call.
If (0<x<1) then (x)
x = "Dog" and y="Man" then x+y=="DogMan"



 Defeasible judgement
A judgement (AB) is called defeasible, denoted (A B) if the addition of some judgements (C) may lead to invalidating it (C,AB). We can capture this as a modal condition
\[A\overset{D}{\vdash} B \qquad \equiv\qquad (A\vdash B)\wedge \big(\diamond \big( \exists C. (C,A\nvdash B)\big)\big)\]%255Cwedge%2520%255Cbig(%255Cdiamond%2520%255Cbig(%2520%255Cexists%2520C.%2520(C%252CA%255Cnvdash%2520B)%255Cbig)%255Cbig)?scale=1)
Do not worry about the symbols if they don’t help you. You can break it down by saying

You much have A leading to B, and
It is possible to add further evidence C where C together with A no longer leads to B.

The propositions “C” that occur in a defeasible judgement are called defeaters. Identifying defeaters is a mix of common sense and subject matter expertise.

 A common sense defeater

You click on the image file leading to it being displayed in the browser.
A=“You click on the image file”
B=“It is displayed in the browser”
Together (AB)
It is possible that the image type is not supported by the browser.
C=“Image type is not supported”. (A defeater)
Together (A,CB)

Therefore (AB) and ((C)(A,Cb). So (A B) is a defeasible proposition..

In this example it is likely that common sense convinces you that “C=Image not supported” would defeat the rules. But in the following example it would only be someone with specific knowledge that could inform us about the defeaters.


 A expert dependent defeater
Consider the following three

A = The container is bowl shaped.
B = The container holds liquids.
C = The liquid is helium.

Our common sense will tell use that (AB), e.g. water is help in a bowl, oil is held in a bowl, and so one. This is a sound judgement. However, an expert in low-temperature superfluids would be able to inform us that liquid helium exhibit zero-viscosity and therefore has no friction the side of the bowl and will creep up the sides and pour over the edges. This defeats the claim and so (AB). Of course this could only be expressed to us through a subject matter expert as our daily experiences do not encounter liquid helium.
Alfred Leitner, 1963, Public Domain.


 Was the first entailment just wrong?
When we first deal with default logic from the lens of deductive reasoning it is tempting to want to revisit the initial entailment (AB) and claim this was in error. There are at least two responses to give to this feeling. First of all, humans built logic and did so in the hopes of solving their problems. So if default logic makes for easier reasoning on some problems we should not be shy to use it even if it is not the right tool for some other applications. The second response is that if we think long enough there is very little outside of formal mathematics which would ever deserve the judgement (AB) because nearly every claim we will make will be couched in some default assumptions often unspoken and too difficult to uncover. So in a practical sense we would get nothing done if we insisted on beginning without defaults. Thus if we are making a specification of a program and want to explain a feature as
“You click on the image leading to the image displaying in the browser”
We are not behaving irrationally. We are merely lacking the later specificity that will unpack this discussion. And it gives us a compact digestible goal to begin aiming at.
And in case you think this is a choice only faced by practical sciences just take a look at the question of solving (x^2-2=0). I natural default is to assume that (x=) is two solutions. That is until you meet a subject matter expert who wants numbers to represent binary values modulo 2. Defaults are natural, embrace them and your reasoning will be easier on others.



 * Select All
(A B)

A is valid
B is valid
A leads to B
Some condition C can defeat A leading to B
Possibly a condition C that defeats A leading B
B is both valid and invalid



 * Select All
You are designing a specification for a print option of your document. You have

A = “Select Print Document”
B= “A paper copy will come out of the printer”.

Your design is that (AB). Select some proposition that would be reasonable to include as “defeaters” to this claim. Keep in mind the original three criteria for default logic.

Paper jam
No toner
No paper
There are other print jobs
There are voltage drop in the power socket.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Week 7
Day 1 Relations and Orders
We saw with deduction that one of the ways to build a new data type is to modify what we mean by “equals”. In programs we override equality. But you are likely familiar with other ways we relate data. For example, some numbers are large, others are small, that means (xy). Likewise some expressions in reasoning benefit from organization.

 General Relations
To turn data like 541 or a PDF into a value we can judge we need to create a relation. Here are some samples relations.

P(541) = “541 is positive”. Something we can judge, and we judge it is true.
P(541) = “541 is even.” Something we can also judge, but this time we judge it is false.
Q(MyCV.pdf) = “MyCV.pdf has page numbers.” Something we can judge. Is it true? We’d have to read the file to find out.


 Propositions
A Proposition is a sentence we can claim and judge. The outcome depends on our mode. Recall from Week 1 we have three forms of propositions

() for Theory is generally True () and False ()
() for Computation is generally True () and False () but must be supported by evidence so it may not come to an end if the evidence never comes.
() for Practice is generally True (), False () along with a host of gray are, perhaps Maybe, or Unknown, or Likely, Unlikely, etc. We will here simplify and just allow a single third value +.



 Relations
So what is a Relation? First choose the appropriate proposition category (Theory, Computation, or Practice). Then a Relation is a function form lists of types (X_1, X_2,, X_n) into (). That is
(P:X_1X_n)

P(x) = “x is positive”. This is not something we can judge yet, but as soon as we replace the variable by a value we will be able to judge it. In fact this sort of claim is simply true of false, Theory proposition applies.. So this is a function from data into propositions but it only makes sense when given decimal numbers (). It is a Relation (P:{,})
P(x,y) = “x +y =0”. This is a either true or false, so we can judge this once given decimal numbers of x and y so this is a relation (P:{,})
Q(x) = “x has page numbers”. Here x is a file, so File is our input type. However, the concept of “has page number” is clear for documents but it means nothing for images, videos and so many other documents. This suggests a practical proposition of Prop={true, false, undefined}. This is a relation (Q: -> {}). In common software syntax this might be def hasPageNumbers(x : File) : Option[Boolean]. The Option wrapper allows us to give back a value of True/False when it makes sense, or nothing when the input file is not a document.



 General Relation Vocabulary

Valence or Arity is the number of inputs to a relation. E.g. P(x), Q(x) are valence 1, also called unary. P(x,y) is binary, valence 2.
Homogeneous: a relation (R:X_1X_n) where for each (i,j), (X_i=X_j). In this case we often write (R:X^n).
Heterogenous: a relation that may not be homogeneous. In general a homogeneous relation is also heterogenous but not the other way around.

Mathematical Conventions
Mathematics tends to study relations (R:X_1X_n) more fully than other subjects and much of mathematics is in the Theory camp of reasoning. Because of this most of mathematics sees relations as just true and false. When this is the case then it is enough to know just the values which are true.
({(x_1,, x_n)X_1X_n R(x_1,, x_n) })
Because of this, much of mathematics will define relations not by a function but by a subset, that is, mathematics will often write
(RX_1X_n)
Even if this is bit short cited on the part of mathematicians not to consider the nuance of relations in computation and in practice, it is still a notation used broadly and you can introduce that notation meaning in fact (R:X_1X_n). Just add that clarity to your discussion in text.



 Binary Homogeneous Relations
Amongst the most used relations are binary homogeneous relations
(R:XX)
In this case we generally prefer an infix notation. Example, instead of (R(x,y)) we choose some symbol, maybe = or < or == etc. and write things like
(x=y), (x<y), x==y, x!=y, (xy)
Since we need to keep talking about many binary homogeneous relations we will continue to use R as a generic name
(xRy)

 Reflexive law
A binary homogeneous relation (R:X^2) is called reflexive if
(x.(xRx))

In number equality is reflexive (x=x), less than is not reflexive (5<5) is false, but less-than or equal is reflexive (xx)
In programming if one data type B extends another A it means every method for A is a method for B as well, though B may have further methods. Under this definition A has all the methods that A has so A extends A. However, in writing a program you may not be allowed to write A extends A as that leads the programming language to get confused with circular reasoning. This is a difference in definitions, so even experts can disagree on this one with good reason.
A daughter inherits traits from her father, but a daughter does not inherit traits from herself. So inheritence is not generally reflexive.

Reflexive Closure
In some situations it is convenient to assume a relation is reflexive even if it is not. Think of promoting (x<y) into (xy). This literally means
(xy := (x=x) (x<y))
We can do this to absolutely any binary homogeneous relation (R:X^2)
(xy := (x=x) (x<y))
The resulting relation (R^=) is called the reflexive closure. The notation we usually use is to add part of the equal sign to the original symbol. Here are some examples

(< )
()

In other situations we want to remove reflexivity. We can do this as well.
(xy := (xx) (xy))
The notation similarly strikes out the equal portion.


 Transitive Law
So what makes something an order? While humans make the rules, and thus can change them, by far the most popular definitions agree on one rule, the transitive law.
( (a < b )(b< c) (a< c))


 Symmetric and Anti-symmetric laws
Two further relations laws are commonly encountered.

Symmetric: (xRy yR x)
Anti-symmetric: (xRy yRx x=y)

As we have seen there is a notion of “closure” for each of these. We simply force a relation to be symmetric. However, the closure for anti-symmetric is more sublte because it is forced to change the notion of equality. So this creates what we early called a partition.



 Special Relations
Now mostly because of the popular use there are a bunch of combinations of these four rules that get names and you might be expected to know them in your future so we lets give them here.

 Equivalence relation
Definition. A homogeneous binary relation (R:X^2) is called an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, transitive, and symmetric.
Equivalence relations usually uses language like this
(x=y), (xy), (xy), x==y, x.equals(y), equals(x,y)
You may also here the words “congruent” or “equivalent” or “isomorphic” as synonyms to equivalence relations. As always, it is ok to ask someone to explain their terms if you are not sure what they mean. And if you use a term, be able to explain it yourself.


 Order relations
Definition. A homogeneous binary relation (R:X^2) is called an order relation if it is transitive. It is furthermore

A pre order if it is transitive and reflexive
A partial order if it is transitive, reflexive, and anti-symmetric.
A total order if it is transitive, reflexive, anti-symmetric, and for every (x,yX), (xRy) or (yRx).

There are many traditional order languages but some common ones include
(x< y), (xy), (xy), (xy)
One of the reasons that transitive is so hard to avoid is that in almost all logics, entailment itself is transitive:
\[\begin{array}{rl}
P & \vdash Q\\
Q & \vdash R\\
\hline
P & \vdash R
\end{array}\]
So once we get going with propositions it is often hard to avoid the transitive condition.

text:
Overview When Reasons beyond evidence are Wrong
In this module we will be dealing with possible responses to mistakes and unexpected behaviors. This is especially important as we reason beyond the evidence since this places us in stations where errors and confusion are to be expected. So the theme of this module is
Logical reasoning when evidence is inconsistent.
The type of reasoning this often entails was primarily invented to study large philosophical and sometimes religious questions. But over many centuries and especially in the recent decades it has become a pillar of computational reasoning because so often computation is an unable to have all the evidence required to make sound judgement. So decision are made under best plans and back up plan is created to recover when those assumptions are shown to be false.

 Learning Objectives

Explain the meaning of inconsistency in reasoning.
Define monotonic and non-monotonic reasoning.
Recognize scenarios with of non-monotonic problems.
Recognize two major strategies (Default vs. Adaptive) logic for addressing non-monotonic problems.
Locate a story problem as within a Default Logic or Adaptive Logic solution space.
Apply one strategy from Default, Resp. Adaptive, Logic to solve the problem.

You click on the image file leading to it being displayed in the browser.
A=“You click on the image file”
B=“It is displayed in the browser”
Together (AB)
It is possible that the image type is not supported by the browser.
C=“Image type is not supported”. (A defeater)
Together (A,CB)

Therefore (AB) and ((C)(A,Cb). So (A B) is a defeasible proposition..

In this example it is likely that common sense convinces you that “C=Image not supported” would defeat the rules. But in the following example it would only be someone with specific knowledge that could inform us about the defeaters.


 A expert dependent defeater
Consider the following three

A = The container is bowl shaped.
B = The container holds liquids.
C = The liquid is helium.

Our common sense will tell use that (AB), e.g. water is help in a bowl, oil is held in a bowl, and so one. This is a sound judgement. However, an expert in low-temperature superfluids would be able to inform us that liquid helium exhibit zero-viscosity and therefore has no friction the side of the bowl and will creep up the sides and pour over the edges. This defeats the claim and so (AB). Of course this could only be expressed to us through a subject matter expert as our daily experiences do not encounter liquid helium.
Alfred Leitner, 1963, Public Domain.

When we first deal with default logic from the lens of deductive reasoning it is tempting to want to revisit the initial entailment (AB) and claim this was in error. There are at least two responses to give to this feeling. First of all, humans built logic and did so in the hopes of solving their problems. So if default logic makes for easier reasoning on some problems we should not be shy to use it even if it is not the right tool for some other applications. The second response is that if we think long enough there is very little outside of formal mathematics which would ever deserve the judgement (AB) because nearly every claim we will make will be couched in some default assumptions often unspoken and too difficult to uncover. We are not behaving irrationally. We are merely lacking the later specificity that will unpack this discussion. And it gives us a compact digestible goal to begin aiming at.
And in case you think this is a choice only faced by practical sciences just take a look at the question of solving (x^2-2=0). I natural default is to assume that (x=) is two solutions. title: Changing conclusions
text:
Changing conclusions
In this module we will be dealing with possible responses to mistakes and unexpected behaviors. This is especially important as we reason beyond the evidence since this places us in stations where errors and confusion are to be expected. So the theme of this module is
Logical reasoning when evidence is inconsistent.
The type of reasoning this often entails was primarily invented to study large philosophical and sometimes religious questions. But over many centuries and especially in the recent decades it has become a pillar of computational reasoning because so often computation is an unable to have all the evidence required to make sound judgement. So decision are made under best plans and back up plan is created to recover when those assumptions are shown to be false.

 Learning Objectives

Explain the meaning of inconsistency in reasoning.
Define monotonic and non-monotonic reasoning.
Recognize scenarios with of non-monotonic problems.
Recognize two major strategies (Default vs. Adaptive) logic for addressing non-monotonic problems.
Locate a story problem as within a Default Logic or Adaptive Logic solution space.
Apply one strategy from Default, Resp. Adaptive, Logic to solve the problem.

Programming has a cute name for fixing little unintended errors: “Debugging”. Why the word “bug?” Why not “failure”?

title: Relations and Order
text:
We saw with deduction that one of the ways to build a new data type is to modify what we mean by “equals”. In programs we override equality. But you are likely familiar with other ways we relate data. For example, some numbers are large, others are small, that means \(x\leq y\). Likewise some expressions in reasoning benefit from organization.


To turn data like 541 or a PDF into a value we can judge we need to create a relation. Here are some samples relations.

P(541) = “541 is positive”. Something we can judge, and we judge it is true.
P(541) = “541 is even.” Something we can also judge, but this time we judge it is false.
Q(MyCV.pdf) = “MyCV.pdf has page numbers.” Something we can judge. Is it true? We’d have to read the file to find out.



A Proposition is a sentence we can claim and judge. The outcome depends on our mode. Recall from Week 1 we have three forms of propositions

\(\text{Prop}\) for Theory is generally True \(\top\) and False \(\bot\)
\(\text{Prop}\) for Computation is generally True \(\top\) and False \(\bot\) but must be supported by evidence so it may not come to an end if the evidence never comes.
\(\text{Prop}\) for Practice is generally True \(\top\), False \(\bot\) along with a host of gray are, perhaps Maybe, or Unknown, or Likely, Unlikely, etc. We will here simplify and just allow a single third value +.



So what is a Relation? First choose the appropriate proposition category (Theory, Computation, or Practice). Then a Relation is a function form lists of types \(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n\) into \(\text{Prop}\). That is
\(P:X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\to \text{Prop}\)

P(x) = “x is positive”. This is not something we can judge yet, but as soon as we replace the variable by a value we will be able to judge it. In fact this sort of claim is simply true of false, Theory proposition applies.. So this is a function from data into propositions but it only makes sense when given decimal numbers \(\mathbb{R}\). It is a Relation \(P:\mathbb{R}\to \{\top,\bot\}\)
P(x,y) = “x +y =0”. This is a either true or false, so we can judge this once given decimal numbers of x and y so this is a relation \(P:\mathbb{R}\times \mathbb{R}\to \{\top,\bot\}\)
Q(x) = “x has page numbers”. Here x is a file, so File is our input type. However, the concept of “has page number” is clear for documents but it means nothing for images, videos and so many other documents. This suggests a practical proposition of Prop={true, false, undefined}. This is a relation \(Q: \text{File} -> \{\text{true, false, undefined}\}\). In common software syntax this might be def hasPageNumbers(x : File) : Option[Boolean]. The Option wrapper allows us to give back a value of True/False when it makes sense, or nothing when the input file is not a document.






Valence or Arity is the number of inputs to a relation. E.g. P(x), Q(x) are valence 1, also called unary. P(x,y) is binary, valence 2.
Homogeneous: a relation \(R:X_1\times \cdots\times X_n\to \text{Prop}\) where for each \(i,j\), \(X_i=X_j\). In this case we often write \(R:X^n\to \text{Prop}\).
Heterogenous: a relation that may not be homogeneous. In general a homogeneous relation is also heterogenous but not the other way around.

Mathematical Conventions
Mathematics tends to study relations \(R:X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\to \text{Prop}\) more fully than other subjects and much of mathematics is in the Theory camp of reasoning. Because of this most of mathematics sees relations as just true and false. When this is the case then it is enough to know just the values which are true.
\(\{(x_1,\ldots, x_n)\in X_1\times \cdots \times X_n \mid \Gamma \vdash R(x_1,\ldots, x_n) \}\)
Because of this, much of mathematics will define relations not by a function but by a subset, that is, mathematics will often write
\(R\subset X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\)
Even if this is bit short cited on the part of mathematicians not to consider the nuance of relations in computation and in practice, it is still a notation used broadly and you can introduce that notation meaning in fact \(R:X_1\times \cdots \times X_n\to \text{Prop}\). Just add that clarity to your discussion in text.




Amongst the most used relations are binary homogeneous relations
\(R:X\times X\to \text{Prop}\)
In this case we generally prefer an infix notation. Example, instead of \(R(x,y)\) we choose some symbol, maybe = or < or == etc. and write things like
\(x=y\), \(x<y\), x==y, x!=y, \(x\subset y\)
Since we need to keep talking about many binary homogeneous relations we will continue to use R as a generic name
\(xRy\)


A binary homogeneous relation \(R:X^2\to \text{Prop}\) is called reflexive if
\(\forall x.(xRx)\)

In number equality is reflexive \(x=x\), less than is not reflexive \(5<5\) is false, but less-than or equal is reflexive \(x\leq x\)
In programming if one data type B extends another A it means every method for A is a method for B as well, though B may have further methods. Under this definition A has all the methods that A has so A extends A. However, in writing a program you may not be allowed to write A extends A as that leads the programming language to get confused with circular reasoning. This is a difference in definitions, so even experts can disagree on this one with good reason.
A daughter inherits traits from her father, but a daughter does not inherit traits from herself. So inheritence is not generally reflexive.





In some situations it is convenient to assume a relation is reflexive even if it is not. Think of promoting \(x<y\) into \(x\leq y\). This literally means
\(x\leq y \qquad := (x=x) \vee (x<y)\)
We can do this to absolutely any binary homogeneous relation \(R:X^2\to \text{Prop}\)
\(x\leq y \qquad := (x=x) \vee (x<y)\)
The resulting relation \(R^=\) is called the reflexive closure. The notation we usually use is to add part of the equal sign to the original symbol. Here are some examples

\(< \leadsto \leq\)
\(\subset \leadsto \subseteq\)

In other situations we want to remove reflexivity. We can do this as well.
\(x\lneq y \qquad := (x\neq x) \wedge (x\leq y)\)
The notation similarly strikes out the equal portion.



So what makes something an order? While humans make the rules, and thus can change them, by far the most popular definitions agree on one rule, the transitive law.
$ (a < b )(b< c) (a< c)$



Two further relations laws are commonly encountered.

Symmetric: \(xRy \Rightarrow yR x\)
Anti-symmetric: \(xRy \wedge yRx \Rightarrow x=y\)

As we have seen there is a notion of “closure” for each of these. We simply force a relation to be symmetric. However, the closure for anti-symmetric is more sublte because it is forced to change the notion of equality. So this creates what we early called a partition.



Now mostly because of the popular use there are a bunch of combinations of these four rules that get names and you might be expected to know them in your future so we lets give them here.



Definition. A homogeneous binary relation \(R:X^2\to \text{Prop}\) is called an equivalence relation if it is reflexive, transitive, and symmetric.
Equivalence relations usually uses language like this
\(x=y\), \(x\equiv y\), \(x\cong y\), x==y, x.equals(y), equals(x,y)
You may also here the words “congruent” or “equivalent” or “isomorphic” as synonyms to equivalence relations. As always, it is ok to ask someone to explain their terms if you are not sure what they mean. And if you use a term, be able to explain it yourself.



Definition. A homogeneous binary relation \(R:X^2\to \text{Prop}\) is called an order relation if it is transitive. It is furthermore

A pre order if it is transitive and reflexive
A partial order if it is transitive, reflexive, and anti-symmetric.
A total order if it is transitive, reflexive, anti-symmetric, and for every \(x,y\in X\), \(xRy\) or \(yRx\).

There are many traditional order languages but some common ones include
\(x< y\), \(x\leq y\), \(x\subset y\), \(x\sqcup y\)
One of the reasons that transitive is so hard to avoid is that in almost all logics, entailment itself is transitive:
\[
\begin{array}{rl}
P & \vdash Q\\
Q & \vdash R\\
\hline
P & \vdash R
\end{array}
\]
So once we get going with propositions it is often hard to avoid the transitive condition.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
* 06-0 | Overview & Objectives

 * Overview
If we are going to go beyond the evidence then we are going to need ways to get new evidence from the conditions we have. So let us assume we have access to a bunch of data that is unprocessed and imagine that we have to turn this in new propositions. This calls for a new class of function, but in fact you already know of many examples. Take for instance 541 and 1024. There is nothing we could say about these two numbers as being true or false. But if we say the first is smaller than the second suddenly we get a truth value, in fact, it is such a primitive truth it is even computational:
( < 1024) by the evidence that (541+ 483 = 1024)
There are others, “positive”, “heavy”, “cloudy”, “salty”, on and on. We have many ways to taking lists of data and judge it. These are called relations and they are the work horse of inductive arguments because they give us a way to generate new propositions where previously we just had data.


 * Objectives

Find ways to create new evidence from data, a process called relations.
Organize properties of relations around patterns that can be used recursively.
Familiarize ourselves with relations that are common to the sciences.
Develop infrastructure to discover, create, and store relations for computation.
Adjust theoretical relations to practical conditions.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
section: Week 6 Day 2 Pattern Making & its Co-operators
text:
Week 6 Day 2 Pattern Making & its Co-operators

 The life of a file.
One day Dada created a file. She named the file "Top-Secret-Read-Immediately.txt" and started typing out a story, each line adding to the story so that file grew. Almost as quick as things started, the story was over. Dada transmitted the straight to Codaydeh.
Codaydeh immediately opened the file and started to scroll, each line appearing one after other. The story was amazing! What a mystery, what would happen next? Codaydeh scrolled further but nothing happened! The file just stopped, mid sentence. There was nothing more there. This couldn’t be right? Had some of the file been cut off in transmission? Or was Dada suddenly interrupted?


 Pattern Matching
The allegory of sending a file is an archetype of a form of reasoning we all face in everyday life but which presents several challenges to computation. While we would like to think of the file as one piece of data, its creation and its uses are spread apart, often separated by time and space. The separation means that the data will need a number of intermediate uses. We have already seen how we make a data type that breaks down into parts, an “Inductive Type”. This is like the letter writer Dada. There are prescribe number of ways to make the data (introduction rules)
(1: A^{d_1}A) (2: A^{d_2}A),…, (m: A^{d_m}A)
We can shorten this one one function
(: A^{d_1}A^{d_2}A^{d_m}A)
There is only one way to use this data: match each pattern of introduction (construction) and give each of those a role.



Screenshot 2026-02-22 at 9.16.11 PM.png


There is only one elimination rule (use) for the packaged data and it is determined by identifying the uses of the individual means to package the data. Need a little more review? Go through the lab 6 slides here.


 Pattern Making
Now let’s take the perspective of the letter reader. When Codaydeh receives a transmission he knew just what to do and starts taking in line by line text. There is only once source of the data but many uses. The data could be broken into words, then characters, those could be printed in some font, shown an a screen, saved to a file, who knows. But we don’t need to know the use to know the work is to take this single source and divide it up into parts we can use. That means we can focus on the many elimination rules but need only one introduction rule. The trick is to reverse the semantics, all arrows go the opposite direction. Let us start by reversing the operators.

 Co-operators of Co-induction
Suppose we expect that our algebra packaged data up using operators (^{d_1}^{d_n}). Then when we get a data from () then we should expect it was made from one of the terms (^{d_i}). So we just need to reverse this. That is, we need a function (^{d_1}^{d_2}). How do we make it? Let make (n=2) to keep things easy.
Step 1. Remember that (^{d_1}^{d_2}) is type based on OR, and so it has 2 introduction rules, one for (_1:^{d_1}^{d_1}^{d_2}) and (_2:^{d_2}^{d_1}^{d_2}).
Step 2. We need to test the incoming (u:) to know if it came from the left (^{d_1}) or right (^{d_2}). Whichever one it is we can make a function (^{d_1}) or (^{d_2}) and then compose it with (_1) or (_2).



Screenshot 2026-02-24 at 10.23.23 PM.png


The point is we can get form () to (^{d_1}^{d_2}).
Now the precise mechanics to allow this is subtle and requires the programming language called “destructors” or “unapply”. In particular there is not function (^{d_1}) because not every input comes from that side. We test to be sure but it means that this side of our program is technically not “tapeable function”. So there is a special process within the logic that lets us use this as “partial function”. You can ignore this, but it feels right to tell you that sometimes logic needs to go deeper.
Fortunately most modern programming languages include some nice notation to hide the mechanics and make it easy to use. Here’s a program that hides the work. We have a file that can have an End Of File (EOF) or we can have a character a:Char and a file tail:File and we want to add a to the file at position p. This would formally be the following function type.
(: ^0) and ((a,p) : ^1)
which means when unified as a single operator we have
(displaystyle : (^0{a:} {p:} ^1))
Thus the co-operators will reverse this array
(displaystyle : (^0{a:} {p:} ^1))
Let’s call this co-operator unpack and see how close we can get with software.


 OCaml Example
type file =
| EOF
| Insert of char * int * file

let unpack (f : file) : (file array, (char * int) * file array) Either.t =
match f with
| EOF -> Either.Left [||]
| Insert (c, p, rest) -> Either.Right ((c, p), [|rest|])
This approach shows the two possible returns, a File array, or a file array indexed by a character and a position. However it falls short in that it does not have the lengths of these arrays which are in fact known to us. We can achieve this by removing the array type and using the specific number.


 Scala Example
enum File:
case EOF
case Insert(c: Char, p: Int, rest: File)

def unpack(f: File): Either[Array[File], ((Char, Int), Array[File])] =
f match
case File.EOF => Left(Array.empty[File])
case File.Insert(c, p, rest) => Right(((c, p), Array(rest)))


 Java Example
import java.util.Optional;

sealed interface File permits File.EOF, File.Insert {
record EOF() implements File {}
record Insert(char c, int p, File rest) implements File {}
}

class FileUnpack {
static Object unpack(File f) {
return switch (f) {
case File.EOF eof -> eof;
case File.Insert ins -> new CharFilePair(ins.c(), ins.p(), ins.rest());
};
}

record CharFilePair(char c, int p, File rest) {}
}


 Agda Example
open import Data.Char
open import Data.Nat
open import Data.Sum using (_⊎_; inj₁; inj₂)
open import Data.Product using (_×_; _,_)

data File : Set where
EOF    : File
Insert : Char → ℕ → File → File

unpack : File → File ⊎ ((Char × ℕ) × File)
unpack EOF = inj₁ EOF
unpack (Insert c p rest) = inj₂ ((c , p), rest)


 Co-recurse: the unique introduction rule.
Now that we have seen how to unpack operators with co-operators we now need to link them to other co-operators. We continue to reverse the picture.



Screenshot 2026-02-24 at 7.31.42 PM.png


We can use this to convert our file into glyphs and display it on a screen. We can also use it to convert JSON into a screen image or convert to another format like HTTP or UPD to transmit it through the internet. The game keeps going.

Codaydeh scrolled further but nothing happened! The file just stopped, mid sentence. There was nothing more there. This couldn’t be right? Had some of the file been cut off in transmission? Or was Dada suddenly interrupted?



The allegory of sending a file is an archetype of a form of reasoning we all face in everyday life but which presents several challenges to computation. While we would like to think of the file as one piece of data, its creation and its uses are spread apart, often separated by time and space. The separation means that the data will need a number of intermediate uses. We have already seen how we make a data type that breaks down into parts, an “Inductive Type”. This is like the letter writer Dada. There are prescribe number of ways to make the data (introduction rules)
\(\text{case }1: A^{d_1}\to A\) \(\text{case }2: A^{d_2}\to A\),…, \(\text{case }m: A^{d_m}\to A\)
We can shorten this one one function
\(\text{combined case}: A^{d_1}\sqcup A^{d_2}\sqcup \cdots\sqcup A^{d_m}\to A\)
There is only one way to use this data: match each pattern of introduction (construction) and give each of those a role.



Screenshot 2026-02-22 at 9.16.11 PM.png


There is only one elimination rule (use) for the packaged data and it is determined by identifying the uses of the individual means to package the data. Need a little more review? Go through the lab 6 slides here.



Now let’s take the perspective of the letter reader. When Codaydeh receives a transmission he knew just what to do and starts taking in line by line text. There is only once source of the data but many uses. The data could be broken into words, then characters, those could be printed in some font, shown an a screen, saved to a file, who knows. But we don’t need to know the use to know the work is to take this single source and divide it up into parts we can use. That means we can focus on the many elimination rules but need only one introduction rule. The trick is to reverse the semantics, all arrows go the opposite direction. Let us start by reversing the operators.


Suppose we expect that our algebra packaged data up using operators \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \cdots \sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_n}\to \mathbb{U}\). Then when we get a data from \(\mathbb{U}\) then we should expect it was made from one of the terms \(\mathbb{U}^{d_i}\). So we just need to reverse this. That is, we need a function \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\). How do we make it? Let make \(n=2\) to keep things easy.
Step 1. Remember that \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\) is type based on OR, and so it has 2 introduction rules, one for \(\iota_1:\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\) and \(\iota_2:\mathbb{U}^{d_2}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\).
Step 2. We need to test the incoming \(u:\mathbb{U}\) to know if it came from the left \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\) or right \(\mathbb{U}^{d_2}\). Whichever one it is we can make a function \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\) or \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\) and then compose it with \(\iota_1\) or \(\iota_2\).



Screenshot 2026-02-24 at 10.23.23 PM.png


The point is we can get form \(\mathbb{U}\) to \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\).
Now the precise mechanics to allow this is subtle and requires the programming language called “destructors” or “unapply”. In particular there is not function \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\) because not every input comes from that side. We test to be sure but it means that this side of our program is technically not “tapeable function”. So there is a special process within the logic that lets us use this as “partial function”. You can ignore this, but it feels right to tell you that sometimes logic needs to go deeper.
Fortunately most modern programming languages include some nice notation to hide the mechanics and make it easy to use. Here’s a program that hides the work. We have a file that can have an End Of File (EOF) or we can have a character a:Char and a file tail:File and we want to add a to the file at position p. This would formally be the following function type.
\(\displaystyle \text{EOF}: \mathbb{U}^0\to \mathbb{U}\) and \(\displaystyle \text{Insert}(a,p) : \mathbb{U}^1\to \mathbb{U}\)
which means when unified as a single operator we have
\(displaystyle \text{all-ops} : \left(\mathbb{U}^0\sqcup \bigsqcup_{a:\text{Char}} \bigsqcup_{p:\text{Int}} \mathbb{U}^1\right)\longrightarrow \mathbb{U}\)
Thus the co-operators will reverse this array
\(displaystyle \text{co-ops} : \mathbb{U} \longrightarrow \left(\mathbb{U}^0\sqcup \bigsqcup_{a:\text{Char}} \bigsqcup_{p:\text{Int}} \mathbb{U}^1\right)\)
Let’s call this co-operator unpack and see how close we can get with software.

OCaml ExampleScala ExampleJava ExampleAgda Example


type file =
| EOF
| Insert of char * int * file

let unpack (f : file) : (file array, (char * int) * file array) Either.t =
match f with
| EOF -> Either.Left [||]
| Insert (c, p, rest) -> Either.Right ((c, p), [|rest|])
This approach shows the two possible returns, a File array, or a file array indexed by a character and a position. However it falls short in that it does not have the lengths of these arrays which are in fact known to us. We can achieve this by removing the array type and using the specific number.


enum File:
case EOF
case Insert(c: Char, p: Int, rest: File)

def unpack(f: File): Either[Array[File], ((Char, Int), Array[File])] =
f match
case File.EOF => Left(Array.empty[File])
case File.Insert(c, p, rest) => Right(((c, p), Array(rest)))


import java.util.Optional;

sealed interface File permits File.EOF, File.Insert {
record EOF() implements File {}
record Insert(char c, int p, File rest) implements File {}
}

class FileUnpack {
static Object unpack(File f) {
return switch (f) {
case File.EOF eof -> eof;
case File.Insert ins -> new CharFilePair(ins.c(), ins.p(), ins.rest());
};
}

record CharFilePair(char c, int p, File rest) {}
}


open import Data.Char
open import Data.Nat
open import Data.Sum using (_⊎_; inj₁; inj₂)
open import Data.Product using (_×_; _,_)

data File : Set where
EOF    : File
Insert : Char → ℕ → File → File

unpack : File → File ⊎ ((Char × ℕ) × File)
unpack EOF = inj₁ EOF
unpack (Insert c p rest) = inj₂ ((c , p), rest)







Now that we have seen how to unpack operators with co-operators we now need to link them to other co-operators. We continue to reverse the picture.



Screenshot 2026-02-24 at 7.31.42 PM.png


We can use this to convert our file into glyphs and display it on a screen. We can also use it to convert JSON into a screen image or convert to another format like HTTP or UPD to transmit it through the internet. The game keeps going.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Week 7 Overview
We are after inductive reasoning (reasoning beyond the evidence) and to do that we we now turn to that generates new evidence from data we have. This is the concept of an “Relation”. Think of a number, maybe it is 541. But is that number “True”? No! Numbers do not get talked about as “True” or “False”. Lets try another example. Think of a file on your computer. I’m thinking of my CV (what professors call their Resume). It is a PDF file. But it isn’t “True” or “False” either.
This is the point of this unit. We are often surrounded by data but none of it is directly evidence because it is not in the form we can use in logic. It is not in the form of data we can judge as being valid (true, false, or other). So one way to reason beyond the evidence we have is to start converting some of the vast data we have into evidence by introducing a device that turns data into judgement. This is called a Relation

As plots

As hierarchy/Hasse diagrams

Reflexive
Transitive
Symmetric/Anti-symmetric

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
section: Week 6 Day 1 Lists, Trees, & their Algebra
text:
Week 6 Day 1 Lists, Trees, & their Algebra
When we reason inductively we look at evidence we have, conjecture about possible options, and compile a strategy that works through the cases we identify. When our concerns are computational we need all our evidence to come in the form of data, data of various types. And the strategy is to develop transformations of our data. That means functions of a special shape we call operators. All the operators together form the so-called “algebra” of our induction. Many times the operators will be used over and over again, in what we call “recursion”, reflecting the idea that sometimes complexity comes from repeating simpler ideas over and over again. Think of (4n); that is simply (n+(n+(n+n)))) so it is addition repeated 3 times. Let’s begin with an archetype situation where we need induction.
Induction & Coconspirators
Once we create data inductively we will need a strategy to take such complex data apart, and for that we reverse the constructions in a process known sometimes as “coalgebra”. Instead of operators we reverse the direction and have “cooperators” and instead of recursion we make streams of “corecursion”. But all this is too abstract to take in without some examples. Coalgebras will come next lesson!

 * Lectures
YouTube video player

 Defining the operators of the List algebra
Let us write List[A] to mean the type of data which we regard as a list of terms of type A. For example, List[Int] is a list of integers, List[String] is a list of String objects, List[List[Int]] is a list of lists of integers, and so on. To make a list we have basically 2 options

Make an empty list, traditionally called “nil” nil:List[A] also denoted []:List[A].
For every constant a:A, there is a unique operator that pre-pends a to the list. Traditional notations include cons(a): List[A]-> List[A] or a more operator looking notation like a::_.

Technical point: sometimes it is convenient to treat all empty lists as equal, but the way we have done it so far []:List[Int], []:List[String] would make two empty lists, one for integers, one for strings. In some programming languages you can unify these types by creating a single empty list of type List[Any] . The idea is that when the time comes to decide, any type of entries will work. After all a list with nothing in it doesn’t need to have a specific type. That model doesn’t quit match the algebra so we leave that technical choice to the side, but you might want to try it on your own.


 Example of List Building by induction
An integer would be the letter “i” and so the plural, a list of integers, becomes “is” (“eyes” not “iz”), which in our notation could be is:List[Int] = 5::[4::[1::[]]]. The brackets serve as parenthesis and most programming languages will let you remove them, e.g. 5 :: 4 :: 1 :: []. In fact programming languages offer lots of syntax alternatives called “syntactic sugar” such as [5,4,1]. In this situation there is one nil operator but also one operator for every integer! So if integers are 32-bits, that means (2^{32}^9) cons operators!


 Operators as Formation and Introduction rules
What makes this induction is the use of operators to build up the data. Operators can come be many, e.g. one nil operator, and as many a::_operators as there are terms a:A. On a formal level we think of the application of operators as “introduction rules” (constructors/setters). Let us look at the sequent version of these rules.

Formation ()
Introduction(Nil case): (:)
Introduction(Cons(a) case): ()



 Using the algebra: Elimination and computation rules
The elimination rules and the associated computation rules are so prescribed for these data types that they are often not even explained. These are so common they even have their own special names: “Principle of Induction” and “recursion” respectively. Here they are as sequence for Lists.

Elimination(“Principle of Induction”): ( { extract(as) : ( ) } ).
Computation(“Recursion”): (extract([]) := Left()) because you can extract nothing from an empty list. Otherwise ( { extract(head :: tail) := Right( head, tail) } )

Don’t get too strict about these names. Many authors use them in slightly different ways.


 A sample use
`> as:List[String] = [“dog”, “cat”, “mongoose”]
def length_of_list(as:List[A]): Int =
as match {
case [] => []
case head :: tail => 1 + length_of_list( tail )
}`
> length_of_list(as) 3


 Ways to think about many name operators
Arguably we might prefer to think of constructing lists as taking as input both a head a:A and tail tail:List[A]. But that leads to a very complicated algebra and so it is easier for us to reason about the parts that are the same, the List[A]. You might find it helpful to think of similar situations you might encounter already.
Think of this as an operation similar to say the an exponent, e.g. (x^2) or (x^3). You can imagine a calculator button for each operation, and you can imagine a bigger calculator, like a computer, could make one for larger powers in fact one for every integer. Having multiple operators with similar names is normal in your everyday computation.



 * Some Demonstrations
Induction

 So what do we have in total?
An “algebraic structure”, or simply “an algebra” refers to any set, or type of data, (A) equipped with operators (:)
(:A^{||}A)
Here (||) means the number of inputs to the operator, e.g. 2 for binary, 1 for unary. This called the valence (or arity) of the operator. Remember that (A^n) means lists of n terms form (A), e.g.

(A^2={(a_1,a_2)a_1, a_2:A})
(A^1={(a_1)a_1:A})
(A^3={(a_1,a_2,a_3)a_1, a_2,a_3:A})
(A^0={()}), that is right, the list with nothing in it is still one thing, so (A^0) has one term, just like (10^0=1) and (x^0=1).

For example, the decimal numbers () have many operators including addition, multiplication, negatives, zero, and one. So (={+,, -, 0, 1}) and the functions are

(+:^2) because we add 2 numbers.
(+:^2) because we multiply 2 numbers.
(-:^1) because we negate 1 number. Warning: it is possible to subtract numbers as well but technically that would be a different operator because it would 2 numbers to subtract. Let us keep things easy and just use negatives.
Zero is a constant, which in other words means a function that depend on no inputs, we write it (0:^0). Remember (^0={()}) has only one term, and so the function (0) sends that one term, the empty list (()) to the correct constant (0.000000….). In programs we might write def zero() : Reals = 0.000, notice the () is the single input to this function.
One is another constant we write it (1:^0), it too needs no inputs. Again the empty list () is sent to 1.0000, i.e. def one() : Reals = 1.00000.



 A tree algebra
Having made the case that recursion uses algebra, we can think of a binary tree as having two operator: root & branch.

sealed trait Tree[A:Type] case Root(a:A) extends Tree[A] case Branch(left:Tree[A], right:Tree[A]) extends Tree[A]
In math notation (root(a:A):^0) and (branch : ()^2)

title: Lists, Trees, & their Algebra
Inductive Reasoning
text:
We are now launching our second of three major units on reasoning. So far we have focussed on
Deductive Logic: reasoning from the evidence provided.
Now we will focus on a much more realistic but nuanced form of reasoning where we have incomplete evidence and still need to make logical decisions.
Inductive Logic: reasoning beyond the evidence provided.


If you read the definition “reason beyond the evidence” you might begin to worry if this is scientific, certainly it would seem dubious as mathematics which tries to be completely proof based. But what if you attempt to read a complex math formula like the following one.
\[
\frac{\left(\sqrt{9-x^2}\right)(x-18)}{1-x+2x^2-4x^3+8?}
\]
For most of use this formula will be too long to absorb all at once. Instead we are very likely to begin to read it from top-to-bottom, left-to-right under the hypothesis that it will indeed reveal itself as a complete mathematical formula. When we read the numerator we don’t yet have the evidence that the denominator will be a math formula. We are reasoning beyond our evidence. And in fact it is only when we get to the very end that we find in disappointment that it was not a standard math formula because it had a stray typo, an ? that should probably have been something else. But look back, was this any less “logical” to proceed under a hypothesis that we had a formula? Probably not. We can imagine that most of the time we don’t encounter flaws and this induction—reasoning beyond the evidence—was every bit as “logical” as our examples of deductive logic.



Much of the data we make or use is complex which literally means it is made out of parts, like a building complex that has several smaller buildings linked together. An example of this is JSON blob that stores social network data as a mix of GPS coordinates, text messages, images, id numbers and much more. Reasoning about complex data doesn’t have to be “complex”, as in “complicated”, but it does benefit from a strategy. The strategy that logic attaches to the study of complex data is known as induction. What it means in this case is that we do not try to understand the entire JSON blob all at once. Instead we learn a series of simpler rules to reason locally under the assumption that when we see the whole data it will make sense. At any one stage we are forced to “reason beyond the evidence we have”. In retrospect the logic we have seen up to this point should be known as deductive. Induction comes from the word “induce” and the idea of induction is to study complex events as mix of smaller evidence that that induce us towards an understanding of the whole.




Recognize inductive reasoning.
Use pattern matching idioms in software.
Apply recursion.
Model the algebra of induction in both producing and consuming roles.

Elimination(“Principle of Induction”): ( { extract(as) : ( ) } ).
Computation(“Recursion”): (extract([]) := Left()) because you can extract nothing from an empty list. Otherwise ( { extract(head :: tail) := Right( head, tail) } )

Don’t get too strict about these names. Many authors use them in slightly different ways.


 A sample use
`> as:List[String] = [“dog”, “cat”, “mongoose”]
def length_of_list(as:List[A]): Int =
as match {
case [] => []
case head :: tail => 1 + length_of_list( tail )
}`
> length_of_list(as) 3


 Ways to think about many name operators
Arguably we might prefer to think of constructing lists as taking as input both a head a:A and tail tail:List[A]. But that leads to a very complicated algebra and so it is easier for us to reason about the parts that are the same, the List[A]. You might find it helpful to think of similar situations you might encounter already.
Think of this as an operation similar to say the an exponent, e.g. (x^2) or (x^3). You can imagine a calculator button for each operation, and you can imagine a bigger calculator, like a computer, could make one for larger powers in fact one for every integer. Having multiple operators with similar names is normal in your everyday computation.



 * Some Demonstrations
Induction

 So what do we have in total?
An “algebraic structure”, or simply “an algebra” refers to any set, or type of data, (A) equipped with operators (:)
(:A^{||}A)
Here (||) means the number of inputs to the operator, e.g. 2 for binary, 1 for unary. This called the valence (or arity) of the operator. Remember that (A^n) means lists of n terms form (A), e.g.

(A^2={(a_1,a_2)a_1, a_2:A})
(A^1={(a_1)a_1:A})
(A^3={(a_1,a_2,a_3)a_1, a_2,a_3:A})
(A^0={()}), that is right, the list with nothing in it is still one thing, so (A^0) has one term, just like (10^0=1) and (x^0=1).

For example, the decimal numbers () have many operators including addition, multiplication, negatives, zero, and one. So (={+,, -, 0, 1}) and the functions are

(+:^2) because we add 2 numbers.
(+:^2) because we multiply 2 numbers.
(-:^1) because we negate 1 number. Warning: it is possible to subtract numbers as well but technically that would be a different operator because it would 2 numbers to subtract. Let us keep things easy and just use negatives.
Zero is a constant, which in other words means a function that depend on no inputs, we write it (0:^0). Remember (^0={()}) has only one term, and so the function (0) sends that one term, the empty list (()) to the correct constant (0.000000….). In programs we might write def zero() : Reals = 0.000, notice the () is the single input to this function.
One is another constant we write it (1:^0), it too needs no inputs. Again the empty list () is sent to 1.0000, i.e. def one() : Reals = 1.00000.



 A tree algebra
Having made the case that recursion uses algebra, we can think of a binary tree as having two operator: root & branch.

sealed trait Tree[A:Type] case Root(a:A) extends Tree[A] case Branch(left:Tree[A], right:Tree[A]) extends Tree[A]
In math notation (root(a:A):^0) and (branch : ()^2)

 * Lesson Introduction
Imagine you look at the contents of a file, you might imagine a simple document. There will be some special data to describe the format and what version is being used. Then there will be strings of letters that you types along with line numbers. There will be parts of data for the fonts to use and whether it should be in a color. You might have included a photograph or a style. This is no longer sounding as simple as listing letters in an alphabet!
What is called for here is a logic that does not try to understand a document all at once but rather takes smaller incremental steps to evolve the concept. This is a process of reasoning known as induction–going beyond the evidence. Sometimes we have clear guardrails that limit what we can do beyond the evidence, that tracks well for computational judgments. Other times what lies beyond the evidence requires some default assumptions, something better for practical judgement. And sometimes we can tame the practical inductive judgments by modeling and predicting their probabilities creating a theoretical judgment. This will take several modules to unravel but we start with the computational questions of induction.

title: Deductive Reasoning
text:
When we peddle clockwise (when facing the gears) on a bicycle we know the bike will move forward. It is a deduction that one proposition (peddling clockwise) leads to a specific outcome (the bike moves forward).
We can even argue why. We could establish that the motion moves a chain clockwise which moves a gear on the rear wheel clockwise which moves the attached wheel clockwise which means the back of the bike pushes forward. It all locks into place as a solid deduction. We can insert these steps to refine our earlier judgment.
Now what happens if we peddle counterclockwise? If you have experience riding or watching bicycles you know this becomes a delicate question. The argument we just made could be reversed to suggest the bicycle would move backward. But many who have witnessed a bicycle ride will notice peddling backwards does not generally change the direction. Nor does it matter if you stop peddling once in motion. Those conclusions are far less deductive. Those need some intervening knowledge that our photographic evidence has not provided. This is the point of deductive reasoning versus other forms of reasoning. Deduction should proceed from the evidence. Peddling clockwise offers enough evidence for such a deduction. Peddling backwards likely does not (we might using inductive reasoning instead).

title: Deductive Reasoning
text:
Computational Impact
Deduction was one of the first forms of reasoning converted into computation and you may already see why. If you have data that backs up a claim and that claim leads to another claim you will in effect be transforming your input data into output data. This is what you might call a function. This is a deduction made computational and the first leg of the Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence.
Having a definition brings up new questions, for instance, whose “system” do we accept and what counts as “evidence”? You might want to first continue the green loop to explore the two other forms of reasoning (inductive and deductive) or you can take the harder blue track now of digging into how we reason deductively.

title: What is a subset?
text:
What is a subset?
Often the goal of a data set is to explore only parts of it. Mathematicians call this a subset. Getting a data types to replicate subsets can be hard, but a starting point is to just rely on injective functions. That is:

A subset \(S\) of a data type \(T\) is an injective function \(\iota:S\to T\)

You might want to review the lesson on injective before continuing.
What does this really mean? Well suppose it says that we have some new data type \(S\) and a way to associate each term of \(S\) to a unique term in \(T\). That does not require that we use every term in \(T\) and so it is in this sense that \(S\) is just a “sub” amount of the data available in \(T\). Finally the word “set” should play a role too. This is reserved for situations in which we can describe a test of membership. For example, if \(T\) is all the people in Fort Collins and \(S\) is members of my gym, then not everyone is a member, that is only some \(t:T\) would be given a certificate \(s:S\) which proves \(t=\iota(s)\).
Describing subsets in this way means we are interested in the membership and not precisely in how we certify members. For example it might be that when the gym first opened the owner just recognized the small number of clients and so the injective function \(\iota:S\to T\) was just memory. As the gym grows we end up needing a better system. We can change this to an ID card. Here \(S\) becomes the persons with ID cards, for example (Pete, ID#342). We do not want to be stuck using ID cards forever. Perhaps in the future a client login will be preferred. But we still want to maintain the concept of one subset, the members of the gym. We have a computational problem: we need to the ability to replace and upgrade our membership system without changing who exactly is a member.
[Side note, there is a thread of this discussion that deals with how people come and go and membership lists change. Let’s leave that to a discussion of “Modal Membership” where we consider the possible worlds. For now let us stay focussed on the computational question.]
The solution is to decide that two injective functions are equivalent if we can get from one to the other with a bijection, that is, a two-way reversible function. If we have that then we are able to migrate clients form the old system to the new, and if we need to double check or track down a problem, go back to the old system as well without changing anything.
Definition 1: A subset \(S\) of a data type \(T\) is an injective function \(\iota:S\to T\) or any other injective function that is equivalent to it.

 * Objectives

Recognize a subset and membership
Identify the difference between a property and a judgement.
Build a data type for subsets

So a function (f:AB) is surjective when any of the following hold.

For every (b:B) the equation (f(x)=b) has at most one solution (x:A).
There is a right-inverse (/f:BA) such that (f/f(a)=a)
Whenever (hf=kf) then (h=k)



 * Quick Check
You are told (f:AB) is surjective. What can you know about its possible right-inverses?
It may not have a right inverse.
To be surjective you must have a right inverse.
It has at most one right inverse.
This is possible but not required.
It has at least one right inverse
Yes, there is at least a right inverse.


 * Quick Check
A bank user must enter their pin number to access their account. Is the pin function surjective?
Yes
No, there is no reason that every number must be used as someone’s pin. For example the bank may forbid easy to guess numbers like 0000.
Maybe
This is the safest answer. While lots of bank users could increase the odds that every pin is eventually used we cannot be certain that perhaps the bank does not permit some pins that are too easy to guess, like 0000.
No
It is not impossible that with lots of customers every pin eventually is chosen by someone, but we can’t be certain.

How can a program prove a function is surjective?
It cannot, you have to prove that on paper.
No, there are several great ways to prove some program is surjective using another program. All you need is a right inverse, but there are other options too including a cancellation function or a type theory theorem prover.
By providing a right inverse.
Yes. If you program in a right inverse to function then you are giving a proof that the function is surjective. Not only that you are increasing the power of you program because people can use that right inverse to reverse computation and get more done.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
section: math156 Refactoring Code and Logical Equivalence
text:
math156 Refactoring Code and Logical Equivalence
When we design a program from a flowchart we might lock in steps that later we want to re-arrange. This is known as “refactoring”. The purpose of refactoring is to make arguments more clear, make room to reuse arguments, and shorten arguments. The main thing we try not to do when refactoring is change or weaken the software, i.e. change the logic. So it mater now to pause and ask, how can we use the connection of programs to logic as a tool to guarantee that our refactoring is, well, logical? The answer is the subject of proofs. While proofs are huge topic in the sciences and especially within math and logic, what we explore here is a first step.

 Proofs in sequent calculus are trees
Whether complex or simple, realizing a goal as a sentence in logic can help use realize what parts can be altered without changing meaning or making the meaning wider. Sequent calculus is designed to help us isolate these goals and leave behind useful reproducible arguments for anyone who has to maintain our changes in the future.
Sequents are little bricks of reasoning and sequent calculus is how we are permitted to brick them together. Our purpose now is to prove that if we label all the components and logical operators of a design specification we can often restructure it entirely without loosing any of the meaning. And better yet, this type of proof can be passed along reliably to anyone in the future.


 * Objectives

Take apart the building blocks of a task into sequents and identify implicit use of logical operators.
Judge if conjectured alternatives follow from the specification.
Conjecture alternate logical formulations and prove they follow.



 * Specifications for a printer


 Reorganizing the Logic for a printer
YouTube video player


 Proving logical equivalence
YouTube video player

 Natural deduction
One way to describe a tree is as graph in which any two points are connected by a unique shortest path. This property makes it impossible to give confusing directions. When it comes the clearest proofs, the directions are essential. This is what makes given proofs by trees such a powerful tool. It avoids ambiguity. To enforce this rule in our sequent calculus we have used a subtle but important rule:
Natural Deduction Rule for Sequent Calculus: While there can be any number of premises to a sequent, there can be only one conclusion.
So to see the three, all the premises are the leaves, the conclusion is the root. Composing rules just grows branches.


 Critiques of natural deduction
We should emphasize that natural deduction is not actually that natural. Humans reason through a complex network of evidence often bring back into play ideas that appeared earlier and reusing parts of an argument as complex braid of reasoning. To make these into natural deductions requires that we identify all these loops and reuses and correctly clone reused parts and separate the argument. Cloning should give you worry as we have seen since the start that not all logical systems can be credited with the option to reuse hypotheses. So the strength of natural deduction is not that it is close to nature but that it is clear and efficient. The use of the term “natural” seems mostly to have been a political stunt to inculcate strong belief in philosophies of proof in an era where competing philosophies suggested otherwise. The mathematician David Hilbert can be credited largely for this emphasis, though he achieved it at the cost of removing his dissenters from editorial boards and prominent positions. It is a regrettable omission that has had a long and complicated shadow serving to separate math from computer science in a manner that is only in recent years being rectified.
