 * Quick Check
What are some factors to consider when describing “the image” of a function?
The axioms of set theory.
While images have subtle requirements in foundations of classical logic those are generally not noticed at the level of planning and are there merely to make sure that images can be made. You can safely ignore those issues but know that people thought long and hard to set it up properly.
The times, place or mode in which we evaluate the function.
This is a very common need. Often a function is not frozen in time but rather is an evolving concept that has meaning only once we figure out the state of some state machine. As program user you may need to track that state and implement a modal logic.
Every function (f:AB) has an image but real life often does not have a fixed concept of a function. It may be that the values (f(a)) depend on factors that are in the environment. These can include things like what values in a database, which can change. Meanwhile computer need explicit predictable outcomes. One solution is to move to a modal logic, by adding a state machine. The meaning of the function’s outputs can consult the value of the current state to describe the world in which it lives. The idea is to think about the possible worlds and what can be reached by the state we are in. If the world we are in can reach the outcome then we include in the image. Once we are done building in the modalities we can finally simplify to the classical image:
(Im(f)={ f(a) aA} = { bBaA, f(a)=b})

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
section: Math 156 When (y=f(x)) has exactly one solution
text:
Math 156 When (y=f(x)) has exactly one solution

 Bijective: (y=f(x)) always has exactly 1 solution.


 (y=f(x)) has exactly one solution
YouTube video player


 * Fill-in-the-Blank
A function (f:XY) is bijective when for every (yY), (y=f(x)) has exactly one solution.


 * Flashcards
Instructions - Injective
(f:XY) has a left inverse (f:YX^?) - Onto
Jargon for “Surjective” - One-to-one
Jargon for “Injective” - One-to-one correspondence
Jargon for “Bijective” - Bijective
(f:XY) has a two-sided inverse (f^{-1}:YX) - Surjective
(f:XY) has a right inverse (/f:YX) - Right invertible / “cancellable”
(uf=vf) leads to (u=v) - Left invertible / “cancellable”
(fu=fv) leads to (u=v) - (/f)
(f:XY), (/f:YX) where (xX. ((f/f)(x)=x)) - (f)
(f:XY), (f:YX) where (xX, ((ff)(x)=x)


 What if your function is “none of the above”?
Pay attention that what is not being said is that (y=f(x)) sometimes have at least/at most/exactly one solution and sometimes not. Functions can have a mix of solution patterns but they only get the name surjective/injecitve/bijective when that pattern applies to all (yY). This means there are many functions that are none of the above. However, an important and crucial theorem of function is that they always factor into this pattern.
Theorem. Every function (f:XY) is the composition (f=ibc) where

(i) is injective and we call it the “image of (f)”,
(b) is bijective, and
(c) is surjective and we call the “co-image of (f)”.

Perhaps it is better to see this with an example. Imagine we think of customers ordering off of a menu in the morning. Not everything on the menu will be ordered. And items that sell can be said to have appealed to clients who have similar taste profiles. So we can break down the ordering process into 3 stages



Flow chart of customer ordering off of a menu as related to their profile and items sold.



Stage 1: Customer taste profiles (e.g. sweet tooth, picky eater, diet conscious, ….)
Stage 2: Match menu selection to each profile.
Stage 3: The sold item must all appear somewhere on the menu

This decomposition over simplifies the real life, for example even a regular customer profile can surprise us with a new order every now and then. But we take this theoretical observation more seriously by thinking of these functions as described in practical logics which allow for occasional inconsistencies. The field of Machine Learning is dedicated to tools that construct such functions as reasonably accurate approximations of customer profiles and their most likely menu choices.
What we do with the data after is still open to creativity. Perhaps we lower food costs by making our menu a closer to match to items that sell. Or perhaps we market to new customers increase the profile and sell more high-priced items from the menu. The math is here to do the job of point out how the data moves and to do so in regular predictable ways for which we can solve. You and your users get to imagine what becomes possible because of the math.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text: Overview

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Math156 Overview

 Our progress this far

Identify context, implicit and explicit (import, include, using, etc.) and the logic that requires (e.g. Constructive, Classical, Paraconsistent, Modal, Linear, etc.).
Develop logical operators to capture forms of reasoning we agree to consider valid in that context, e.g. AND (), OR (), IMPLIES (), NOT (), FOR ALL (), THERE EXISTS (), NECESSARY () and POSSIBLY () are common.
Wrap these with data types so that we can narrow our logical context to avoid contradictions.



 Final Objective: Combining data types
Our final objective is to combine the data types we just made into more complex structures similar to how we combine logical operators to make complex reasoning. Don’t be alarmed by the term “complex” here. We mean it in the spirit of a building “complex” as one made from smaller parts and not in the colloquial sense of “complicated”. It is nevertheless true that the more parts a system has the more we have to be mindful about the resulting meaning. So it is unavoidable that some data types do become complicated.


 * Objectives

Define Injective, Surjective, Bijective
Characterize injective, surjective, bijective by equivalent properties
Syntactic properties of right/left/two-sided invertiblity
Semantic properties of the commutative-diagram left/right cancellation properties.
Identify subsets / Filtered data types as injections,
Identify partitions / data types with overridden equality as surjections
Develop intersections / pullbacks to combine data on what is common
Develop unions / push-outs to unify data with overlaps.
Develop further diagram skill with Venn diagrams and Hasse diagrams

We now have several logics in front of us and are on our way to turning this into software. One lesson we are learning is to keep concepts simple and build up complexity from small steps we can trust. So now comes the problem of mixing two context. In our first video we will encounter a new problem this brings. A paradox that forces us to add to our logic. The result is what today is known as “Higher Order Logic”, which include several sublogics with names like “Set Theory”, “Type Theory”, “Classes”, “Kinds” and “Sorts”. The same sentence, evidence, or data can be judged differently in two contexts that need to be used together.




Your project uses 2D and 3D points. Will you need a higher order logic? - Yes *


Correct: The arithmetic storage and display of 2D points is different from 3D points and you cannot blend the two without errors. So your will need some higher order logic to separate the context. For example you might create two different types of data. - No *
Think about the point (2,1) and (1,0,1). Is there really any way that you could use these interchangeably without causing some errors?




Perhaps the simplest and most common solution to higher-order logic problems is to annotate the data. Annotations are a general term for all the symbols, superscript, subscripts, highlights, colors, etc. that we might add to text to indicate there is something special going on. Here are three of the most common forms of annotations.

(xX) Here (x) is the data and (X) the annotation. The symbol () read as “in” is meant to read as if the data (x) is in the context of (X). This is especially common in mathematics circles where might write (5) to say “5 is in the real numbers” (real numbers are just decimal numbers).
x:X or X x. Here x is the data and X the annotation. The symbol : read as “has type” is meant to read as if the data x is in the context of the data type X. This is especially common in programming circles where might write Float x or x:Float to read as “x is a floating point number.




You read the following code. Are you likely to be using higher-order logic?
def convert(file, format):
s = read(file)
return save(s,format)

Yes


Unlikely. While the names of the function and the variables give us clues that the data have special roles, there is nothing in the code that annotates this for the program and so we should assume we are operating under the conditions that any data could be coming in or out of this function. It will mean we should expect errors form confusion could occur and perhaps we should plan for this. - No *


Correct:. While the names of the function and the variables give us clues that the data have special roles, there is nothing in the code that annotates this for the program and so we should assume we are operating under the conditions that any data could be coming in or out of this function. It will mean we should expect errors form confusion could occur and perhaps we should plan for this.





Later you get a pull-request with an update to the code that reads like this. Are the modification suggestive of higher-order logic?
def convert(file:File, format:Extension):File
var s:String = read(file)
return save(s,format)

Yes




Correct: The use of annotation signals. These may help our computer program check for errors and use the data correctly according to the logic we intend. - No *
The annotations are a clue about narrowing of data and is uses.

text: (20 mins) What is a subset?

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Math156 What is a subset?
Often the goal of a data set is to explore only parts of it. Mathematicians call this a subset. Getting a data types to replicate subsets can be hard, but a starting point is to just rely on injective functions. That is:
Definition 1: A subset (S) of a data type (T) is an injective function (:ST)
You might want to review the lesson on injective before continuing.
What does this really mean? Well suppose it says that we have some new data type (S) and a way to associate each term of (S) to a unique term in (T). That does not require that we use every term in (T) and so it is in this sense that (S) is just a “sub” amount of the data available in (T). Finally the word “set” should play a role too. This is reserved for situations in which we can describe a test of membership. For example, if (T) is all the people in Fort Collins and (S) is members of my gym, then not everyone is a member, that is only some (t:T) would be given a certificate (s:S) which proves (t=(s)).
Describing subsets in this way means we are interested in the membership and not precisely in how we certify members. For example it might be that when the gym first opened the owner just recognized the small number of clients and so the injective function (:ST) was just memory. As the gym grows we end up needing a better system. We can change this to an ID card. Here (S) becomes the persons with ID cards, for example (Pete, ID#342). We do not want to be stuck using ID cards forever. Perhaps in the future a client login will be preferred. But we still want to maintain the concept of one subset, the members of the gym. We have a computational problem: we need to the ability to replace and upgrade our membership system without changing who exactly is a member.
[Side note, there is a thread of this discussion that deals with how people come and go and membership lists change. Let’s leave that to a discussion of “Modal Membership” where we consider the possible worlds. For now let us stay focussed on the computational question.]
The solution is to decide that two injective functions are equivalent if we can get from one to the other with a bijection, that is, a two-way reversible function. If we have that then we are able to migrate clients form the old system to the new, and if we need to double check or track down a problem, go back to the old system as well without changing anything.
Definition 1: A subset (S) of a data type (T) is an injective function (:ST) or any other injective function that is equivalent to it.

 * Objectives

Recognize a subset and membership
Identify the difference between a property and a judgement.
Build a data type for subsets

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
*04-1 | Solving y=f(x) organizes data

 * Lesson Introduction
In the 1800’s Georg Cantor began to ask questions about infinity which lead him to need a vocabulary for data that was much more rich than any which had existed before. What he invented would eventually be known as as Set Theory, and it comes in many flavors perhaps the most famous one by Ernest Zermelo. However, when we look at types of data we nearly have all we need already. So what is missing?
One way to detect that types are an incomplete theory is to look at one of the most important types, the function (f:XY). Ever heard someone ask for the “range” (or image) of a function? They want to know not just what values are possible, that is the codomain (Y), they want to know what actual values come out. That’s a question of whether (y=f(x)) has a solution for (x) given (y).
Other questions we might ask whether two inputs come out the same, e.g. what are all the monitors I can buy for $500? Once more that is a question of how many solutions (x) I have to (500f(x)).
So since solving (y=f(x)) questions is often the crux of a question, we should have data types to help with that. This is Set Theory.

* 04-0 | Subsets & Partitions Overview & Objectives

 * Overview
When you get a membership to a shop, club, school or organization you are no longer just anyone. You belong to something. And you might even be grouped within that membership with membership tiers (gold, silver, bronze) or (freshman, sophomore, junior, senior, grad). It is so natural to make instructions that only make sense for members.
“All students must sit a final by the end of the course.”
or to use these groupings
“Seniors can register in the 7th week of the prior semester.”
So since we reason so well with membership and grouping we do well to add these to our evolving tools for logic. Members are historically called subsets. Groupings are called partitions. Now you saw the work we put into make the data types we have, and sure subsets and partitions will take work as well. Fortunately we have a lot of tools already so we can use them in clever ways to make the process quicker.


 * Questions & Targets

Develop language and diagrams to articulate combinations of subsets and partitions.
Part of any good plan is now how much data we have or will make, so we will use subsets and partitions to develop a robust theory of sizes.

Design a program that combines your customer orders with your supplier’s inventory.

title: Equations from Diagrams
text:
We often benefit from thinking with pictures. One reason this can be better than words on their own is that we can often use a picture two show a complex set of conditions with few actual symbols. The complication however is that pictures are often one example and not a general claim as we might be hoping to argue. For this reason it is important to clarify our language of pictures and to be precise enough that others can read this without confusion. Having now built up (1) Types of data, (2) Functions between types (3) Composition of types, we are now in a position to draw pictures that put these constructions together. The key tool is what we call a “Commutative Diagram”



Identify a commutative diagram
Convert commutative diagrams into equations
Convert equations of functions into commutative diagrams.
Use the Story-board style to communicate the evolution of a commutative diagram.




Let’s take apart the story into two major lessons. The first of these is the concept of a “commutative diagram”. The idea here is known two most of us as the way we read a flow chart. We have nodes with a rows and if we follow a path of arrows then we are following the cumulative effect of applying one transformation after another. If we start to think of this in the logic we are building we can think of the arrows as implication, or if they concern data we call them functions instead of implications. The nodes then become data types.

Nodes: Data types
Arrows: Functions between data types
Composition: passing data through multiple functions.

You may be familiar with composition of functions and its properties, here is a refresher. The takeaways are that

Definition ((gf)(x)=g(f(x)))
Associativity ((h(gf))=(hg)f))
But non-commutative ((gf)) does not in general equal ((fg)).

Notice above all that we are looking at equations. Equations are parts of mathematics we can test and use to constrain questions and crucially to solve for unknowns. It is a form of “Algebra”. If we bring equations into the design of programs we will find the algebra confines us a bit towards solving the questions in the right way. If we break an equation we have a bug. So we can make tests that try different values of input in the equation and see if they hold. If not we look for a bug. This equation being well inside our system of code is a local test. We do not need to wait for the eventual full strength program to find the mistakes. This is a type of debugging known as “Unit Testing”. Designing our programs to hide equations is one of the main ways we can separate off small problems that are less complex and spot mistakes early.


In software composition can often be written in the opposite order. For example, myFile.as_CSV().convert_JSON() is an often legal programming syntax which means to take the data myFile, apply the function as_CSV to it, then apply the function convert_JSON is applied after that. If x=myFile, f=as_CSV is and g=convert_JSON, then the logic reads as ((gf)(x)). This runs in reverse of the words we see in the program. The complication is that even in programs we can often write the order composition in multiple ways. The code below is the same composition but done more in line with the math style.
convert_JSON( as_CSV( myFile ) )




So now that we see that function composition is not generally “commutative”, i.e. (gffg) in most cases, whenever this does happen we should take notice. Below we see a flow chart of two events: Brushing Hair and Brushing Teeth, vs. Socks On and Shoes On.



Screenshot 2026-02-01 at 9.58.33 AM.png


From this model we see some events commute, others do not.

A commutative diagram (Brush~HairBrush~Teeth = Brush~TeethBrush~Hair)
A non-commutative diagram (Shoes~OnSocks~on Sock~On Shoes~On)

Over time the term “Commutative Diagram” has been relaxed to count any equation of function compositions. So while originally this was about the commutative law (gf=fg) it now includes any flowchart where two paths between the same points commute.

A diagram of functions between types is said to “commute” if any two paths between the same points give equal values.




Now let us focus on the “Universal” nature of our diagrams. Suppose our Dad character had suggested that the child keep only one domino and one string. This would have been enough to eliminate to both a string and a domino. It is in some sense a representation of the data. Yet, the son could clearly complain that this is also to throw away a lot of the data. This would mean the “heap” strategy the kid uses is in a measurable way superior as it did not loose any information. How can the son communicate this?



YouTube video player
The added ingredient here is a timeline, a comic strip, that shows the diagram evolving from given assumption through to a final property.

S["String"]
I["Int"]
flowchart TD
S["String"]
I["Int"]
P["Pair"]
P --> S
P --> I
flowchart TD
C["Competing Pair"]
S["String"]
I["Int"]
H["Pair"]
C --> S
H --> S
H --> I
C --> I
flowchart TD
C["Competing Pair"]
S["String"]
I["Int"]
H["Pair"]    C -->|new Pair| S
C --> S
H --> S
H --> I
C --> I
With the son’s approach to a heap he can repeat everything his father’s method can so it is at least as good. In real life a software package that implements logic like this is making a guarantee that no information is being overlooked. The main idea is to




Design a pattern of flow from your new data types to the given data (elimination rules “getters”)
Repeat that same pattern of flow with a competitor solution.
Verify that your type of data can transform the competitor’s solution into your own uniquely (introduction rule, i.e. “constructors/setters”). Think of this as migrating their solution into your own. The uniqueness here means you don’t have to get caught up in future choices of how to convert. Doing so means you program is now brittle and will depend on configurations and is, well, not universal.




A good idea is worth repeating, but often that really means repeating with some variation. The variation we want to explore is when the roles of the arrows are all reversed behavior can occur in reverse as well. When we do that we are in effect swapping the elimination rules with the introduction rules. With logic that means for example to swap AND with OR, True with False, and many similar dualities. It is often a strong way to get a new functionality without much new work. In the exercises you will explore this duality.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Math156 Dual logic and Programs
Is a good idea is worth repeating? Well in math and logic once we have solved a problem we don’t really need to solve it again. Rather what we mean in this situation is that we can repeat the spirit of the idea but with some useful changes. The variation we want to explore here are when the roles of the arrows are all reversed behavior can occur in reverse as well. Think of this as swapping inputs with outputs, saving a file verses reading a file, opening a window verses closing a window, and so on. When we do that we are in effect swapping the elimination rules with the introduction rules of some data types. With logic that means for example to swap AND with OR, True with False, and many similar so-called dualities. It is often a strong way to get a new functionality without much new work. But sometimes these dualities actually uncover missing parts of the original problem which help us make a better understanding of the entire logic.

 * Objectives

Dualize the logic and diagrams associated to it.
Create the semantics for AND as dual to OR
Recognize the diagrams of for all () and for some () as dual.
Identify ({a:A} B(a)) and ({a:A}B(a)) data types as wrapping quantifiers.



 * Dual Logic and Diagrams of OR


 Diagram logic of OR and its dual AND
YouTube video player


 Data types for quantifiers
Now that we approach mastering the logic of AND, OR, IMPLIES, and NOT we have missing only the QUANTIFIERS (, ) (qualifiers (,) will occur later). We already saw that to make “for all” was really just a repeated use of “AND”. So it may come as little surprise to discover that the data types for all are repeated use of pairs, sometimes called “tuples” but they can include such things as structures and arrays as well. These data types have become known as “dependent types”. We will work through the “Dependent Pair” type here and in exercises you will explore “Dependent Functions”.

In programming X(1)+X(2) adding more terms as need is a sum of types but dependent pairs take on notation as diverse as <i,x>, i**x, but I believe in time it will converge the math notation (x_i). The only problem is that the LaTeX way to use subscripts is x_i which now clashes with the snake-case style of program names. This is easy to fix but as of today it is not yet settled.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
section: math156 HIgher-Order logic by Data Types
text:
math156 HIgher-Order logic by Data Types
The word “data types” is synonymous with computer programs since the 1940’s when Konrad Zuse and others began to think of clever encodings of data such as “Floating Point Numbers”. But before that Types had already been envisioned in work of Bertrand Russell in 1902 and later clarified by Alonzo Church and Haskell Curry to avoid major problems in the foundations of mathematics and logic. This is generally a good sign. If an idea emerges from two or more unrelated areas then there is bound to be value in comparing the goals and resolving them into a one unified concept. Today this is known as “Type Theory” and it offers an excellent translation between the mechanical needs of computers and the fluid abstractions of human reasoning. To get start we will make our first type the first logical operator “AND”. This is a bit of a long one but it will end with actual code you can run yourself. Focus on how we move from the sequents to an eventual program.

title: Logical Operators
text: Identify the logical notions in a context by focusing on what does not change, like the flagpole rather than the flag.

title: Logical AND by Syntax And Semantics
text:
The English word “AND” is a bit too generic to make a reliable logical operator. For instance, we might write

12 is positive and even
Study and you will get good grades.

In the first sentence 12 is given two independent properties happen to coexist. Meanwhile the second sentence seems to indicate that the first property (studying) is responsible for the second (good grades). If you need further confirmation that something is different about these two uses consider swapping the order.

12 is even and positive
You will get good grades and study.

Arguably the meaning of the first sentence is unchanged but the second really has changed in meaning.


In order to be extra clear about our logic we want to set aside the words in natural language an use instead symbols or words in special fonts so as to treat the rules with some rigor that cannot miscommunicate out meaning. To so this we start to make a system that resembles arithmetic with is various additions, subtractions and other operators. When we calculate with any symbols we get what is known as a “Calculus”
So far we have seen ()-calculus and now we will be looking at two further Calculi, Propositional and Sequent. This is as good a place as any to pause and mention the list of “calculi” that exist in this course.

Integral Calculus – the calculation of area and volume.
Differential Calculus – the calculation of rates of change.
Propositional Calculus – the way to compute with of propositions.
Lambda Calculus – the method of creating functions (funny name owing to a funny notation).
Sequent Calculus – the method to write down logic.

As a cultural warning, when some says they are studying “Calculus” chances are they mean one of the first two. Our main objective is to start making logical operators and we will focus on “AND”. In assignments you will explore “OR” and “NOT”



Identify Premise and Conclusion from a logical expression.
Use sequent calculus notation to write down logical operators such as AND, TRUE.
Demonstration the use of introduction and elimination rules.







YouTube video player



Sequent Calculus



Sequents means “parts of as a sequence” and the entire idea is to separate the premise from a conclusion. The devices to separate can just be a line, a long space, a word like “entails” but the most common one today is the turnstyle ⊢also said “vdash” since that is how you look it up as a font.
Sequents calculus is the use of sequence to calculate truth in a specified logic. If our logic only has “and” we can only calculate how make an and (introduction) and how to apply an and (elimination). All this must be written in a language.

(L)anguage : the alphabat, symbols, and grammar to be used in the sequents. If your sequents do not parse in the grammar then they don’t count.
(I)ntroduction : what premise or premises do you need to get ot use your logical operator?
(E)limination : what premises along with context do you need to use a logical operator?

The LIE components of a logical operator are a good way to remember the steps.



There is another way we can describe logical operators that get closer to our appreciation of what our data means. For example, 12 is even and positive is true because each of “12 is even” and “12 is positive” are true. If this is all we care about we can ignore the precise form in which we get the facts and focus purely on the values. This is known as “Semantic” reasoning.
When it comes the semantics of AND we insist on one rule:
Only True AND True should be True 
However this still leaves us lots of room to explore meaning.


In classical logic, what experts call “KL” (the German initials) we insist every event is judged as true () or false () with no middle values allowed (that rule is called the “Law of the Excluded Middle (LEM)”). That means that (PQ) can take only 4 combinations.
(P)(Q)(PQ)
()()()
()()()
()()()
()()
()
Many times this information is recorded more compactly as a table where (P) and (Q) label the rows and columns



LaTeX:


In fact when computing we often replace the symbols with 0 () and 1 () and notice this is the multiplication rules of these numbers



LaTeX:


Notice we could be using very different algorithms to calculate AND through semantics. We might be looking things up in a table or multiplying integers, or using transistors in special configuration called a logic-gate. The point is, if we look at AND as is values instead of its syntax we have the freedom to engineer how we actually apply AND. That can be a powerful feature.



Finally, much of life is not so certain and while we may describe some things as true () we might struggle to conclude that all other things are false (). For that many logics have been created that use further values. Sometimes it is a U for “Unknown”. Some times a “M” for mixed” (maybe a concept that has elements of truth and falsity), or “F(x)” for a “fuzzy truth (0x)” to measure quantities that vary continuously.
I like to use the symbol (+) because it seems typographically between () and () and reminds me we could slide the bar up or down to introduce many subdivisions of “truth”. Obeying the rule of and: ONLY TRUE AND TRUE IS TRUE, we are still permitted to assign the remains values in different ways. For example, perhaps (+) should be (+), meaning, if you have something true and something partially true, then the whole thing is partially true. Of course context gets to decide what will count as the new meaning of AND. We close by detailing one of the ANDs as defined by the logician Kleene.



LaTeX:


In words: truth and truth is true; truth and partial truth is partially true but any value and a falsity is false. There are clearly many ways that this captures the mode of a logic for AND even when we cannot be certain that our data is good enough to make things exactly true or false. And to make this semantics into arithmetic, suppose we used 1 for (), 0 for (+), and -1 of (). Then (PQ) becomes merely ((P,Q)). For example ((1,0)=0) which is what it means to have True and Partially true being only Partially true.
As you develop your logic you may have many other ways to approach operators like this one. But resist the urge to call it an AND unless it obey the main rule: Only True and True is True.

title: Quantifiers
text:
\(\forall\), \(\exists\), \(=\), and \(!^n\)
Once more we can look to natural language to get a hint about what logical operators we will find useful. Think of giving out the same instruction to an ever growing list of employees:

Andrew, Brenda, Carlos, Diego, Ehud, Fari, and Georgio must wash their hands before preparing food.

There a number of disadvantages to this approach. For one thing we are letting natural language get away with some imprecise form. Notice there is only one use of the word AND yet the Language of AND works in pairs <this> AND <that>. So the proper form would need us to pair up the instructions for which we invent parentheses

( (Andrew AND (Brenda AND Carlos)) AND (Diego AND (Ehud AND Fari) ) AND Georgio must wash their hands before preparing food.

Of course this is one of many ways we could pair up the AND’s without actually making the logic any easier to explain.
Since logic is invented by humans for human use, it makes sense to create a version of AND which is much more forgiving about repeated use. This would allow us to get the idea into a precise language we could use in reasoning and making future programs. What should this “repeated AND” be called? Pause to think of how you might say the instructions in simpler way. Here are some options that come to my mind.

All employees must wash their hands before preparing food.
Each employee must wash their hands before preparing food.
Each and every employee must wash their hands before preparing food.

The natural languages we use on each other have many choices for style and emphasis. We can see the basic form is not working to avoid listing all the people. Instead it indexes them into a single category “Employee”. It states the rule they must obey “Wash hands” and then quantifies who in the employee list has this requirement: ALL/EACH/EVERY.






Tip



The word any is often tempting to use as a quantifier, but within natural language it can vasilate between mean all or some, which which quite a different meaning.

“All employees must wash their hands.”
“Did any employee wash their hands?”

As a habit you may do better to practice choosing a term that is less likely to be misunderstood.




The logical operator “For all” is denoted \(\forall\) as an upside-down letter “A” (for “All”). To express it we follow the L.I.E.



The grammar of a universal quantifier is given by \[
\tag{$L_{\forall}$}
\langle universal\rangle ::= \forall \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
\] In words we say “For all \(x\), \(P(x)\) is valid” where \(x\) is a variable and \(P(x)\) is a predicate. Variations include “\(P(x)\) holds, for all \(x\)” and “for every \(x\), \(P(x)\) is valid”.

Notice this is another example of binding a variable. So just as with substitution rules and the Paradox of the trapped variable, we need to be careful to rename \(x\) when substituting.

Proposition 1. \(\forall n.(n<n+1)\).
Here the variable is \(n\) and the predicate is \(n<n+1\).
It is not necessary that the predicate actually depend on the variable, for example
Proposition 2. \(\forall n. (2+2=4)\).




We have not forgotten how to spell LIE but we are skipping ahead to the elimination rule because this is what truly organizes what “for all” does. When the manager asserts that “All employees wash their hands!” the meaning is found by applying this claim to any single employee. For example this means “Brenda must wash her hands!” And a new employee “Henri must wash his hands!” Notice the application no longer features “All” nor a variable “employee”. Thus it is an elimination of the structure of the operator.

\[
\tag{$E_{\forall}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\\ \Gamma & \vdash c \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash P(c)\end{array}
\]
In words:

If context \(\Gamma\) leads to “For all x, P(x) is valid” and context also leads to a value c for x, then P(c) must hold in \(\Gamma\).”





Now that we know how to use the “for all” operator we can guess what we need to know to discover an example of a “for all” operator. Basically we need to reverse what we want as a conclusion. We need to know that if context can make a constant value c for x lead to P(c) being valid, then context is saying P(x) is valid “for all x”. This is quite similar to turning a substitution into a function by function abstraction. The major difference is that instead of a function that output data we think of universal quantifiers and proving a proposition.

\[
\tag{$I_{\forall}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\end{array}
\]
In software, a universal quantifier uses a computational judgement, hence evidence (data) must be produced for each \(P(x)\). In other words \(\forall x.P(x)\) in a Brouwerian judgment is synonymous with a function \(x\mapsto P\).

Notice the premise now has an unknown constant c which together with context leads to P(c). How do we come up with that? We do that through a mix of assumption (hypothesis, axioms, laws) and proofs. For example, a manager or a health inspector make a rule that all employees must wash their hands. Can they really know that this has always been obeyed? Perhaps not but in theory that is how it should work. Once we begin to work in practice or in computation we might find we need to relax our rules. We saw this already with AND where we derived new logic based on include partial truths. We can do the same with “for all” but in order that we call something a “for all” we should keep at least on feature that the theory exhibits. And that is the elimination rule.
For example, if we relax to accept that perhaps some employee neglects to wash their hands we should be within our rights to fire the employee and the health inspector can close the restaurant. When it comes to “for all” it is must important to protect the outcome that clean hands handle food than it is to protect the way introduce the law.








The grammar of an existential quantifier is given by \[
\tag{$L_{\exists}$}
\langle existential\rangle ::= \exists \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
\] In words we say “There exists an \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid” where \(x\) is a variable and \(P(x)\) is a predicate. Variations include “\(P(x)\) holds, for some \(x\)” and “there is at least one \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid”.





\[
\tag{$I_{\exists}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\end{array}
\]





\[
\tag{$E_{\exists}$}
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\\ \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash Q\end{array}
\] In words:
> If context \(\Gamma\) leads to “There exists an x such that P(x) is valid” and context also leads to a value c for x, then P(c) must hold in \(\Gamma\) and hence Q must hold in \(\Gamma\).






\(x=y\) means “\(x\) is identical to \(y\)” and can be expressed in terms of the universal quantifier as follows: \[
x=y \equiv \forall P.(P(x) \leftrightarrow P(y))
\] In other words, “\(x\) is identical to \(y\)” is equivalent to “for all predicates \(P\), \(P(x)\) is valid if, and only if, \(P(y)\) is valid”.


\(x=x\)







NoteProof



For a predicate \(P\) and data \(c\) in the context, if \(P(c)\) is valid then \(P(c)\) is valid, i.e.  \[
\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma,c & \vdash P(c)\end{array}
\]
$P(c)P(c). Hence by the introduction rule for the universal quantifier, \(\forall P.(P(x) \leftrightarrow P(x))\) is valid. By the Leibniz Law of Identity, \(x=x\) is valid.


A major issue in programming is how to provide this notion.

x == y
boolean equals(Object that) {
  return this == that;
}




In affine logic we remove the option to duplicate assumptions as this can related to physical resources. In the stricter linear logic we further require the use of every assumption.

$! x.P(x) $ means “there exists exactly one x such that P(x) is valid”. This is a counting quantifier. It can be expressed in terms of the existential and universal quantifiers as follows:


In a classical logic, the uniqueness quantifier can be expressed as follows: \[
\exists ! x.P(x) \equiv \exists x.(P(x) \wedge \forall y.(P(y) \Rightarrow x=y))
\] In words, “there exists exactly one \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid” is equivalent to “there exists an \(x\) such that \(P(x)\) is valid and for all \(y\), if \(P(y)\) is valid then \(y\) must be equal to \(x\)”.



Meanwhile a rule like contraction clearly seems suspect in concepts like “have a USB port” or “have an egg” where counting seems crucial for the logic. A logic that cares about such counting is often called a “linear logic” (if it needs an exact match) or an “affine logic” (if it is upper bounded by a count). You can find in programming languages like Idris and Rust that allow for these logics. They are especially useful when we care to track that all our files are and memory are used and released as expected, and to boost the security guarantees of vulnerable software. It is hard to ease drop on data if you can only read it once.

The following Idris code shows how to specify that a value can only be used once. Hence the following fails because it used the value hasUSB twice because the preceeding number 1 instruct Idris to use that value exactly once.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner) -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB = hasUSB && hasUSB 
It also fails if you do not use the value at all.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner) 
                    -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB = false 
Idris is only happy if you use the inputs exactly once, so you need to give it to options. Each gets used exactly once and captures the idea of our logic.
canKeyAndMouse : (1 hasUSB : PortScanner,
                  1 hasOtherUSB : PortScanner)
                  -> Bool
canKeyAndMouse hasUSB hasOtherUSB = 
                    hasUSB && hasOtherUSB


Rust makes a similar idea practical with ownership. A value once used transfer ownership and in effect disappears and cannot be reused. This is why the following could would fail.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");
send_to_captain(data);
// Next line causes error; data moved.
send_to_criminal(data); 
Here is a safe use of data.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");
send_to_captain(data);
// Next line causes error; data moved.
send_to_criminal(data); 
Unlike Idris, Rust does not require you to use the value.
let data = String::from("Pa$$w0rd");  
// data never used, but that's ok

Though nothing should stop you from learning languages like Idris and Rust, this article should convince you firstly of valuable uses for different than expected logic. When your situation demands you can involve future study and coding assistants to select the programming language that supports your logic best.






In a context \(\Gamma\), given a predicate \(P(x)\), if every object \(c\) in the context \(\Gamma\) leads to \(P(c)\) being valid, \(\forall x.P(x)\) is valid. \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle universal\rangle & ::= \forall \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
&  (L_{\forall})
\\[5pt]
& \begin{array}{rl} \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\end{array}  
& (I_{\forall})\\[5pt]
& \begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\\ \Gamma & \vdash c \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash P(c)\end{array}
& (E_{\forall})\\
\end{aligned}
\]

In a context \(\Gamma\), given a predicate \(P(x)\), if there exists an object \(c\) in the context \(\Gamma\) that leads to \(P(c)\) being valid, \(\exists x.P(x)\) is valid. \[
\begin{aligned}
\langle existential\rangle & ::= \exists \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
&  (L_{\exists})
\\[5pt]
& \begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\end{array}  
& (I_{\exists})\\[5pt]
& \begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\\ \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash Q\end{array}
& (E_{\exists})\\
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
x=y & \equiv \forall P.(P(x) \leftrightarrow P(y)) &  (\text{Leibniz Law of Identity})\\[5pt]
\end{aligned}
\]



\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle counting\rangle & ::= !^{\langle \mathbb{N}\rangle} \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle \text{Predicate}\rangle\\
\frac{\Gamma, c_1,\ldots, c_n\vdash P(c_1),\ldots,P(c_n)}{\Gamma\vdash !^{\leq n} x.P(x)}(I_{!^n})\\
\exists ! \langle \text{variable}\rangle . \langle\text{Predicate}\rangle
\exists ! x.P(x) & \equiv \exists x.(P(x) \wedge \forall y.(P(y) \Rightarrow x=y)) &  (\text{Counting quantifier})\\
\end{aligned}
\]

\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\end{array}
\]
In software, a universal quantifier uses a computational judgement, hence evidence (data) must be produced for each \(P(x)\). In other words \(\forall x.P(x)\) in a Brouwerian judgment is synonymous with a function \(x\mapsto P\).

Notice the premise now has an unknown constant c which together with context leads to P(c). How do we come up with that? We do that through a mix of assumption (hypothesis, axioms, laws) and proofs. For example, a manager or a health inspector make a rule that all employees must wash their hands. Can they really know that this has always been obeyed? Perhaps not but in theory that is how it should work. Once we begin to work in practice or in computation we might find we need to relax our rules. We saw this already with AND where we derived new logic based on include partial truths. We can do the same with “for all” but in order that we call something a “for all” we should keep at least on feature that the theory exhibits. And that is the elimination rule.
For example, if we relax to accept that perhaps some employee neglects to wash their hands we should be within our rights to fire the employee and the health inspector can close the restaurant. When it comes to “for all” it is must important to protect the outcome that clean hands handle food than it is to protect the way introduce the law.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
5000 Years of Modern Computing
Dual logic and Programs
text:
Is a good idea is worth repeating? Well in math and logic once we have solved a problem we don’t really need to solve it again. Rather what we mean in this situation is that we can repeat the spirit of the idea but with some useful changes. The variation we want to explore here are when the roles of the arrows are all reversed behavior can occur in reverse as well. Think of this as swapping inputs with outputs, saving a file verses reading a file, opening a window verses closing a window, and so on. When we do that we are in effect swapping the elimination rules with the introduction rules of some data types. With logic that means for example to swap AND with OR, True with False, and many similar so-called dualities. It is often a strong way to get a new functionality without much new work. But sometimes these dualities actually uncover missing parts of the original problem which help us make a better understanding of the entire logic.

Recognize the diagrams of for all () and for some () as dual.

Notations

title: “There exists (())” as repeated ORs
text:
“There exists (())” as repeated ORs
A good idea is worth repeating. Just as we often want to make the repeated use of “AND” precise we also like the repeated use of OR in many arguments.
Andrew, Brenda, Carlos, Diego, Ehud, Fari, or Georgio must unload the truck.
The intent here is to gather all of these employees into a group any one of which would be enough to unload the truck. Once more to prevent changing the sentence every time employee’s change we invent a new logical operator.

Some employees must unload the truck.
There exists an employee that must unload the truck.

History has favored the word “exists” over “some” and other natural words for this logical operator and similar to the for all captured by an upside-down A, the “Exists” is capture by a reversed E, ().

 There Exists ()

 Language of “There exists”



LaTeX: universal::= . 


For example, (n.(2n=n+1)). Here the variable is (n) and the predicate is (2n=n+1). It is not necessary that the predicate actually depend on the variable, for example (n. (2+2=4)).


 Introduction Rule of “There exists”
In the logic of () the immutable rule is the introduction rule. That means that variations to adapt to other logics should only consider the operator a version of “exists” if that operator at least satisfies the “existence” introduction rule. How we use the existence is given room to be adapted. So if you had to invent your own introduction rule for “there exists” what would you need as a premise?
Perhaps you came up with the rule that to claim “existence” you have to have had evidence for it at some point. That evidence may be indirect, given to you by a trusted source that you cannot reveal, or completely open and obvious to others. But we cannot escape the need that in the context we had an instance of the property. In symbols we write this as follows.
(
\[\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash c \\ \Gamma & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \exists x. P(x)\end{array}\]
)
In words:
If context () leads to a value c and context can validate P(c), then context can claim that there exists x for which P(x) holds.


 Elimination Rule for “There Exists”
The way we use “there exists” is similar to disjunctive dilimma (OR) in that we cannot really predict how a claim of existence will be used so what we really mean is that whatever follows from any one witness should be enough to satisfy the resulting logic. For example, if a manager knows (x.P(x))=“Some employee will unload the truck”, and they know that having the truck unloaded (P(c)) by any employee c means then can begin serving food (Q), then they can begin serving food having no concern as to which particular employee unloads the truck. We gather this into the following rule.
(
\[\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \exists x.P(x)\\ \Gamma, c, P(c) & \vdash Q\\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash Q\end{array}\]
)

title: Necessary (), Possible () and Modal Logic
text:
Necessary (), Possible () and Modal Logic
The logical operator (,, , , ) have experienced nearly 200 years of use and have had time to seep into mathematics. In fact mathematics is somewhat unaware of most of the logical operators have been invented in the last century preferring to contrive all situations into tortured exhibitions of those symbols alone—a project known as “Logicism” which was shown to be impossible in the 1930s. But we are not mathematicians, we are mathematicians that want to compute and the means we will pay attention to progress in the rest of the world of logic. Of the many topics that have had substantial gain for logic arguably Modal Logic has been the most important. This is a logic that admits that reasoning often depends on the mode in which we find the question. Change the mode and you change the reasoning. The two major operators we will survey from this form of logic are obvious to natural language: necessary () and possible ().
I love this type of logic but every video I ever made about it pales when compared to Attic Philosophy. So we are in for a treat today as we watch a true expert bring us the goods.
YouTube video player

 Necessary () & Possibly ()
The basic of “necessary” is to clarify if a claim is true in all modes. This might sound like a variation on () except that unlike (), “necessary” () does not depend on a variable. It rather qualifies an entire sentence. Here is an comparison

You need to login to use your bank software.
For every user, there is a login process to get to the bank software.

While there is a relationship between these two sentences, the first expresses in a clear way that the intent is to enforce security. The second merely explains that security is available to everyone. These are not the same logic.

 Language of For All
\[\langle necessary\rangle ::= \Box \langle\text{Sentence}\rangle\]
\[\langle necessary\rangle ::= \diamond \langle\text{Sentence}\rangle\]
For example, ((x)((1/x) is defined) “It is necessary that (x) for (1/x) to be defined”. Programs are often filled with logic of this sort with annotations or documentation that declare what is necessary. Here is one such example.
function div(m,n) @assert n != 0; return m/n end function


 Semantics of Necessity
While syntax drives many operators, necessity is best explored first by its semantics. We do with through what is known as possible worlds. We list all the modes that our logic will consider treating each as a “world”. For example, a company may provide access to its files in several ways as illustrated.



Screenshot 2026-01-24 at 4.12.51 PM.png


Here are some of the semantics we can read from this chart

It is possible to reach common data (C) from mobile phone M, written ((MC)).
It is necessary to be in the office to reach storage files F ((OF))
It is possible to reach sensitive data (S) from mobile phone M, but only if we go through the app. Depending on your context you might not care that it takes two steps and write simply ((MS)) but if you do care about the steps you might be more verbose with (((MA)S), the extra necessity makes it clear that while mobile can get to sensitive data it is necessary that it does that through the app.

Possible World Semantics are substantial improvement over traditional “true-false” logic because we can often express the complexity of real life with diagrams. When it comes to programming this stuff there are many tools, but the main one is known as “State Machine”. While there are small differences you can roughly equal “State Machine” with “Possible Worlds.”

title: “For All” () as repeated ANDs
text:
“For All” () as repeated ANDs
Once more we can look to natural language to get a hint about what logical operators we will find useful. Think of giving out the same instruction to an ever growing list of employees:
Andrew, Brenda, Carlos, Diego, Ehud, Fari, and Georgio must wash their hands before preparing food.
There a number of disadvantages to this approach. For one thing we are letting natural language get away with some imprecise form. Notice there is only one use of the word AND yet the Language of AND works in pairs <this> AND <that>. So the proper form would need us to pair up the instructions for which we invent parentheses
( (Andrew AND (Brenda AND Carlos)) AND (Diego AND (Ehud AND Fari) ) AND Georgio must wash their hands before preparing food.
Of course this is one of many ways we could pair up the AND’s without actually making the logic any easier to explain.
Since logic is invented by humans for human use it makes sense to create a version of AND which is much more forgiving about repeated use. This would allow us to get the idea into a precise language we could use in reasoning and making future programs. What should this “repeated AND” be called? Pause to think of how you might say the instructions in simpler way. Here are some options that come to my mind.

All employees must wash their hands before preparing food.
Each employee must wash their hands before preparing food.
Each and every employee must wash their hands before preparing food.

The natural languages we use on each other have many choices for style and emphasis. We can see the basic form is not working to avoid listing all the people. Instead it indexes them into a single category “Employee”. It states the rule they must obey “Wash hands” and then quantifies who in the employee list has this requirement: ALL/EACH/EVERY.

 For all
The logical operator “For all” is denoted () as an upside-down letter “A” (for “All”). To express it we follow the L.I.E.

 Language of For All



LaTeX: universal::= . 


For example, (n.(n<n+1)). Here the variable is (n) and the predicate is (n<n+1). It is not necessary that the predicate actually depend on the variable, for example (n. (2+2=4)).


 Elimination of For All
We have not forgotten how to spell LIE but we are skipping ahead to the elimination rule because this is what truly organizes what “for all” does. When the manager asserts that “All employees wash their hands!” the meaning is found by applying this claim to any single employee. For example this means “Brenda must wash her hands!” And a new employee “Henri must wash his hands!” Notice the application no longer features “All” nor a variable “employee”. Thus it is an elimination of the structure of the operator. We write it like this:
(
\[\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\\ \Gamma & \vdash c \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash P(c)\end{array}\]
)
In words:
If context () leads to “For all x, P(x) is valid” and context also leads to a value c for x, then P(c) must hold.”


 Introduction Rule for For All
Now that we know how to use the “for all” operator we can guess what we need to know to discover an example of a “for all” operator. Basically we need to reverse what we want as a conclusion. We need to know that if context can make any constant value c for x lead to P(c) being valid, then context is saying P(x) is valid “for all x”.
(
\[\begin{array}{rl} \Gamma, c & \vdash P(c) \\ \hline \Gamma & \vdash \forall x.P(x)\end{array}\]
)
Notice the premise now has an unknown constant c which together with context leads to P(c). How do we come up with that? We do that through a mix of assumption (hypothesis, axioms, laws) and proofs. For example, a manager or a health inspector make a rule that all employees must wash their hands. Can they really know that this has always been obeyed? Perhaps not but in theory that is how it should work. Once we begin to work in practice or in computation we might find we need to relax our rules. We saw this already with AND where we derived new logic based on include partial truths. We can do the same with “for all” but in order that we call something a “for all” we should keep at least on feature that the theory exhibits. And that is the elimination rule.
For example, if we relax to accept that perhaps some employee neglects to wash their hands we should be within our rights to fire the employee and the health inspector can close the restaurant. When it comes to “for all” it is must important to protect the outcome that clean hands handle food than it is to protect the way introduce the law.


 Relaxing Notation
Finally as you talk to people and different programming problems you may find that the language of “for all” can slip into an incorrect style. We might say “2n is even, for every integer n”. That is strictly speaking the wrong form and it can lead to unfortunate confusion. But on the other hand insisting that everyone keep to precise grammar makes conversations boring and artificial. Use your judgement. If the meaning is confused then change it. But if there is little risk for confusion be relaxed with the ways that other around you might slightly break these rules.

title: A Library of Logic
text:
Public domain, Wikimedia Commons


To plan a computation you need the right logic, like the rules of a game. If you encounter a board with 8 x 8 alternating squares perhaps you mean to play chess or perhaps checkers. In a game of checkers, pieces can jump each other but in chess some pieces like pawns cannot move through obstacles. This does not upset anyone because the rules of each game are specific to that world. It is the same way with reasoning. There is no hard rule that can never be broken. Between different logics we get different answers. What unifies our reasoning is that some rules get used in similar ways from one situation to the next, not unlike how games fit into genres (role play, games of total chance, games of strategy, action games and so on). Once you play enough games of one kind you get faster and better at games with similar rules. Likewise, all you need to be successful at reasoning is to know how to learn the rules of each game and to choose games, I mean logics, you know and enjoy.

title: Curry-Howard-Lambek Correspondence
text:
Recall we opened these articles with a discussion of dividing 541 tiles into rows of 101 tiles each. This lead us to uncover a relationship between proofs, programs, and diagrams. In this article we will switch out the use of precise numbers and start to work towards a more precise translation between the sorts of proofs, programs, and diagrams we see with a simple division algorithm.


Perhaps the most important point of the experiment was to clarify the aim. Notice that we ended with two claims that both had to be true at once. The first was that \(541=5\cdot 101 + 36\), which reflects the idea that we keep track of all the tiles. The second was that \(36 < 101\) which reflected the goal of tiling as many rows as possible. One of the most important lessons in solving a problem is to actually state clearly what problem you aim to solve. Let us do that now, but with \(m\) tiles placed in rows of \(n\) tiles each.

Claim. When counting with natural numbers \(0,1,2,...\), if we are given \(m\) and \(n>0\), then there exists natural numbers \(q\) and \(r\) such that \[
m = qn + r \text{ and } r < n.
\]

Notice the mathematics has forced us to express many unsaid but important facts. We only want to talk about counting numbers, what mathematics calls natural numbers. So we won’t be seeing a remainder of say \(2.3\) or \(\sqrt{\pi}\). Second, we have separated clearly the result from the method used to justify it. There is no discussion here of the steps we performed. So why should anyone believe our claim? To convince them we next include what mathematics calls a proof, an argument that convinces our audience.

Proof. We proceed by considering the number of tiles \(m\) and the number of tiles per row \(n\). We repeatedly subtract \(n\) from \(m\) until the remaining number of tiles is less than \(n\). The number of times we subtracted \(n\) is the quotient \(q\), and the remaining number of tiles is the remainder \(r\). By construction, we have \[
m = qn + r \text{ and } r < n,
\] which completes the proof.

If we now stand back and think of \(m\) tiles stretched in rows of length \(n\) we can see this method will find \(q\) rows with a remainder \(r<n\) of left over or rejected tiles where \[
m=qn+r\text{ and }r<n.
\]
This is the a complete solution but the specifics were never the point. Lets inspect how we solved it. Perhaps the most important point was to know what we accomplished. Notice when we concluded we had two terms: the quotient \(q\) and the remainder \(r\). Saying those words meant \(541 = 5\cdot 101 + 36\) and \(36 < 101\). What we did was prove this
There were two phases. One was a step in which we were forced to stop, when the tiles remaining are too few. We call this a base case. The second situation, called a recursive case, is when we have enough tiles to complete a full row. We take that away from the tiles we had and start the problem all over with new numbers. This is programming strategy called a recursion. In fact the specific mix of recursion here is so special it has a nickname called a loop.
Many a programmer has been helped by seeing this in a diagram known to many as a flow-chart, though others have suggested the name string diagram. We read a flow chart as system of pipes that moves the data from each node to the next in the direction of the arrows. Each node does something to the data as described inside the label. A label on an edge acts like a filter. So if the data does not match the filter then you cannot move your data through that arrow. The name “loop” may make more sense when we review the shape of the flow-chart.

Flow-Chart as Visual LanguageFlow-Chart as a Written Language



---
title: Dividing m tiles into n tiles per row.
---
flowchart TD 
    %% Nodes
    Start[q=0, r=m]
    Ask{Is r less than n?}
    Yes[Stop]
    No[Replace r with r-n]
    Update[Increment q by 1]
    %% Arrows
    Start --> Ask
    Ask -->|True| Yes
    Ask -->|False| No
    No --> Update
    Update --> Ask

Remark. A flow-chart need not be thought of as picture. In fact the picture is intentionally meant to allow for a lot of variability. You can move a node around for example without interrupting the flow. So the flow-chart is actually the collection of relationships and their labels. So it is a language which might be written in words, spoken allowed, or drawn in pictures.
For example, in the second table we record the same flow-chart by list in words and symbols all the nodes, arrows, and labels. For instance Start[q=0, r=m] represents a starting node with label “q=0, r=m”. In another line Ask -->|True| Yes represents an arrow from the “Ask” node to the “Yes” node with the label “True”.
Our examples includes a few technical terms like flowchart TD and is wrapped by the symbols ```. Those are details that allow our computer to interpret our diagram language and create the picture shown in the first tab. The specific technology we chose was Mermaid. Learning a graphical language like this can be useful when changing designs as well as in sharing concepts with anyone who cannot see your screen. It is also enormously helpful when inputting a diagram to a chatbot or AI assistant.





To wrap up, we saw three ways to think of division:

A Proof: an argument to confirm the division is possible.
A Program: as a list of steps to carry out division.
A Diagram: a language (often visual) to express division in steps.

Each way to think is as good as the next but each seems to emphasize our understanding differently.




Now that we have an algorithm to divide we should ask what were the Babylonian clay tables, for since it did not appear in anything we just described.
You might discover that you get faster if you can build on what you already have computed before. For example, suppose the day before you had already laid 440 tiles 101 tiles wide and you left your self a memo, reminding you that this wall stood 4 rows high with 36 remaining tiles. Together that means: \[
440 = 4\cdot 101 + 36 \quad \text{and} \quad 36<101.
\] So you from your memo you could work back to today’s problem by adding back the 101 for the first row you placed down to get: \[
\begin{aligned}
541 & = 101+440  = 101 + 4\cdot 101 + 36, & 36 \lt 101\\
541 & = 5\cdot 101 + 36, & 36 \lt 101.
\end{aligned}
\] So we can tile 5 rows high with 36 tiles remaining. The real savings here is the ability wall off (:eye_roll:) steps and solve them independently. That way if you have more than one way to solve it you can simply choose the solution you find most efficient. By invoking the previous day’s lesson of dividing \(440\) tiles by \(101\), we save time and effort in solving the current problem.
If we wanted to emphasize the steps instead of the outcomes we could put these in a diagram where events lead from one state to another. State here is a term used to mean where everything is, for example, “my house is in such a messy state” is a way to saying the items in your home our not where they belong. The state in our division problem refers to all our numbers and equations.

flowchart TD

    D["541=(1+4)*101+36"]

    C -->|increment q=4, keep r=36| D

    classDef greenNode fill:HoneyDew,stroke:ForestGreen,color:ForestGreen,stroke-width:2px

The Babylonian clay tablets are their memos for division. To use them you first subtract the denominator from your numerator until you find the ratio on the clay table memo which has recorded with it the division result for that pair. You then take that known result and add back what you subtracted to get your answer. In our example \(541/101\) was reduced to \(440/101\) which had a memo \(4+36/101\). As we subtracted only \(1\) denominator we now add it back to get \(541/101=1+4+36/101=5+36/101\).
Programming where you save facts as memos to speed up future work is called memoization, closely related to memorization though the latter is the word that captures all the different tricks, mnemonics, and repetition techniques humans use to recall information.
If you followed all of this then you indeed know how to divide with remainder. What matters now is to explain this without specific numbers but in preparation for any future possible choices. As simple as that sounds we might find doing it forces is to be much more explicit about what some of the ideas of tiling really meant. Let us go through this in three different ways.


If we had \(m\) tiles to place in rows of length \(n\), if \(m<n\) we cannot even get started. We can diagram that step in the process like this.




Proof

Diagram

Program





As \(m\lt n\) it follows that \(m=0\cdot n + m\) with \(m\lt n\). So use \(q=0\) and \(r=m\).

\] So \(1+q\) and \(r\) solve the division problem for \(m\) and \(n\).

We now tie the two strategies together by considering both cases.

ProofCommutative DiagramProgram


Claim. For any non-negative integers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(n>0\), there are integers \(q\) and \(r\) such that \(m=qn+r\) and \(0 \le r < n\).
Proof. If \(m\lt n\) then

\(m=0\cdot n+m \lt n\); so, use \(q=0\) and \(r=m\).

Otherwise,

 Take \(k=m-n\). As \(n>0\), it follows that \(m\gt k\). Hence, division of \(k\) by \(n\) is a smaller problem which we assume was previously solved. So take \(k=q\cdot n+r\) with \(r\lt n\). Add \(n\) to both sides and factor: \[
m = n+ k  = n+qn + r  = (1+q)n + r
\] So \(1+q\) and \(r\) solve the division problem for \(m\) and \(n\).

\(\Box\)


In this complex diagram any two paths with the same start and end points represent equal results. We call this a commutative diagram. Like a bike ride from you home to the office, you can take different paths but the commutes are the same.

# Division Algorithm as a Python program
def div(m, n):
    if m < n:
        return 0, m
    else:
        k = m - n
        q, r = div(k, n)
        return 1+q, r
 
# Random test of the left side
m = random.randint(0, 100);  j = random.randint(0, 100)
n = m+j+1
@assert div(m,n) == (0, m)
 
# Random test of the right side
n = random.randint(0, 100);  k = random.randint(0, 100)
m = n + k
q, r = div(n, n)
@assert div(n+k, n) == (1+q, r)








You must be asking yourself how reading about division using a tiles is going to prepare you to work with Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, or anything else modern.
First a social point. Babylonians were a society that built giant pyramids called ziggurats, fountains, gardens, predicted eclipses well into the future, and yes tiled marvelous gates still on display today. So having division on the mind is not a sign of intellectual weakness. Often difficult concepts arise amongst simpler ones and offer a less threatening path to get to the hard stuff.  We will touch on many state-of-the-art topics in mathematics, computation, and data science. Yet, I will prefer simple setups so that anyone can participate. You never know when you might need to explain what you are planning to a client, a boss, a coworker, a loved one who wants to connect with what you do, or a young person learning from you. These stories are for them.

Now for the scientific merit. We are free to interpret division as a program, perhaps to lay tiles, but also repurposed to for any use of a quotient and remainder. At the same time it was a proof that natural numbers \(m\) and \(n\neq 0\) can always be related by \(m=q\cdot n+r\) with \(0\le r<n\). Lastly there was a diagram which served as a language to often more precise than natural speech and writing, to present division and the composition of a bunch of smaller believable claims or steps. So division, as presented, is equal parts a program, a proof, and a logic. Division is not alone in this relationship.

Curry-Howard-Lambek Correspondence. Precise proofs, working programs, and commutative diagrams are interchangeable.

These articles are an exploitation of this correspondence. Sometimes a proof will seem more obvious than its program. Other times a program is where we start. Often there is a diagram that explains both better. That logic does not see these as different just means you are entitled to use anyone of them to get started and transfer the impacts to the others. When we are lucky the correspondences go back-and-forth in reinforcing cycles.
I once discussed this concept with a fellow mathematician who replied:


This is either profound or wrong! :eye_roll:

–Anonymous colleague of the Hausdorff Institute for Mathematics.

I warn you now that it wont be my purpose to defend this correspondence to the extent that the three names authors have. You can take up later study, follow the many scholar before and after that contribute to its evolving meaning, and perhaps uncover questions that remain unanswered. These articles will focus instead on the impacts of the correspondence.
