title: Proofs, Programs, and Diagrams
text:
division
Of course today we have apps and devices that do all this for us and increasingly Artificial Intelligence (AI) is taking on many more complex chores. Looking back at something this old and familiar gives a predictable occurrence of a pattern that underpins why AI is not only possible, but inevitable, and on the whole not that mysterious. It is the start of the Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence that links mathematical proofs, computer programs, and the linguistics of diagrams.
Math, computation, and language play very different roles in our lives. Math gives us guarantees. Computation accesses answers our minds are too slow and imprecise to ever achieve. Language, well that’s what we use to spread our questions and answers, communication. So if they are interchangeable then perhaps it is no longer a surprise that a machine can talk to us like we talk to people while also providing certainty and efficiency. It is not all of language that is equal to computation, just the small sliver that relates to diagrams. Humans appear to have a substantial extension of language beyond diagrams so we probably have more to say than computation ever will. Yet, the power to relate these three achievements of our species surprises many to the point of seeming unbelievable. To see how it came to be known we can start with the story of division.

title: Proofs, Programs, and Diagrams
text:
Division by repeated tiling
Suppose we have \(541\) tiles and we need to make a wall that is \(60\) tiles wide. The problem is that 2-3 tiles per row break or do not match and cannot be used. How many rows can we expect to tile?
You could answer this by putting down your first \(60\) tiles leaving \(541-60=481\) tiles.

Then we repeat until there are fewer than \(60\) tiles. The steps would be   Wait a moment! This is getting repetitive and tedious. But then you remember that yesterday you had the same problem but instead of \(541\) tiles you had \(361\) tiles. So you can skip repeating your work and just look up the work you did yesterday. \(361\) tiles over rows of \(60\) gave you 6 rows with 1 tile left over. That is, \[
361 = 6\cdot 60 + 1\text{ and } 1 < 60
\] Or to use common terminology, \(361/60=6\text{ remainder }1\) which in fraction form is: \[
\frac{361}{60} = 6 + \frac{1}{60}\text{ i.e.: `` }6\text{ and }\frac{1}{60}\text{ ''}.
\] Since you got to this number by subtracting 60 away 3 times, you can just add 60 back in 3 times. \[
541 = 3\cdot 60 + 361 = 3\cdot 60 + 6\cdot 60 + 1= 9\cdot 60 + 1.
\] In other words, \[
\frac{541}{60} = 9 + \frac{1}{60}\text{ i.e.: `` }9\text{ and }\frac{1}{60}\text{ ''}.
\] Assuming we reject 3 tiles per row for a total of \(9\cdot 3=27\not\leq 1\) we likely will not have a enough remaining tiles to make all 9 rows. We should get a few extra tiles or stop at 8 rows.

Probably you can imagine this working with \(m\) tiles spread out \(n\) tiles wide. The goal would be to predict the number of rows \(q\) and the number of tiles \(r\) left over such that \[
m = q\cdot n + r \text{ and } 0 \le r < n.
\] Despite the low-tech brick-layer story, a surprising amount of mathematics and programming has occurred here which might be better expressed by diagramming the stages. Think of the diagram as a system of pipes with filters. Material or data can flow from one shape to the next along the direction of the arrow so long as it matches the conditions of the label. Once we arrive at a shape we follow the instruction of the shape’s label before continuing. If you are unable to see the diagram you can select the source option which reads out the shapes and arrows and their labels.
---
title: Dividing m tiles into n tiles per row.
---
flowchart TD 
    %% Nodes
    Start[q=0, r=m]
    First_Question{Is r less than n?}
    First_Yes[Stop]
    First_No_Second_Question{Already know r = q' n + r' with r' < n?}
    Second_Yes[Set q to q+q', r to r']
    Stop[Stop]
    Second_No[Replace r with r-n]
    Update[Increase q by 1]
    %% Arrows
    Start --> First_Question
    First_Question -->|True| First_Yes
    First_Question -->|False| First_No_Second_Question
    First_No_Second_Question -->|True| Second_Yes
    First_No_Second_Question -->|False| Second_No
    Second_No --> Update
    Update --> First_Question
    Second_Yes --> Stop
    %% Optional colors and shapes
    classDef stopNode fill:FireBrick,stroke:DarkRed,color:white,stroke-width:2px
    class First_Yes,Stop stopNode

 Are flow-charts pictures?
A flow-chart need not be thought of as picture. In fact the picture is intentionally meant to allow for a lot of variability. You can move a node in a flow-chart to another location without interrupting the flow. So the flow-chart is actually the collection of relationships and their labels. So it is a language which might be written in words, spoken allowed, or drawn in pictures.
In fact, in our example we gave two ways to record the information in the flow-chart. The first was as a visualization of nodes and arrows. The second option just writes in words what the relationships are. For instance Start[q=0, r=m] represents a starting node with label “q=0, r=m”. In another line First_Question -->|True| First_Yes represents an arrow from the the first question node to the the first yes answer if the the first question was found to be true.
Our example source includes a few technical terms like flowchart TD and is wrapped by the symbols ```. That allowed our computer to interpret our diagram language and create the picture shown in the first tab. The specific technology we chose was Mermaid for Markdown. Learning a graphical language like this can be useful when changing designs as well as in sharing concepts with anyone who cannot see your screen. It is also enormously helpful when inputting a diagram to a chatbot or AI assistant.







ImportantDiagrams are not pictures



In these articles the word “diagram” will be meant in the broad sense of a chart, plan, or scheme. So while many diagrams can be given as visualizations, all our concepts of diagrams will be completely accurate when presented as words or programs.




 What was on the clay tablets?
Instead of remembering the work we did yesterday we could leave a memo to ourselves and anyone else of all the previous days’ divisions. This is essentially what was recorded on the clay tablets. The process of division was then to reduce the problem until we could find a memo which matched. If we never found a previous day’s division to match, well then the algorithm would continue reducing the remaining tiles until there were not enough tiles for a new row. The type of process is known as memoization (not to be confused with memorization which is the human process of recalling information).

title: Proofs, Programs, and Diagrams
section: Division was never the point, the Curry-Howard-Lambeck correspondence was.
text:
Division was never the point, the Curry-Howard-Lambeck correspondence was.
Now pause, ignore the task, and ask yourself what exactly did we just write down in our division task?
One perspective is that we gave a list of steps to follow, a program for tiling, which results in writing down two numbers which we name quotient (number of rows) and remainder. Another perspective might argue that we started out being asked for a quotient and remainder, and we simply wrote down a proof that we could find them. Another reader might argue that the diagrams (either the progression of tiling or the flow-chart) were the main communication tool. The interchangeable perspective of proofs, programs, and diagrams when properly labeled and explained turn out to be a condition that is always present.

Curry-Howard-Lambek Correspondence. Proofs of mathematical claims, programs to compute results, and diagrams of relationships between data are interchangeable.

These articles are an exploitation and exploration of this correspondence. This discovery mergers mathematics, computation, and language. In some form this idea goes back to pre-history, but modern day credit is given to those who made it precise and clear. Haskell Curry (1900-1982) was a mathematician and computer scientist, William Howard (1926-2026) was a logician, and Joachim Lambek (1922-2014) a mathematician-linguist. By making this precise we now know that programs have the benefit of 5000 years of civilization’s progress. There is a very real sense that a talented programmer is doing the same work as a great mathematician, and that a carefully sketched business model is a type of computation and mathematics. To master even one of these areas is to master them all, a fact that should humble the arrogant and embolden the timid.
Taken seriously, the Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence means that programming is not a recent invention of the digital age. Since proofs count as programs, all of Euclid’s Elements could be seen as programs. That is a much richer history than you might have expected if you looked simply at the programming section of a library. This fact is reinforced by other recent observations. Famously Alan Turing clarified that all computations behave by fixed rules of computation, the rules of what today we call a Universal Turing Machine in his honor. Armed with that insight, Minsky, Malzek, and Lambek were able to show that those rules were already true of the simple abacus! Truthfully, computers in some form have existed for as long as we have recorded human writing. We just have faster ones today.

One of the places we are seeing the swiftest impact of this correspondence between math, computation, and language is in the field of Artificial Intelligence (AI), specifically Large Language Models (LLMs). Many of the major advance in AI are owed to Program Synthesis where a prompt in natural language gets converted into a mix of programs to run in a conventional programming environment and their results fed to mathematical proofs to test and verify. The Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence not only explains why this was possible, but predicts it was inevitable. These are three sides of the same triangle.

At the moment our statement of the Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence is too vaguely stated and runs the risk of being misrepresented in mystical terms. It is not a free lunch. It takes work to use all these concepts interchangeably without distorting the original intent. It reminds me of a conversation I once had on the topic with a fellow mathematician who replied:


This is either profound or wrong!

–Anonymous colleague of the Hausdorff Institute for Mathematics.

In the coming articles more details will be added to ensure that what we exploit is factual. Yet, I warn you now that it wont be my purpose to defend this correspondence to the extent that the three named authors have. You can take that up in followup studies. These articles will focus instead on the impacts of the correspondence in improving day-to-day problem solving with computation as a support.

title: Proofs, Programs, and Diagrams
text:
Summary

Division is a fact about integers, a program, and scheme relating addition and multiplication.
The Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence shows the division example is true of all proofs, programs, and diagrams.
This correspondence is a part prediction and part explanation for artificial intelligence.

title: Proofs, Programs, and Diagrams
section: Where to go next: Deductive, Inductive, and Abductive reasoning
text:
Where to go next: Deductive, Inductive, and Abductive reasoning
The logician Charles Sanders Peirce (1839-1914) laid out a spectrum for reasoning that still largely organizes the field today and which will serve as the first branches of this project.

Deductive Reasoning: to judge from the evidence.
Inductive Reasoning: to judge beyond the evidence.
Abductive Reasoning: to find the best hypothesis for the evidence.

title: Archetypes
text:
Archetypes and why I tell stories
You must be asking yourself how reading about division using a tiles is going to prepare you to work with Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, or anything else modern. After all, almost every programming language already lets you divide by typing m/n or m div n or with a button \(\div\). In fact an operation this basic would be etched into the silicon of modern micro-processors “chips”. So why even discuss division?
Firstly, the Babylonians built giant pyramids called ziggurats, fountains, gardens, predicted eclipses well into the future, and yes laid tile-bricks like those in marvelous Ishtar gates still on display thousands of years later. So having division on the mind is not a sign of intellectual weakness.

Secondly, be assured that these articles focus on many state-of-the-art topics in mathematics, computation, and data science. Examples like division are chosen as enduring examples, known as archetypes, which use stories of events that are so familiar they are easily personalized. Think for a moment about the same story but where we replace tiles with eggs in cartons, or the products manufactured in an assembly line. Production will be successful if it can fill the packaging with a remainder large enough to cover the expected number of rejects. Want a computer related story? Shift to discussing the transmission of a file in fixed-size packets with an expected error rate in the transmissions. The story of tiling is not one story, but a skeleton to retell your own way.
Always be prepared to give an account of what you know in the language your audience wants to know it. The first time might be in an interview that lands you the job. Later you can use that skill to get the trust of a boss or client. You may become a mentor or teacher. And finally we should not forget those friends and family who just want to connect with what we do. Surely it is up to the person who understands to make the larger effort to be understood. These stories are for others. Use them, personalize them, and you might find your own understanding deepened as well.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
systematically argue from your evidence.


Plan a computation with the right logic, like the rules of a game.




































Identify the logical notions in a context by focusing one does not change, like the flagpole not the flag.



Choose the right type for your data so that all the tools that use it are the best for the job.



Identify membership of data in subsets and create equivalence between members through partitions like membership categories.




systematically work beyond your evidence


Structure data and arguments around cases and patterns.



Use relations to convert data into new propositions.



Make efficient logical deductions using defaults, like assuming a bird can fly, and recover to errors using adaptive and dynamic logic.



Make informed guesses and measure the likelihood of a proposition.




Argue to the best hypothesis of your evidence


Identify the correct meaning of proximity so that your measurements get closer to the destination and do not wonder off course.



Create measurements so that the whole is the sum of its parts allowing it become a data feature and used in machine learning.



Project data to single numbers called “features” by treating features as integrals.



Machine learn by taking a shot at a feature, measure the error, and back propagate the correction through derivatives.

title: Avoiding technology?
text:
Having brought up AI and the inter-operability of proofs, programs, and diagrams; there may be some fears about how to compete with the speed and scale of a machine. To offer some perspective, let us close with a story where mathematics could not have been done without new technology. I don’t mean something with huge numbers and minute details where our life spans and fragile bodies are the problem. I mean problems which eventually humans managed to show could never be done no mater how long we or machines work. Perhaps you have heard of some of these “impossible” problems, such as

Trisecting angle: can you use a ruler and compass to divide any angle into thirds?
Squaring the circle: can you start with a circle and construct a square with the same area using only a ruler and compass.
Solving quintic equations: can you find a general solution for polynomial equations of degree five using radicals like \(\sqrt{x}\), \(\sqrt[3]{x}\), etc.?

At different stages in history these and many problems like them were brought up and found no solution. Only in the last 200 years have we found that the mathematics necessary to explain why they were not solvable. They were “unsolvable”. It is a beautiful story in human achievement to dream up problems that cannot be solved and to be able to prove that they cannot be solved. But that is not the story I want to tell.
Instead, I want to point out that life did not require that we only use a ruler and compass, nor that we limit ourselves to formulas that only involve \(n\)-th roots and arithmetic. We are far more creative species. And with that creativity we invented other tools. It turns out that if you draw an angle on paper there are simple rules to fold the angle into thirds! The limitation was the ruler and compass.
See for yourself and try it on your own angles.


And here is an interactive proof for why it works.
Angle Trisection with Origami (Tim Brzezinski’s GeoGebra demonstration of Hisashi Abe’s angle trisection fold.)


In fact, Archimedes had found a method to trisect an angle using a marked ruler and compass already in 200 BC. A similar fate befell the other “unsolvable” problems of antiquity. They were not actually “unsolvable” as problems so much as they were lessons that if you limit your toolbox you might get stuck.
Technology is not just about making things faster, cheaper, and more precise. Sometimes it is the switch between the impossible and the possible.


Speaking of not avoiding technology, there are some technologies today that seem to balance the changing needs of different software systems and the humans who make and maintain them. This includes diagram languages like Mermaid and minimal coding support like Markdown. No matter how smart or creative you are it means nothing if you cannot communicate!
Unlike Emily Dickinson—whose only serious technology was the ’Em-dash” —you face way too many options. You can change fonts, change colors, visualize a graph, embed video, sonify data, make a python demo, make a webpage, make an app, put a minimal working example on github and much much more. It is too much time not on task.
So what to do? My suggestion is to get familiar with some fast-production tools. Top of this list for me is “MarkDown”. It is a play on the name “MarkUP” which is the M in programming languages like HTML, MathML, XML (but not ML, OCaML, UML which have nothing to do with the web). The idea of “MarkDown” is to use low-use characters on your keyboard to the maximum effect.



There are numerous places you get started with Markdown. I will mention 2 options.

Web app (no install) StackEdit.io/app#
Install an IDE. If you don’t already have a favorite then start with VS code. Once installed add MarkDown previewer as a module from the library and you will have the swiss-army knife of coding experiences.







NoteMy Opinion



Students in computer science are often encouraged or required to use systems called VI/VIM or Emacs. There is a lot of history and some valid reasons. For example you might need to work on a network and not have access to your usual windows and buttons. But in reality those barriers are easily overcome and users tend to specialize in only one of VI/Emacs meaning that they have a 50/50 chance that they chose the right one for the future they face.
The reality is that VI/Emacs skill are more a source of pride & culture than actual functionality. I would encourage newcomers to begin with a full powered IDE such as VS Code. VS Code is open source, highly supported, has numerous tutorials and lets you both button push for the tasks you don’t yet know, and begin to use keyboard commands as you grow as programmer. If money is not issue an AI agent directed tool like Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, or GitHub Copilot can further accelerate your productivity.



Fastest guide I can find https://ashki23.github.io/markdown-latex.html
A slower guide the explains how it works https://www.markdownguide.org/getting-started/
A tutorial https://www.markdowntutorial.com/

title: Choosing a Logic
text:
Logical arguments play by rules, which is what makes people believe logical arguments. However, these rules change from context to context, much like the rules of a game. See for yourself.

Suppose you read the manual and find to facts:

“If you are an Administrator then you can add users.”
“If you are an Administrator then you can remove users.”

Logically, this is the same as the single sentence.

“If you are an Administrator then you can add and remove users.”


If you wanted to explain the reasoning you could give further examples, for instance replace (Administrator, Add User, Remove User) with (Teacher, Teach, Grade) or (Chef, Cook, Clean). To emphasize the logic we might also begin to strip away artifacts of language and leave the main content. \[
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{If Teacher} & \text{then} & \text{can Teach} \\
\text{If Teacher} & \text{then} & \text{can Grade} \\
\hline
\text{If Teacher} & \text{then} & \text{can Teach and Grade}
\end{array}
\qquad
\begin{array}{rcl}
\text{Chef} & \to & \text{cook} \\
\text{Chef} & \to & \text{clean} \\
\hline
\text{Chef} & \to & \text{cook and clean}
\end{array}
\] where \(\to\) reads as “implies” or “if … then …”. Mathematicians like to use \(\Rightarrow\) as well for that job but \(\to\) is the symbol used in logic and other sciences and our choice here too. Thinking like a mathematician you would soon give up on examples and replace their roles with variables \((A, B, C)\) and write the argument as \[
\tag{Rule of Implied Conjunction}
\begin{array}{rcl}
A & \to & B \\
A & \to & C \\
\hline
A & \to &  B \text{ and } C.
\end{array}
\] Congratulations, you have just found a rule of “formal logic”, formal here refers to “form”, i.e. shape of the argument, not that the argument needs cloth napkins and a top hat.
Now let us keep the form (shape) of the argument but change the topic. Notice your belief in this form of reasoning quickly vanishes.

On a laptop:

“If you have a USB port then you can connect a mouse.”
“If you have a USB port then you can connect a keyboard.”

However,

“It may not be true that if you have a USB port you can connect a mouse and a keyboard.”

Obviously you need two USB ports to connect both, and the hypothesis is only clear about having one.

It is striking that most human reasoning knows intuitively not to use the form of argument we used on example 1 with example 2. We could replicate the same experiment and replace (USB port, Mouse, Keyboard) with (Egg, Cookies, Brownies) or variaables (A, B, C) and had we begun with this example we would have instead derived a fallacy instead of a rule! \[
\tag{Fallacy of Implied Conjunction}
\begin{array}{rcl}
A & \to & B \\
A & \to & C \\
\hline
A & \not\to &  B \text{ and } C.
\end{array}
\] Note that in notation, a “strike through” such as \(\not \to\) (or \(\not\Rightarrow\)) of a symbol means it is not true, so the fallacy is that \(A\) does not lead to \(B\) and \(C\).


What we believe as logical depends very much on context. The rule of conjunction made sense for the topic of being an administrator but was fallacy of conjunction when dealing with resources. Both are used correctly in everyday reasoning but they seem to say the exact opposite beliefs. This is the entire point of this article: to make a convincing argument is to play by rules within an agreed to context. Like the rules of a video game which are not always the same from logic to logic. Each logic is a universe of its own. Play with enough logics and you might be quicker to pick up rules of a new one and you will also start to appreciate what it is you really like about the rules of your favorite game, I mean, logic.

Makes up a scenarios that the Rule of Implied Conjunction is true and another scenario where the Fallacy of Implied Conjunction is true. What are the differences between the two scenarios?

When you start to look for context you might not find it in an obvious place. Often, the context is implicit meaning no one bothered to tell you, so it must be dug up from experience and observation. Fortunately in computation we do a better job of signalling context explicitly often with keywords like import. But be warned about wildcards like * which often abbreviate explicit context leaving us to hunt amongst a lot of possible files.



When you play a playground game it matters to agree on the rules otherwise you might make a splendid play only to have your opponent accuse you of cheating. It is the same with math and computation. Python reads the task as a command to concatenate (glue together) the two lists into one. This is a versatile operation and you could imagine using it to make a lot of useful programs. Berzanson et. al.’s Julia observes the logic of adding the internal numbers, what is known as “vector addition”. That understanding tracks with centuries of mathematical and scientific uses. So there is a strong case to want that within programs instead. While we are hear lets mention that Julia’s strengths are speed and scientific computing libraries. title: Logical Judgments
text:
When we speak of reasoning we often ground our language in terms about “truth”. Philosophers still debate what this term should mean and obviously context helps considerably. We pickup the story after the philosophers. That is, we want to begin with the assumption that the meaning of truth and its possible values is already told to us and we now want to explore what we can do with that knowledge. Now it may seem the values of truth are obvious: “true” and “false”. Certainly that is the attitude of much of mathematics. Yet, that is a simplification that was rejected almost as soon as it was suggested.


A proposition is a statement that can be assigned a truth value. When it is assigned such a value we call that a judgement.




A judgement is Boolean if it is either “true” (\(\top\)) or “false” (\(\bot\)). The name is in honor of George Boole (1815-1864) who first demonstrated that logic could be studied in part as a form of arithmetic on two values. The Boolean values are often denoted as \(\mathsf{Prop}=\{\top, \bot\}\).






Warning



Classical mathematics uses Boolean judgement which means that all proposition are explicitly true or false and never both. Since mathematics is uninterested in things that are false it makes no sense (other than learning) to include proposition that are false. As such the custom has emerged in mathematics to use the word “Proposition” only for those statements judged as true. This is a local custom of the field and propositions as used elsewhere are permitted to take on any truth value.
This book will take the more general meaning of this word preferring terms like “Theorem” for true propositions.





A judgement is Popperian if it can be falsified. The name is in honor of Karl Popper (1902-1994) who emphasized that experiments can rule out a theory but not actually prove it. This means that statements that have not been falsified are left with no judgement. The existence of a disproof can be written as a short flowchart \[
P\overset{x}{\longrightarrow }\bot\text{ that is,  ``$x$ is evidence that $P$ leads to falsity''.}
\] So \(\mathsf{Prop}=\{x:P\to \bot\}\) is the context of all statements \(P\) that could be judged as false. The purpose of a scientific experiment is to find such an \(x\) and thus falsify the proposition. If no such \(x\) can be found then we gain confidence that \(P\) might be true.
Note that the opposite of false is unknown which is not the same as true in Popperian judgement. Let us try out some Popperian judgments.

Existing Proposition \(P\): Heavy objects fall faster than light objects.
Experiment/Data \(x\):

Hypothesize \(P\)
Drop a bag of bricks (heavy object) and a bag of feathers (light object) from a tall building.
Observe heavier object does not fall faster than light object.
Conclude that assuming \(P\) leads to a falsehood, in symbols \(x: P\to \bot\).


Notice if we had not assumed \(P\) then experiment \(x\) would not have created anything false. It would just have been a piece of data. To make a falsehood requires we hypothesis a proposition is true and then use that truth in combination with our experiment or other judgments to arrive at something we judge to be false. The precise conditions will be described in the later chapter on implications. For now let us agree there is a common-sense understanding of this argument and a skeptics concerns will be addressed in the future.

Proposition \(P\): \(2^{2^n}+1\) is prime.
Use a Popperian judgment to value this proposition as false and to describe your evidence \(x:P\to \bot\).

In mathematics which tries to be Boolean we would take the false result of this exercise as evidence to claim it is a “false proposition”. Mathematicians call these counter examples of a proposition. Notice however that the Popperian judgement is evidence based and merely gives some limits on where the proposition is true. So often the more exciting questions that develop from Popperian judgments are to ask “Where is the proposition true?”






NoteFermat Primes Question



Are there infinitely many primes of the form \(2^{2^n}+1\)?


The similar question for Galileo is the unproven proposition:

Galileo’s Proposition \(Q\): All objects fall at the same speed (in a vacuum).

Notice there is no experiment that can prove \(Q\) but every experiment that fails to falsify \(Q\) adds credence to the proposition. So Popperian judgment is one-sided.



Somewhat the opposite to Popperian judgments are judgments in the philosophy of L. E. J. Brouwer.
A judgement is Brouwerian if it can be verified. The name is in honor of Luitzen Egbertus Jan Brouwer (1881-1966) who saw mathematics as the study of proof, not truth. He advocated a judgement where proofs are the values of propositions instead of true and false.
Similar to Popper the proof is the data in \(\mathsf{Prop}\), only now the idea is to begin with the assumption that there is at least one thing that is true (truth \(\top\) itself) and from that find evidence to transform that truth in to a proof of \(P\). \] So \(\mathsf{Prop}=\{x:\top \to P\}\).

Let us compare a Boolean judgment with a Popperian and Brouwerian judgment.

Proposition \(P\): If \(n\) is an even natural number then \(n^2\) is also even.

In a Brouwerian judgment to claim this is true is to provide a proof.

To be even means we have evidence \(k\), a natural number, where \(n=2k\). From that we derive \[
n^2=(2k)^2=2(2k^2)
\] So we produced evidence \(2k^2\) that \(n^2\) is even. So from a truth, \(n=2k\), we derived another truth \(P:\) \(n^2\) is even.


Meanwhile a Boolean judgement forget about process and just assert if something is true or false. Since we have already proved it we can now just declare it is true.






NoteBoolean Judgment, i.e. Value



\(P\) is true.


In particular we have the following relationship.


If a proposition has a Brouwerian judgment of true then it has true in Boolean judgement.
If a proposition has a Popperian judgment of false then it has false in Boolean judgement.


Note that a theoretical judgment does not necessarily mean that we know it’s truth value. It just means truth values exists and it does not depend on any state.

Proposition The number of times that \(p\) and \(p+2\) are both prime is infinite.
Boolean Value? Unknown!

So when we think of truth we often resort to propositions in Brouwerian judgment and convert them to Boolean truth. Likewise if we think a Boolean proposition should be false, we just need to create an example and use Popperian judgment to show it is false.
when we think of falsity we often resort to propositions in Popperian judgment. So if we want to prove something is false in Boolean judgment we just need to create an example, a model where the proposition is false. Because that means there can never be a Brouwerian proof of it being true. Similarly if we want to prove something is true in Boolean judgment we just need to create a Brouwerian proof of it being true. Because that means there can never be a Popperian example of it being false.
Both Popperian and Brouwerian judgments emphasize just one side of the truth table (false for Popper and true for Brouwer). This does not make them incapable of judgments the other way, for example they may exhaust all other possibilities, but usually requires some context or assumptions to understand that there is an exhaustible list of options. So these judgments leave open the possibility of having one-sided propositions.



Engineers, lawyers and data scientist often work with judgments that are inconsistent. It could be that one sensor gives one reading and another a different reading,or a judge gets conflicting stories from witnesses, or that two copies of what are supposed to be the same data are just not equal. Have a judgement for that setting is crucial.
A judgment is Paraconsistent (“beyond consistent”) if it can be both true and false. These logics are older than Boolean but were rebuilt in with stricter structure in the 1900’s by several logicians includeing Newton da Costa (1929-2024), Stanisław Jaśkowski (1906-1965), and Lotfi Zadeh (1921-2017). There are many variations.

\(\mathsf{Prop}=\{\top, +, \bot\}\) (3-valued judgments of Kleene or Łukasiewicz) where \(+\) plays a role described with are “paradox” or “unknown” depending on the context.
\(\mathsf{Prop}=\{\top, \bot, \text{missing},\text{error}_1, \text{error}_2,\ldots\}\) where the extra values assume a role based on the definitions of an apparatus or programming language.
\(\mathsf{Prop}=\{ 0\leq \varepsilon\leq 1\}\) (fuzzy judgments) is a decimal value representing the degree of truth with \(1\) being absolutely true and \(0\) absolutely false. It is not uncommon to see the range shifted say to \(-1\leq \varepsilon\leq 1\) or \(-\infty\leq \varepsilon\leq \infty\). This shifts the arithmetic but not the intent of the judgment.

There are also variations which are one-sided such as discussing degrees of truth without degrees of falsity and vice-verse.

Proposition \(P\): A thermometer reading above a \(100^{\circ} F\) indicates a fever.
The thermometer is read three times with values \(99.2^{\circ} F\), \(100.4^{\circ} F\), and \(99.5^{\circ} F\).

In a three-valued logic we could judge \(P\) as \(+\) (both true and false) as it was true in one reading and false in others.

In a Fuzzy judgement we could assume there was a positive in 1/3 of the trials and report a 33% positive test.

text:

The Boolean values are often denoted as \(\mathsf{Prop}=\{\top, \bot\}\).

Classical mathematics uses Boolean judgement which means that all proposition are explicitly true or false and never both. Since mathematics is uninterested in things that are false it makes no sense (other than learning) to include proposition that are false. As such the custom has emerged in mathematics to use the word “Proposition” only for those statements judged as true. This is a local custom of the field and propositions as used elsewhere are permitted to take on any truth value.
This book will take the more general meaning of this word preferring terms like “Theorem” for true propositions.

text:

title: Trees: a source of unambiguous reasoning
text:
Now look at the examples of math and program parse diagrams and you will notice a difference to parsing of many natural languages: the graphs have only one path between any two nodes. This is such an important property that it has a name: trees.



A tree is a diagram of nodes and edges in which between any two nodes there is exactly one path that does not revisit a node.
A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a diagram of nodes and oriented edges in which we cannot go in circles following the direction of any arrows.


flowchart LR
    A --- B
    A --- C
    B --- D
    B --- E
    E --- C
In the graph above there are two different paths from A to E, the first through B and the second through C. So this is not a tree. But if we remove even one edge on one of these two paths then we get a tree. For example:
flowchart LR
    A --- B
    A --- C
    B --- D
    B --- E


When we add direction to the edges of a graph we can consider paths that only follow the arrows and so a graph which is not a tree can nevertheless become a directed acyclic graph (DAG) that is not a tree. For example:
flowchart LR
    A --> B
    A --> C
    B --> D
    B --> E
    E --> C


The non-redundant paths in a proper maze (one in which there are no alternate paths) form a tree.



Start to A, option to turn left or continue straight. From left curve around a wall to trap 1. Continuing straight to B. Option to turn right or continue straight. If right reach trap 2. Continue straight weaves around a corner to the exit.


flowchart LR
    Start --- a
    a --- Trap1["Trap 1"]
    a --- b
    b --- Trap2["Trap 2"]
    b --- End
Note that the non-redundant paths in an improper maze (one in which there can be alternate paths) form a DAG.

The point of trees is that they have unique paths so when we given instructions between two nodes these cannot be misinterpreted. So when it comes to understanding logic, if we can organize the grammar to only build trees then we are guaranteed that everyone who reads the logic in that grammar understands it the exact same way we meant it. No double meanings and no ambiguity can exist. This is a perfect property to have if we can get it. Fortunately context-free grammars do exactly that. The only missing element is to know where to begin reading nodes of the tree. So let us choose one node as the start.

A tree is rooted if we designate one node as the root and all edges are oriented away from the root. The root is the starting point of the tree and all other nodes are its descendants. The nodes furthest from the root are called leaves.


The parse diagram of a context-free grammar is a rooted tree. In particular when we parse a sentence in the language of a context-free grammar we always get the exact same diagram.
We call this now the parse tree or the abstract syntax tree (AST).


Draw the path tree of the following maze. Make sure to reach each deadend.





Trees have been so successful at organizing our intension with programs that they ought to be useful in organizing other forms of reasoning, including proofs of judgments. In fact, the Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence seems to make this a requirement. So what we do now is replace “parse trees” with “proof trees”. This process today goes by Natural Deduction and it is the backbone of most of modern mathematical logic.
Recall our earlier proof of the proposition

Theorem: If \(n\) is even then \(n^2\) is even.







NoteProof



To be even means we have evidence \(k\), a natural number, where \(n=2k\). From that we derive \[
n^2=(2k)^2=2(k\cdot 2\cdot k)
\] So we produced evidence \(j=k\cdot 2\cdot k\) that \(n^2\) is even. So from a truth, \(n=2k\), we derived another truth \(P:\) \(n^2\) is even.


As a diagram this proof is the following tree:
flowchart TD
    Premise1["n is even"] ---|evidence k| Result1["n=2k"]
    Premise2["m=ab"] ---|"Associative x(yz)=(xy)z"| Result2["m^2=a(bab)"]
    Result1 ---|sub m=n, a=2,b=k| Result3["n^2 = 2j"]
    Result2 ---|sub j=bab| Result3
    Result3 ---|definition| Result4["n^2 is even"]
By writing the proof as a tree we start to notice that we got information from context of natural numbers, such as the associative property of multiplication. The combination of events ends with the claim we want.

A proof by Natural Deduction is a whose diagram is a tree rooted at the conclusion. The leaves of the proof tree are called the premises and the internal nodes are called deductions.




In many forms of logic we are permitted to reuse a premise multiple times in a proof. You saw that in our earlier example of the properties of administrators who can both add and remove users. Yet it was not always true as we saw with resources like a USB port which can only be used by one device. Now when a judgment style is allowed to reuse a premise we often do not bother to track how many uses we make. The effect can be that within the writing of a proof we simply state the premise we use once and extract from it multiple facts. Strictly speaking this does not diagram as a tree. For example:
flowchart TD
    Premise["P"] -->|use 1| Result1["Q"]
    Premise -->|use 2| Result2["R"]
    Result1 -->|combine| Result3["S"]
    Result2 -->|combine| Result3
This is however a directed acyclic graph (DAG) since there is no cycle in the diagram. So the implicit assumption made by the author is that we are permitted to copy a premise for reuse. Doing so separates the DAG into a proof tree as required. Here’s the above DAG converted into a tree by copying the premise:
flowchart TD
    Premise1["P"] -->|use 1| Result1["Q"]
    Premise1Copy["P"] -->|use 2| Result2["R"]
    Result1 -->|combine| Result3["S"]
    Result2 -->|combine| Result3
This brings up the question of how important it is to insist on only one conclusion to a list of premises. If we have a lot of facts that follow why not simply list them all?
flowchart TD
    Premise["P"] -->|use 1| Result1["Q"]
    Premise -->|use 2| Result2["R"]
In reality this is a perfectly standard form of proof. Mathematics often follows a proof in natural deduction with “Corollaries” or “scholia” which are just terms meant to say that we extract a different consequence form the existing argument. Since the interpretation of DAG verses tree is immaterial to many systems of judgment this causes relatively little harm to clarity. Yet be on the look out for those judgments that consider the total number of uses of our premise. Some things do not last forever and there the reuse of a premise can be highly illogical.

Below is a proof of the Division Algorithm we created in our first topic. Draw the proof tree for this proof.

Theorem (Division Algorithm): For natural numbers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(n>0\) there exist unique integers \(q\) and \(r\) such that \(m=q\cdot n+r\) and \(0\le r<n\).


Proof: If \(m< n\) then take \(q=0\) and \(r=m\) so that \(m=0\cdot n+r\). Otherwise \(-n+m\) is smaller than \(m\) and there is a some memoized (previously found) \(q\) and \(r<n\) where \(-n+m=n\cdot q+r\). Add \(n\) to both sides so that \[
m=n+-n+m-n=n+n\cdot q+r=n\cdot (1+q)+r
\] So \(m=n\cdot q'+r\) with \(r< n\). \(\Box\)

If some step appears to use some fact you know from the context of natural numbers, e.g. \(n+n\cdot q=n\cdot (1+q)\), you may state it as a premise. These will indicate what hidden assumption this proof depends on. Often these offer clues for future inventions, such as inventing division of polynomials.
Warning If you involve support online you may fine a far more complicated answer than you are expected to use here. For example you make see \(\exists\) (“There exists”) and \(\wedge\) (“and”). While it is ok to use, consider replacing the symbols with words and seek an explanation that would make sense to your Babylonian tile setter as well.




It is not always obvious how to take a proof in words and turn it into a tree or DAG. You can remind yourself why this must by asking: what sense is there in going in circles in your proof? Unfortunately, even seasoned mathematicians are not always conscious that proofs are trees. Making things worse is the goal of many authors to introduce a flare to their writing of proofs reorganizing sentences, inserting digressions, and changing words just for variety. A surprisingly problematic unnecessary rule by many authors is to never start a sentence with a symbol. In implementing this rule many authors take to reordering the information of a proof, giving the conclusion before the premise or using a variable before telling readers it is a variable. It is not entirely whims of authors to blame. Proofs are written often a lines of text and if we consider a tree or DAG described row by row top to bottom we can see we are forced to fold information into pockets of our text not unlike the build of a maze.
The issues notwithstanding, knowing that proofs exist as trees suggests strategies to reorganize a proof once we have constructed it. We can diagram the tree and then organize the layout so that nearby connections remain together whenever possible. We can give diagrams as part of the proof when the connections get complicated. We can prune branches and give them as individual smaller trees (“refactoring”). So while flattening a tree into a linear discussion is never a clean job, avoid being a lazy author so that your proofs do not become a maze.




Trees are diagrams in which any two nodes have a unique path between them. They give unambiguous instructions.
Context-free grammars parse as trees while remaining capable of expressing formulas and programs.
Proofs, when organized by Natural Deduction are trees rooted in the conclusion and whose leaves are the premises.

This brings up the question of how important it is to insist on only one conclusion to a list of premises. If we have a lot of facts that follow why not simply list them all?
flowchart TD
    Premise["P"] -->|use 1| Result1["Q"]
    Premise -->|use 2| Result2["R"]
In reality this is a perfectly standard form of proof. Mathematics often follows a proof in natural deduction with “Corollaries” or “scholia” which are just terms meant to say that we extract a different consequence form the existing argument. Since the interpretation of DAG verses tree is immaterial to many systems of judgment this causes relatively little harm to clarity. Yet be on the look out for those judgments that consider the total number of uses of our premise. Some things do not last forever and there the reuse of a premise can be highly illogical.

Below is a proof of the Division Algorithm we created in our first topic. Draw the proof tree for this proof.

Theorem (Division Algorithm): For natural numbers \(m\) and \(n\) with \(n>0\) there exist unique integers \(q\) and \(r\) such that \(m=q\cdot n+r\) and \(0\le r<n\).


Proof: If \(m< n\) then take \(q=0\) and \(r=m\) so that \(m=0\cdot n+r\). Otherwise \(-n+m\) is smaller than \(m\) and there is a some memoized (previously found) \(q\) and \(r<n\) where \(-n+m=n\cdot q+r\). Add \(n\) to both sides so that \[
m=n+-n+m-n=n+n\cdot q+r=n\cdot (1+q)+r
\] So \(m=n\cdot q'+r\) with \(r< n\). \(\Box\)

If some step appears to use some fact you know from the context of natural numbers, e.g. \(n+n\cdot q=n\cdot (1+q)\), you may state it as a premise. These will indicate what hidden assumption this proof depends on. Often these offer clues for future inventions, such as inventing division of polynomials.

title: Trees: a source of unambiguous reasoning
text:
It is not always obvious how to take a proof in words and turn it into a tree or DAG. You can remind yourself why this must by asking: what sense is there in going in circles in your proof? Unfortunately, even seasoned mathematicians are not always conscious that proofs are trees. Making things worse is the goal of many authors to introduce a flare to their writing of proofs reorganizing sentences, inserting digressions, and changing words just for variety. A surprisingly problematic unnecessary rule by many authors is to never start a sentence with a symbol. In implementing this rule many authors take to reordering the information of a proof, giving the conclusion before the premise or using a variable before telling readers it is a variable. It is not entirely whims of authors to blame. Proofs are written often a lines of text and if we consider a tree or DAG described row by row top to bottom we can see we are forced to fold information into pockets of our text not unlike the build of a maze.
The issues notwithstanding, knowing that proofs exist as trees suggests strategies to reorganize a proof once we have constructed it. We can diagram the tree and then organize the layout so that nearby connections remain together whenever possible. We can give diagrams as part of the proof when the connections get complicated. We can prune branches and give them as individual smaller trees (“refactoring”). So while flattening a tree into a linear discussion is never a clean job, avoid being a lazy author so that your proofs do not become a maze.

title: Trees: a source of unambiguous reasoning
text:
Trees are diagrams in which any two nodes have a unique path between them. They give unambiguous instructions.
Context-free grammars parse as trees while remaining capable of expressing formulas and programs.
Proofs, when organized by Natural Deduction are trees rooted in the conclusion and whose leaves are the premises.

title: Gates, Combinators, and Turing and Kleene
text:
One idea that occurred to Schönfinkel and was explored extensively by Curry and Feys is to get rid of the use of variables entirely. Instead focus on a list of allowed operations that can be applied to data. When you think about computation you might realize variables are there as placeholders for data, but that in a physical machine those placeholders hold something, perhaps a voltage that is random, or a voltage that signals all 0s. If we used Turing’s vision of a machine reading paper tape, that tape could have no marks on it. Blanks are still data. So in the concept of a machine there are really no variables at all. Just data of one sort or another. So if a machine is to take on the rule of evaluation functions and it has no variables, then mathematics and computation ought to be describable without variables as well. Such a description of functions is as combinators but most people today will know them as gates and these are the gateway  between Software and Hardware. We can explore this with some examples.



In the Konstants restaraunts, \(K\) is the combinator. When followed by two pieces of data (which can be grouped in parentheses) it yields the first of the two ignoring the second.

K "Curry" "Fries" yields "Curry".
K 3 7 yields 3.
K (3 7) 5 yields 3 7. The parentheses around (3 7) forced us to treat that as one piece of data and so it was the first of the two pieces and thus returned.
Working from the outside in, K (K 3 7) 5 yields K 3 7 (the first term to the outermost \(K\)) which in turn yields 3.
Now working from the inside-out, K (K 3 7) 5 yields K 3 5 (the second \(K\) was applied first to 3 7) which still yields 3.


Viewed form the perspective of the second term, this is a constant function.

The identity combinator I is defined by I x yields x. It simply returns its argument unchanged.

It is worth acknowledging that we are using variables, \(x\), to talk about a system that avoids variables! Well to that we can remark two things. First the use of variables here has no concept of scope, free/bound, local/global. These are variables in their simplest “fill-in-the-blank” form we always felt was logical. Secondly, we can if we want simply use words to avoid the concept of variables. Instead of I x yields x we can say “A machine that outputs whatever it is given.” Brevity and history are the sole reasons to revert to variable language.



The game now is to list a number of combinators that can assist you in building a program. It may surprise you to learn how powerful K together with I can be. For example, the next exercise asks you to confirm that combining K and I is already enough to make a program that manages the concept of if a then b else c.

Let K be represent True and K I represent False (True and false are not something new, just names for K and K I). Next, define a new combinator IF by IF a b c = I a b c. Show that:

IF True 3 7 yields 3
IF False 3 7 yields 7

Because of this behavior, the IF combinator is usually called a conditional combinator and instead of IF a b c we write it:
if a then b else c

So far we chain together our combinators as lists, but once we make a clever little program like if-then-else we might want to compose it with other little programs without physically rewriting all the lines of instructions. We can do that with a combinator specially built to combine two programs into one and apply them in a specified order.

The \(S\) combinator (for Schonfinkle) is defined so that \(S~f~g~x\) yields \(f~x~(g~x)\). It allows us to apply a function to an argument and then apply another function to the same argument, combining the results.

S f g x yields f x (g x). S K K 3 yields K 3 (K 3) which in turn yields K 3 3 which finally yields 3.



Set B to be S (K S) K. Show that B f g x yields f (g x). That is, B behaves like the composition combinator, it applies the program f to the output of the program g.

When you think of the operations of combinators like K, I, and S it may strike you as highly mechanical. That is the right picture to have. And perhaps you are also convinced that in combination they begin to make a tiny bit of sophistication, such as if-then-else, counting, possibly more. Well in fact they can do everything any computer can do.

A system \(\mathcal{A}\) of gates that has gates S, K, and I where for any gates f,g,h

K f g yields f
I f yields f
S f g is always defined
S f g h yields f h (g h) when either is defined.

is capable of carrying out any computation that could be described by substitution of variables. In other words it is a universal computing system, what we call Turing Complete.

Notice the complete absence of substitution and variables so the trapped variable problem just does not exist in computations. Gone also is the requirement that we are secretly depending on infinity to get substitution to work. It was only ever a mistake in vague mathematics and the programming languages used to bridge humans to machines. Put another way, humans who can imagine a place for infinity are beyond what a machine can imagine for itself.

\(S~K~K~x\) yields \(x\). In this sense \(S~K~K\) behaves like the identity combinator \(I\).




Alan Turing is famous for having invented a description of computing that captures the notion of programming.






NoteTuring Complete



A Turing Machine is a model for a machine
A computer is Turing Complete if it can simulate all Turing Machines.




Unfortunately it is not the case that using just these three combinators S, K, and I is a fast way to write practical programs. For example we saw we do not really need I because we can get the same behavior as S K K. But doing three operations instead of one is silly. Modern day CPUs therefore boast over a thousand additional instructions (called applied combinators) and GPUs use a few hundred each designed to better use the time and energy we have to achieve a computation.
As another exercise you can invent counting, additions, binary numbers, decimal numbers and on and on. But those will be very slow. Instead you are better off adding many more combinators to your list to give yourself a solid start.

In the Intel x86 instruction set there is a command to add two numbers. ADD. It takes the next to terms and adds them.

ADD 3 7 yields 10.
Working from the inside-out, ADD (ADD 3 7) 5 yields ADD 10 5 which in turn yields 15.
Working from the outside in, ADD (ADD 3 7) 5 gets stuck! Based on work from the outside we have not yet computed ADD 3 7 and so the outside ADD is stuck waiting on that number before it can continue.

Notice how the ADD operation is not as straight-forward as the K and I or even the IF combinator in that ADD really only makes sense when followed by numbers. This is why it got stuck when working outside-in instead of inside-out. It is striking that something as basic as adding can run into trouble based purely on how we ask the question. To get unstuck we would need to go into the design of the hardware and rewrite the order of operations. This highlights the difference between pure combinators like \(K\) and applied combinators like ADD. This is what is known as an “Applied Combinator”.


A fixed-point combinator \(F\) is one where \(F~g\) yields \(g~(F~g)\). We call this a fixed-point because \(g\) applied to \(F~g\) yields the same result as \(F~g\) itself, so the “point” \(F~g\) is fixed. When introduced as an option for computation they give the programmer a way to have an operation applied to itself repeatedly in a process known as recursion. That is an essential power in modern programming so the ability to create such a combinator (or gate) is highly valuable. The mathematician Alanzo Church (1903-1995) found one such operator he called \(Y\) and Alan Turing (1912-1954) discovered another called \(\Theta\).

There is a tech incubator launched in 2005 called the “Y Combinator” which also hosts “Hacker News”, a website dedicated to articles and announcements on cutting edge technology.






Many readers stop at “Turing Complete” and missunderstand this to mean every computer, given enough time and energy, can do all computations. This is misleading. Think of the job of a sound amplifier. Sounds waves are analog signals which means they use decimal numbers like \(\pi/4\) and \(\sqrt{2}/2\) which are both numbers that use an infinite number of decimal places. The amplifier does not seem to care. It takes in the signal and makes a new signal (also of infinite decimal places) that is louder. It is not possible to explain this simple task using finite strings and substitution rules on a Turing Machine. And yet, clearly sound amplifiers perform their operations without trouble.
It is not only discrete versus analog that seems to separate levels of computing. Increasingly studies of brains and neural networks in cognitive science suggest to researchers that thinking in liveing organisms is not well described by Turing Machines. The subject of realizibility now explores that frontier. If that were not enough, not long after Turing’s work, the mathematician/logician Kleene discovered mathematical consequences that force their to be more computing models beyond what Turing had imagined. While it might have been guessed that Kleene’s higher computing models would also be interchangeable like Turing’s, that turned out to be false. When it comes to computing in its full generality, there really isn’t one computer to rule them all. It is only the most basic level of computing that is interchangeable.









NoteKleene’s need for higher computing



Kleene’s goal was to explain how it is possible to have a claim such as

Proposition P: “There exists a number with some a fixed property.”

where \(P\) is true but doesn’t have a proof. That may sound impossible. Obviously if you have specific value \(c\) that works, then you just have the you, or a computer, return \(c\) as evidence for that property. It seemed that was the only way for such a proposition to be true. However, years earlier a mathemitician Hilbert had made a lot of claims about points existing in geometry that seemed to give no process to explaining what the point even was. And a few years later, the mathematician/logician Godel had shown that in any sufficiently robust theory (such as natural numbers, what we call “PA” for Peano Arithmetic) there are some properties \(P\) which are true but are impossible to prove. Put together in the right way this mean there are some claims of the form “there exists a number \(x\) with property \(P\)” that are true but have knowable value \(c\) for which \(P(c)\) holds. Weird for sure, but lets not follow that tangent.
What Kleene realized is that a proof is just a computation (back to our Curry-Howard-Lambek correspondence). And there is a way to turn anything that is true but not provable into something provable by moving to a more specific logic, “Con(PA)” in the case of natural numbers. So knowing that there is a logic that can prove the previously unprovable claim, there should be a computing model that can compute it. So Kleene built it.
Note, once you build a more specific logic like Con(PA) there will be new Godel exceptions that are true but not provable. So you will need a Con(Con(PA)), and so on. Likewise we get larger and larger models of computing.


A remarkable consequence of Kleene’s effort was the ability to produce a picture of undecideable problems. Through the work of Mandelbrot who invented fractals, nobel laurate Penrose who studied them, and the mathematicians Dude, and Braverman-Yampolsky were able to show that the whether or not a point lies in Julia set (the fractal below) is undecidable in a decimal number computing system. The ability to photograph what we don’t know is to this author far more remarkable than Event Horizon’s photographs of black holes. Bring the topic up with your friends in physics and write to me about how that interaction goes.



Julia set fractal, Solkoll, Public Domian




Let us think of a computation as a collection of gates \(\mathcal{A}\), which can includes constants such as a gate the sets a voltage to 0, or a gate that sets a voltage to 1. A computation is to have some gate \(x\) applies to some get \(y\), \[
x\cdot y  \text{ means apply gate $x$ to gate $y$}
\] For example, I 0 yields 0 and K 1 0, understood as (K 1) 0, yields 1.
, or a gate that adds two voltages together. We can also include combinators like \(S\), \(K\), and \(I\). The collection of all such gates is called a universal computing tower. A universal computing tower is a collection of gates that can be combined to perform any computation that can be described by substitution of variables. In other words, it is a universal computing system, what we call Turing Complete.
What we have actually said is that a computer that takes in a string of finite tokens and applies rules of substitutions is no different to providing gates S, K, and I. There however many examples of analog computing: decimal numbers inputs (which may have infinitely many decimal places) output other decimal numbers. Think of an amplifier on a sound system which takes in sound waves, makes them louder by altering the amplitude, and returns a new wave. There are also studies of neural networks and brains in cognitive science that do not sit comfortably in the Turing computational model because of a similar context where it is best to think of infinite sequences of data being modified to infinite sequences of output.






NoteDeflating infinity



A reader like my younger self might point out that sound waves are moving a finite number of air molecules and thus are ultimately discrete finite problems. Therefore Turing computation is ultimately enough. My older wiser self would now answer that this misses the point.
An analog computer (like an amplifier) can be built from a few gates (some gears or a few electronic parts). Meanwhile, a model of all the air molecules in a concert venue is so vast and chaotic that it would take a computer simulation with roughly as many transistors as air molecules to run. Such a system could never be built or even properly analyzed in theory. Even a digital amplifier will ultimately transfer the process from software to some devices that moves a speaker diaphragm as bulk analog instrument to move the quintillion-trillion molecules of air in a stadium. So the model of 2nd, and higher order computation is meant to capture the reality that we will need to explore and control computations that are not practically described as Turing machines.
Scientist call these sort of separation of models “emergence” where the behavior at some scale becomes so much better explained by a simple model that return to its constituent parts is not useful. A theory that works at different scales is called a Gauge Theory, from the term for trains that work on differently spaced tracks. Computation is a Gauge theory, and Turing Complete computation is the lowest scale of this gauge.


where computations are devised as recieving decimal numbers (which may go on forever) and outputing decimal numbers as their answer. Think by waves and singles vary between all decimal numbers (not a finite set of tokens) and neurologist and so the rules of substitution are not enough to describe the computations. In fact, there are many different ways to compute that are not Turing Complete. The Turing Machine is a very small family of computations.
That is a very small family of computations. It is a misimpression to think that Turing Machines are the only way to compute. In fact, there are many other ways to compute that are not Turing Complete. For example, if we have a machine that takes in a string of finite tokens and applies rules of substitutions but also has the ability to take in an infinite string of tokens and apply rules of substitutions then we have a machine that is more powerful than a Turing Machine. This is known as second order universal computing and it is not uniquely universal. There are many different ways to achieve second order universal computing, each with its own set of rules and limitations.
what any other with misimpression that everything about computation not takes place in a Turing Machine. In reality Turing Machines are successful at only a small family of computations. When we work with data that is analog (signals, waves, etc.) we do not have just counting numbers as input but instead we have such things as decimal numbers.
Second order universal computing is not uniquely universal.





Combinators are operations that can be applied to data.
The \(K\) combinator is a constant function that returns its first argument.
The \(I\) combinator is the identity function that returns its argument unchanged.
The \(S\) combinator allows for the application of two functions to the same argument and combines the results.
The \(B\) combinator behaves like function composition, applying one function to the output of another.
The S, K, I combinators together are sufficient for universal computation.
Applied combinators, like ADD, can be more efficient for specific tasks but may have limitations based on their context.
Fixed-point combinators enable recursion by allowing a function to be applied to itself.

There are also studies of neural networks and brains in cognitive science that do not sit comfortably in the Turing computational model because of a similar context where it is best to think of infinite sequences of data being modified to infinite sequences of output.






NoteDeflating infinity



A reader like my younger self might point out that sound waves are moving a finite number of air molecules and thus are ultimately discrete finite problems. Therefore Turing computation is ultimately enough. My older wiser self would now answer that this misses the point.
An analog computer (like an amplifier) can be built from a few gates (some gears or a few electronic parts). Meanwhile, a model of all the air molecules in a concert venue is so vast and chaotic that it would take a computer simulation with roughly as many transistors as air molecules to run. Such a system could never be built or even properly analyzed in theory. Even a digital amplifier will ultimately transfer the process from software to some devices that moves a speaker diaphragm as bulk analog instrument to move the quintillion-trillion molecules of air in a stadium. So the model of 2nd, and higher order computation is meant to capture the reality that we will need to explore and control computations that are not practically described as Turing machines.
Scientist call these sort of separation of models “emergence” where the behavior at some scale becomes so much better explained by a simple model that return to its constituent parts is not useful. A theory that works at different scales is called a Gauge Theory, from the term for trains that work on differently spaced tracks. Computation is a Gauge theory, and Turing Complete computation is the lowest scale of this gauge.


where computations are devised as recieving decimal numbers (which may go on forever) and outputing decimal numbers as their answer. Think by waves and singles vary between all decimal numbers (not a finite set of tokens) and neurologist and so the rules of substitution are not enough to describe the computations. In fact, there are many different ways to compute that are not Turing Complete. The Turing Machine is a very small family of computations.
That is a very small family of computations. It is a misimpression to think that Turing Machines are the only way to compute. In fact, there are many other ways to compute that are not Turing Complete. For example, if we have a machine that takes in a string of finite tokens and applies rules of substitutions but also has the ability to take in an infinite string of tokens and apply rules of substitutions then we have a machine that is more powerful than a Turing Machine. This is known as second order universal computing and it is not uniquely universal. There are many different ways to achieve second order universal computing, each with its own set of rules and limitations.
what any other with misimpression that everything about computation not takes place in a Turing Machine. In reality Turing Machines are successful at only a small family of computations. When we work with data that is analog (signals, waves, etc.) we do not have just counting numbers as input but instead we have such things as decimal numbers.
Second order universal computing is not uniquely universal.

title: Gates, Combinators, and Turing and Kleene
text:
Combinators are operations that can be applied to data.
The \(K\) combinator is a constant function that returns its first argument.
The \(I\) combinator is the identity function that returns its argument unchanged.
The \(S\) combinator allows for the application of two functions to the same argument and combines the results.
The \(B\) combinator behaves like function composition, applying one function to the output of another.
The S, K, I combinators together are sufficient for universal computation.
Applied combinators, like ADD, can be more efficient for specific tasks but may have limitations based on their context.
Fixed-point combinators enable recursion by allowing a function to be applied to itself.

title: Logical Library summary
text:
A common feature of “fixing” a paradox is that we agree to give up on something. In this example, to give up on constants and variables is to give up a lot of the ways we have learned to talk about science. Yet to put rules on what substitution looks like, goes against the “fill-in-the-box” intuition we spent years building for ourselves.
Whenever we encounter a situation where we limit our thinking by rules we have what is called an abstraction.

An abstraction is to limit a topic by rules.

We will have many opportunities to explore abstraction within computation, but the word is so common you might benefit from some outside examples to connect your learning with what you already experience. In economics, workers do many different jobs but to make it possible to compare their productivity we can limit their jobs to how much money they earn. The money is the abstraction.

An abstract painting such as Marcel Duchamp’s Nude Descending a Staircase the nude figure is limited to having a head, arms, and legs. This allowed the subject of the abstract art to consider the locomotion of descending a staircase rather than the details of a specific person.



Nude Descending a Staircase, by Marcel Duchamp (1887-1968) - Philadelphia Museum of Art, PD-US



Possibly here is a place to imagine how data we collect for computations is typically an abstraction of whatever we want to explore. You have some control in creating abstractions when you compute. Choose your rules wisely, they will have consequences.



Despite the wildly different options for logic there are some, just as we can cluster games into styles we structure logic in styles as well and for the most part in this book you can forget specific names for individual logics and think broadly about these three options.

Theoretical Logic: great for models, precise and non-overlapping concept of truth.
Computational Logic: requires evidence to make a deduction, models scientific experiments and computation fairly well.
Practical Logic: admits the inevitability of contradictory information, good for data and realistic information.
