title: Conjunction and Implication in contexts
text:
So now let us put on the filter of a target form of judgment and see what we gain or loose from our above LIE rules for both operators.

















The best tool language has for clarifying meaning is the use of a grammar. If we keep to a context-free grammar we can be certain that everyone reads the meaning the same. So here is a grammar we can give to “and” to fit our logical purposes. Note, in historical settings the term “conjunction” is often used as synonym for “and”. Using “conjunction” can often solve the annoying problem needing to use “and” as an every day word while also talking about “and” in a logical way.

In symbolic language \(\wedge\) (“wedge” but pronounced “and”) is used to represent the logical operator “and”. The grammar for “and” is given by the following production rule: \[
\tag{$L_{\wedge}$}
\langle conjunction \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \wedge \langle proposition \rangle
\] In natural language we can say “A and B” where A and B are propositions. Alternatives include &, && and AND but we will stick to \(\wedge\) for the rest of this book.

Notice what we have not allowed are some the natural ways that “and” drifts in language, e.g. 

“7 is positive, odd and prime”

would now need to be said more like this:

“(7 is positive) and ((7 is odd) and (7 is prime))”

We forgive most authors who slide back to the more natural language uses of “and” but it will strengthen your understanding to practice this in a precise way for a while.

In a theoretical judgment where we forget about evidence then all we need from propositions is their truth value. We can ask for this in most programming languages by builtin logical operators that are written in a variety of ways. Here are some popular options.

p && q is used in C, C++, Java, JavaScript, and R.
p and q is used in Python, Ruby, and Pascal.
(and p q) is used in Lisp and Scheme.
p ∧ q in Agda

Note that these result in a truth value only, they do not hold on to any evidence.


In a computational judgment we need data (evidence) that proves the propositions. So a proposition \(P\) has data \(x\) that proves it, and a proposition \(Q\) has data \(y\) that proves it. We combine these as a joint proposition

(P,Q) in Scala
Pair<P,Q> in Java.
tuple[P,Q] in Python.
std::pair<P,Q> in C++.
P × Q in Agda.

These are just the propositions, they will need data to be proved.


In a practical judgment of a proposition \(P\) we associate some value \(\varepsilon\) of truth, for example, a percentage of our believe the \(P\) is true. If we have similar proposition \(Q\) with a value \(\delta\) then to judge \(P\wedge Q\) we need to combine these values. Some of the options include

min(ε,δ) assumes whichever the lower of two percentages should be the default.
ε*δ assumes the two percentages are independent and so the product is a reasonable estimate of the joint probability.





Now get into what drives the meaning of “and” by describing what must be present to ensure we can create an instance of its use. Logicians call these introduction rules because they introduce the symbols of the logical operator, in this case \(\wedge\).

In natural language we use “and” when we combine two valid propositions \(P\) and \(Q\) to make a new valid proposition \(P\wedge Q\).
Now in symbolic language to say a proposition is valid is to have judged it in a context. So we start with \[
\Gamma \vdash P
\quad
\Delta \vdash Q
\] for contexts \(\Gamma\) and \(\Delta\). We conclude \[
\Gamma, \Delta \vdash P \wedge Q
\]

The mix of words and symbols is helpful initially but when we start to work with logic it becomes much more of a calculation, a calculus. Because this type of calculus is a movement of sequences it is known as sequent calculus. In the full sequent calculus we can collapse the words to this: \[
\tag{$I_{\wedge}$}
\begin{array}{rl}
    \Gamma &\vdash P\\
    \Delta & \vdash Q\\
\hline
    \Gamma, \Delta & \vdash P \wedge Q
\end{array}
\]

If we think of a program as making verified judgments then it makes sense that a proposition \(P\) has data \(x\) the proved it, and a proposition \(Q\) has data \(y\) that proved it. So to create data the proves both we can just hold on to both \(x\) and \(y\). The notation for this is an ordered pair \((x,y)\). The notations vary between programming languages, here are some popular options. Assuming x and y are already data:

p=(x,y) in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript.
(define p (list x y)) in Lisp and Scheme.
Pair p = new Pair(x,y) in Java.
p = <x,y> in Magma.
auto p = std::make_pair(x, y); in C++.





Once we have conjoined two propositions we can carry them around as a single proposition until we intend to use it. It is at this point that we want the ability reach back and extract the to original propositions. Logicians call these elimination rules because they eliminate the symbols of the logical operator, in this case \(\wedge\). Something new happens with this step because it not one but two uses we expect. So technically we are after two elimination rules.

In natural language we use \(P\wedge Q\) so that we can know \(P\) or that we can know \(Q\), or both. So we need to change from a context that judged \(P\wedge Q\) to a context that judges \(P\) and a context that judges \(Q\). In symbolic language we can write this as two elimination rules: \[
\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P\wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash P
}(E_{-\wedge *})
\qquad
\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P\wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash Q
}(E_{*\wedge -})
\]

when we have a reason \(R\) to know of a proposition \(P\wedge Q\) given to us in a context \(\Gamma\). Then we can say that \(R\to P\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to \(P\) and \(R\to Q\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to \(Q\). In diagram language we could say \(R\to (P\wedge Q)\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to both \(P\) and \(Q\).
flowchart LR
    subgraph panel1["Context Γ"]
        direction LR
        Reason --> PQ["Prop P ∧ Q"]
    end
    subgraph panel2["Context Γ after Elimination"]
        direction LR
        Reason2["Reason R"] -->|π₁| P2["Prop P"]
        Reason2 -->|π₂| Q2["Prop Q"]
    end
    %% Trick to make the subgraph appear in order
    panel1 --- panel2
    linkStyle 5 stroke:transparent,fill:transparent 
    style panel1 fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
    style panel2 fill:#f9f9f9,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px
Finally in symbolic language this would be the following rule to add to our proof tree options.


p[0] in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript.
(car p) for first, (cdr p) for rest, in Lisp and Scheme.
p.fst or x where t=(x y) in Haskell.
p.first in C++.
p.1 in Magma.



Let \(p\otimes q\) be a logical operator that is like \(\wedge\) but it is a resource operator. That is, if we have \(p\otimes q\) then we can use \(p\) or \(q\) but not both. Write down the LIE for this operator.




In order to be extra clear about our logic we want to set aside the words in natural language an use instead symbols or words in special fonts so as to treat the rules with some rigor that cannot miscommunicate out meaning. To so this we start to make a system that resembles arithmetic with is various additions, subtractions and other operators. When we calculate with any symbols we get what is known as a “Calculus”
So far we have seen \(\lambda\)-calculus and now we will be looking at two further Calculi, Propositional and Sequent. This is as good a place as any to pause and mention the list of “calculi” that exist in this course.
As a cultural warning, when some says they are studying “Calculus” chances are they mean one of the first two. Our main objective is to start making logical operators and we will focus on “AND”. In assignments you will explore “OR” and “NOT”



Identify Premise and Conclusion from a logical expression.
Use sequent calculus notation to write down logical operators such as AND, TRUE.
Demonstration the use of introduction and elimination rules.







YouTube video player



Sequent Calculus



Sequents means “parts of as a sequence” and the entire idea is to separate the premise from a conclusion. The devices to separate can just be a line, a long space, a word like “entails” but the most common one today is the turnstyle ⊢also said “vdash” since that is how you look it up as a font.
Sequents calculus is the use of sequence to calculate truth in a specified logic. If our logic only has “and” we can only calculate how make an and (introduction) and how to apply an and (elimination). All this must be written in a language.

(L)anguage : the alphabat, symbols, and grammar to be used in the sequents. If your sequents do not parse in the grammar then they don’t count.
(I)ntroduction : what premise or premises do you need to get ot use your logical operator?
(E)limination : what premises along with context do you need to use a logical operator?

The LIE components of a logical operator are a good way to remember the steps.



There is another way we can describe logical operators that get closer to our appreciation of what our data means. For example, 12 is even and positive is true because each of “12 is even” and “12 is positive” are true. If this is all we care about we can ignore the precise form in which we get the facts and focus purely on the values. This is known as “Semantic” reasoning.
When it comes the semantics of AND we insist on one rule:
Only True AND True should be True 
However this still leaves us lots of room to explore meaning.


In classical logic, what experts call “KL” (the German initials) we insist every event is judged as true \(\top\) or false \(\bot\) with no middle values allowed (that rule is called the “Law of the Excluded Middle (LEM)”). That means that \(P\wedge Q\) can take only 4 combinations.

The point is, if we look at AND as is values instead of its syntax we have the freedom to engineer how we actually apply AND. That can be a powerful feature.



Finally, much of life is not so certain and while we may describe some things as true \(\top\) we might struggle to conclude that all other things are false \(\bot\). \hline

\]

As you develop your logic you may have many other ways to approach operators like this one. But resist the urge to call it an AND unless it obey the main rule: Only True and True is True.

title: Conjunction and Implication in contexts
text:
The best tool language has for clarifying meaning is the use of a grammar. If we keep to a context-free grammar we can be certain that everyone reads the meaning the same. So here is a grammar we can give to “and” to fit our logical purposes. Note, in historical settings the term “conjunction” is often used as synonym for “and”. Using “conjunction” can often solve the annoying problem needing to use “and” as an every day word while also talking about “and” in a logical way.

In symbolic language \(\wedge\) (“wedge” but pronounced “and”) is used to represent the logical operator “and”. The grammar for “and” is given by the following production rule: \[
\tag{$L_{\wedge}$}
\langle conjunction \rangle ::= \langle proposition \rangle \wedge \langle proposition \rangle
\] In natural language we can say “A and B” where A and B are propositions. Alternatives include &, && and AND but we will stick to \(\wedge\) for the rest of this book.

Notice what we have not allowed are some the natural ways that “and” drifts in language, e.g. 

“7 is positive, odd and prime”

would now need to be said more like this:

“(7 is positive) and ((7 is odd) and (7 is prime))”

We forgive most authors who slide back to the more natural language uses of “and” but it will strengthen your understanding to practice this in a precise way for a while.

In a theoretical judgment where we forget about evidence then all we need from propositions is their truth value. We can ask for this in most programming languages by builtin logical operators that are written in a variety of ways. Here are some popular options.

p && q is used in C, C++, Java, JavaScript, and R.
p and q is used in Python, Ruby, and Pascal.
(and p q) is used in Lisp and Scheme.
p ∧ q in Agda

Note that these result in a truth value only, they do not hold on to any evidence.


In a computational judgment we need data (evidence) that proves the propositions. So a proposition \(P\) has data \(x\) that proves it, and a proposition \(Q\) has data \(y\) that proves it. We combine these as a joint proposition

(P,Q) in Scala
Pair<P,Q> in Java.
tuple[P,Q] in Python.
std::pair<P,Q> in C++.
P × Q in Agda.

These are just the propositions, they will need data to be proved.


In a practical judgment of a proposition \(P\) we associate some value \(\varepsilon\) of truth, for example, a percentage of our believe the \(P\) is true. If we have similar proposition \(Q\) with a value \(\delta\) then to judge \(P\wedge Q\) we need to combine these values. Some of the options include

min(ε,δ) assumes whichever the lower of two percentages should be the default.
ε*δ assumes the two percentages are independent and so the product is a reasonable estimate of the joint probability.

title: Conjunction and Implication in contexts
text:
Now get into what drives the meaning of “and” by describing what must be present to ensure we can create an instance of its use. Logicians call these introduction rules because they introduce the symbols of the logical operator, in this case \(\wedge\).

In natural language we use “and” when we combine two valid propositions \(P\) and \(Q\) to make a new valid proposition \(P\wedge Q\).
Now in symbolic language to say a proposition is valid is to have judged it in a context. So we start with \[
\Gamma \vdash P
\quad
\Delta \vdash Q
\] for contexts \(\Gamma\) and \(\Delta\). We conclude \[
\Gamma, \Delta \vdash P \wedge Q
\]

The mix of words and symbols is helpful initially but when we start to work with logic it becomes much more of a calculation, a calculus. Because this type of calculus is a movement of sequences it is known as sequent calculus. In the full sequent calculus we can collapse the words to this: \[
\tag{$I_{\wedge}$}
\begin{array}{rl}
    \Gamma &\vdash P\\
    \Delta & \vdash Q\\
\hline
    \Gamma, \Delta & \vdash P \wedge Q
\end{array}
\]

If we think of a program as making verified judgments then it makes sense that a proposition \(P\) has data \(x\) the proved it, and a proposition \(Q\) has data \(y\) that proved it. So to create data the proves both we can just hold on to both \(x\) and \(y\). The notation for this is an ordered pair \((x,y)\). The notations vary between programming languages, here are some popular options. Assuming x and y are already data:

p=(x,y) in Python, Ruby, and JavaScript.
(define p (list x y)) in Lisp and Scheme.
Pair p = new Pair(x,y) in Java.
p = <x,y> in Magma.
auto p = std::make_pair(x, y); in C++.

title: Conjunction and Implication in contexts
text:
Once we have conjoined two propositions we can carry them around as a single proposition until we intend to use it. It is at this point that we want the ability reach back and extract the to original propositions. Logicians call these elimination rules because they eliminate the symbols of the logical operator, in this case \(\wedge\). Something new happens with this step because it not one but two uses we expect. So technically we are after two elimination rules.

In natural language we use \(P\wedge Q\) so that we can know \(P\) or that we can know \(Q\), or both. So we need to change from a context that judged \(P\wedge Q\) to a context that judges \(P\) and a context that judges \(Q\). In symbolic language we can write this as two elimination rules: \[
\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P\wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash P
}(E_{-\wedge *})
\qquad
\frac{
    \Gamma\vdash P\wedge Q
}{
    \Gamma \vdash Q
}(E_{*\wedge -})
\]

when we have a reason \(R\) to know of a proposition \(P\wedge Q\) given to us in a context \(\Gamma\). Then we can say that \(R\to P\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to \(P\) and \(R\to Q\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to \(Q\). In diagram language we could say \(R\to (P\wedge Q)\) represents that the reason \(R\) leads to both \(P\) and \(Q\).

title: Necessary \(\Box\), possible \(\diamond\) and Modal Logic
text:
Ever go into the setting of an app and flip a bunch of toggles  and  to customize the behavior of the app? You can even configure this book. And when you do you are engaging with a new kind of logic. A logic uniquely of the 20th century (though the ideas of course are found everywhere in history). It is called modal logic.
The logical operator \(\wedge,\vee, \neg, \forall, \exists\) have experienced nearly 200 years of use and have had time to seep into mathematics. In fact mathematics is somewhat unaware of most of the logical operators have been invented in the last century preferring to contrive all situations into tortured exhibitions of those symbols alone—a project known as “Logicism” which was shown to be impossible in the 1930s. But we are not mathematicians, we are mathematicians that want to compute and the means we will pay attention to progress in the rest of the world of logic. Of the many topics that have had substantial gain for logic arguably Modal Logic has been the most important. This is a logic that admits that reasoning often depends on the mode in which we find the question. Change the mode and you change the reasoning. The two major operators we will survey from this form of logic are obvious to natural language: necessary \(\Box\) and possible \(\diamond\).
I love this type of logic but every video I ever made about it pales when compared to Attic Philosophy. So we are in for a treat today as we watch a true expert bring us the goods.




The basic of “necessary” is to clarify if a claim is true in all modes. This might sound like a variation on \(\forall\) except that unlike \(\forall\), “necessary” \(\Box\) does not depend on a variable. It rather qualifies an entire sentence. Here is an comparison

You need to login to use your bank software.
For every user, there is a login process to get to the bank software.

While there is a relationship between these two sentences, the first expresses in a clear way that the intent is to enforce security. The second merely explains that security is available to everyone. These are not the same logic.


\[
\langle necessary\rangle ::= \Box \langle\text{proposition}\rangle
\]
\[
\langle possible\rangle ::= \diamond \langle\text{proposition}\rangle
\]
For example, \(\Box(x\neq 0)((1/x\) is defined) “It is necessary that \(x\neq 0\) for \(1/x\) to be defined”. Programs are often filled with logic of this sort with annotations or documentation that declare what is necessary. Here is one such example.
function div(m,n) 
    @assert n != 0; 
    return m/n;
end function;



While syntax drives many operators, necessity is best explored first by its semantics. We do with through what is known as possible worlds. We list all the modes that our logic will consider treating each as a “world”. For example, a company may provide access to its files in several ways as illustrated.
flowchart LR
    Mobile --> App["Mobile App"]
    App --> Public["Public data"]
    App --> Sensitive["Sensitive data"]
    Home --> Public
    Home --> VPN
    VPN --> Sensitive
    Office --> Public
    Office --> Sensitive
    Office --> Strorage["Storage files"]
Here are some of the semantics we can read from this chart

It is possible to reach public data \(C\) from mobile phone M, written \(\diamond (M\to C)\).
It is necessary to be in the office to reach storage files F \(\Box (O\to F)\)
It is possible to reach sensitive data \(S\) from mobile phone M, but only if we go through the app.

Depending on your context you might not care that it takes two steps and write simply \(\diamond (M\to S)\) but if you do care about the steps you might be more verbose with \(\diamond (\Box(M\to A)\to S)\), the extra necessity makes it clear that while mobile can get to sensitive data it is necessary that it does that through the app.
Possible World Semantics are substantial improvement over traditional “true-false” logic because we can often express the complexity of real life with diagrams. When it comes to programming this stuff there are many tools, but the main one is known as “State Machine”. While there are small differences you can roughly equal “State Machine” with “Possible Worlds.”

title: Summary
Summary
Refactoring Code and Logical Equivalence
text:
Refactoring Code and Logical Equivalence
When we design a program from a flowchart we might lock in steps that later we want to re-arrange. This is known as “refactoring”. The purpose of refactoring is to make arguments more clear, make room to reuse arguments, and shorten arguments. The main thing we try not to do when refactoring is change or weaken the software, i.e. change the logic. So it mater now to pause and ask, how can we use the connection of programs to logic as a tool to guarantee that our refactoring is, well, logical? The answer is the subject of proofs. While proofs are huge topic in the sciences and especially within math and logic, what we explore here is a first step.

 Proofs in sequent calculus are trees
Whether complex or simple, realizing a goal as a sentence in logic can help use realize what parts can be altered without changing meaning or making the meaning wider. Sequent calculus is designed to help us isolate these goals and leave behind useful reproducible arguments for anyone who has to maintain our changes in the future.
Sequents are little bricks of reasoning and sequent calculus is how we are permitted to brick them together. Our purpose now is to prove that if we label all the components and logical operators of a design specification we can often restructure it entirely without loosing any of the meaning. And better yet, this type of proof can be passed along reliably to anyone in the future.


 * Objectives

Take apart the building blocks of a task into sequents and identify implicit use of logical operators.
Judge if conjectured alternatives follow from the specification.
Conjecture alternate logical formulations and prove they follow.



 * Specifications for a printer


 Reorganizing the Logic for a printer
YouTube video player


 Proving logical equivalence
YouTube video player

 Natural deduction
One way to describe a tree is as graph in which any two points are connected by a unique shortest path. This property makes it impossible to give confusing directions. When it comes the clearest proofs, the directions are essential. This is what makes given proofs by trees such a powerful tool. It avoids ambiguity. To enforce this rule in our sequent calculus we have used a subtle but important rule:
Natural Deduction Rule for Sequent Calculus: While there can be any number of premises to a sequent, there can be only one conclusion.
So to see the three, all the premises are the leaves, the conclusion is the root. Composing rules just grows branches.


 Critiques of natural deduction
We should emphasize that natural deduction is not actually that natural. Humans reason through a complex network of evidence often bring back into play ideas that appeared earlier and reusing parts of an argument as complex braid of reasoning. To make these into natural deductions requires that we identify all these loops and reuses and correctly clone reused parts and separate the argument. Cloning should give you worry as we have seen since the start that not all logical systems can be credited with the option to reuse hypotheses. So the strength of natural deduction is not that it is close to nature but that it is clear and efficient. The use of the term “natural” seems mostly to have been a political stunt to inculcate strong belief in philosophies of proof in an era where competing philosophies suggested otherwise. The mathematician David Hilbert can be credited largely for this emphasis, though he achieved it at the cost of removing his dissenters from editorial boards and prominent positions. It is a regrettable omission that has had a long and complicated shadow serving to separate math from computer science in a manner that is only in recent years being rectified.

section: Math156 Sets, Types, & Other Higher Order Logic
text:
Math156 Sets, Types, & Other Higher Order Logic
We now have several logics in front of us and are on our way to turning this into software. One lesson we are learning is to keep concepts simple and build up complexity from small steps we can trust. So now comes the problem of mixing two context. In our first video we will encounter a new problem this brings. A paradox that forces us to add to our logic. The result is what today is known as “Higher Order Logic”, which include several sublogics with names like “Set Theory”, “Type Theory”, “Classes”, “Kinds” and “Sorts”. These are all different attempts to avoid mistakes but remain flexible.

 * Objectives

Identify the limits of first order logic, e.g. that you cannot combine facts from two contexts without contradictions.
Be able to read set theory notation
Use set theory notation to repair problems in first order logic.



 Lectures


 A set theory
YouTube video player


 We need higher order logic when…
The same sentence, evidence, or data can be judged differently in two contexts that need to be used together.


 * Quick Check

Your project uses 2D and 3D points. Will you need a higher order logic? - Yes *


Correct: The arithmetic storage and display of 2D points is different from 3D points and you cannot blend the two without errors. So your will need some higher order logic to separate the context. For example you might create two different types of data. - No *
Think about the point (2,1) and (1,0,1). Is there really any way that you could use these interchangeably without causing some errors?

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Annotation
Perhaps the simplest and most common solution to higher-order logic problems is to annotate the data. Annotations are a general term for all the symbols, superscript, subscripts, highlights, colors, etc. that we might add to text to indicate there is something special going on. Here are three of the most common forms of annotations.

(xX) Here (x) is the data and (X) the annotation. The symbol () read as “in” is meant to read as if the data (x) is in the context of (X). This is especially common in mathematics circles where might write (5) to say “5 is in the real numbers” (real numbers are just decimal numbers).
x:X or X x. Here x is the data and X the annotation. The symbol : read as “has type” is meant to read as if the data x is in the context of the data type X. This is especially common in programming circles where might write Float x or x:Float to read as “x is a floating point number.


 * Quick Check

You read the following code. Are you likely to be using higher-order logic?
def convert(file, format):
s = read(file)
return save(s,format)

Yes


Unlikely. While the names of the function and the variables give us clues that the data have special roles, there is nothing in the code that annotates this for the program and so we should assume we are operating under the conditions that any data could be coming in or out of this function. title: Equations from Diagrams
text:
Diagrams for Types
Data types can be represented with diagrams.

 Learning Materials
Reading
Universal Programs [10:19]
Making Or a Program [15:04]


 Quick Check

What do two paths between the same points in a commutative diagram represent?


Two paths between the same points in a commutative diagram stand for an equation. This coherence condition can be turned into a program test.

title: Equations from Diagrams
text:
Objectives

Identify a commutative diagram
Convert commutative diagrams into equations
Convert equations of functions into commutative diagrams.
Use the Story-board style to communicate the evolution of a commutative diagram.

title: Equations from Diagrams
text:
Reviewing Composition
Let’s take apart the story into two major lessons. The first of these is the concept of a “commutative diagram”. The idea here is known two most of us as the way we read a flow chart. We have nodes with a rows and if we follow a path of arrows then we are following the cumulative effect of applying one transformation after another. If we start to think of this in the logic we are building we can think of the arrows as implication, or if they concern data we call them functions instead of implications. The nodes then become data types.

Nodes: Data types
Arrows: Functions between data types
Composition: passing data through multiple functions.

You may be familiar with composition of functions and its properties, here is a refresher. The takeaways are that

Definition ((gf)(x)=g(f(x)))
Associativity ((h(gf))=(hg)f))
But non-commutative ((gf)) does not in general equal ((fg)).

Notice above all that we are looking at equations. Equations are parts of mathematics we can test and use to constrain questions and crucially to solve for unknowns. It is a form of “Algebra”. If we bring equations into the design of programs we will find the algebra confines us a bit towards solving the questions in the right way. If we break an equation we have a bug. So we can make tests that try different values of input in the equation and see if they hold. If not we look for a bug. This equation being well inside our system of code is a local test. We do not need to wait for the eventual full strength program to find the mistakes. This is a type of debugging known as “Unit Testing”. Designing our programs to hide equations is one of the main ways we can separate off small problems that are less complex and spot mistakes early.

 Software Composition
In software composition can often be written in the opposite order. For example, myFile.as_CSV().convert_JSON() is an often legal programming syntax which means to take the data myFile, apply the function as_CSV to it, then apply the function convert_JSON is applied after that. If x=myFile, f=as_CSV is and g=convert_JSON, then the logic reads as ((gf)(x)). This runs in reverse of the words we see in the program. The complication is that even in programs we can often write the order composition in multiple ways. The code below is the same composition but done more in line with the math style.
convert_JSON( as_CSV( myFile ) )

title: Equations from Diagrams
text:
Commutative Diagrams
So now that we see that function composition is not generally “commutative”, i.e. (gffg) in most cases, whenever this does happen we should take notice. Below we see a flow chart of two events: Brushing Hair and Brushing Teeth, vs. Socks On and Shoes On.



Screenshot 2026-02-01 at 9.58.33 AM.png


From this model we see some events commute, others do not.

A commutative diagram (Brush~HairBrush~Teeth = Brush~TeethBrush~Hair)
A non-commutative diagram (Shoes~OnSocks~on Sock~On Shoes~On)

Over time the term “Commutative Diagram” has been relaxed to count any equation of function compositions. So while originally this was about the commutative law (gf=fg) it now includes any flowchart where two paths between the same points commute.

A diagram of functions between types is said to “commute” if any two paths between the same points give equal values.

title: Equations from Diagrams
text:
Universal Diagrams
Now let us focus on the “Universal” nature of our diagrams. Suppose our Dad character had suggested that the child keep only one domino and one string. This would have been enough to eliminate to both a string and a domino. It is in some sense a representation of the data. Yet, the son could clearly complain that this is also to throw away a lot of the data. This would mean the “heap” strategy the kid uses is in a measurable way superior as it did not loose any information. How can the son communicate this?

With the son’s approach to a heap he can repeat everything his father’s method can so it is at least as good. In real life a software package that implements logic like this is making a guarantee that no information is being overlooked. The main idea is to


 Universal Program Design

Design a pattern of flow from your new data types to the given data (elimination rules “getters”)
Repeat that same pattern of flow with a competitor solution.
Verify that your type of data can transform the competitor’s solution into your own uniquely (introduction rule, i.e. “constructors/setters”). Think of this as migrating their solution into your own. The uniqueness here means you don’t have to get caught up in future choices of how to convert. Doing so means you program is now brittle and will depend on configurations and is, well, not universal.



 Reversing the arrows: Couniversal Design
A good idea is worth repeating, but often that really means repeating with some variation. The variation we want to explore is when the roles of the arrows are all reversed behavior can occur in reverse as well. When we do that we are in effect swapping the elimination rules with the introduction rules. With logic that means for example to swap AND with OR, True with False, and many similar dualities. It is often a strong way to get a new functionality without much new work. In the exercises you will explore this duality.

title: How to make a type of data
text:
How to make a type of data
When we developed structural logic we depended on three ingredients: Language to tell us how to communicate the logic, Introduction rules to tell us how the logic may arise, and Elimination rules to tell us how to draw conclusions. Now as we move to more complex reasoning we find ourselves in confusion as multiple contexts compete for the meaning of our variables. So we need to put up makers that separate context and allow them to coevolve in our reasoning. The simplest tool for this is known as a type and to make one we may actually get rid of push to include data.

Formation the rules we need in place to declare a type, think of this as introduction rules not of proposition but for types.
Introduction the rules we need to introduce data into a type.
Elimination the rules we need to eliminate data from a type.
Computations the rules we need to convert the introduction information it elimination information.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Math156 Dual logic and Programs
Is a good idea is worth repeating? Well in math and logic once we have solved a problem we don’t really need to solve it again. Rather what we mean in this situation is that we can repeat the spirit of the idea but with some useful changes. The variation we want to explore here are when the roles of the arrows are all reversed behavior can occur in reverse as well. Think of this as swapping inputs with outputs, saving a file verses reading a file, opening a window verses closing a window, and so on. When we do that we are in effect swapping the elimination rules with the introduction rules of some data types. With logic that means for example to swap AND with OR, True with False, and many similar so-called dualities. It is often a strong way to get a new functionality without much new work. But sometimes these dualities actually uncover missing parts of the original problem which help us make a better understanding of the entire logic.

 * Objectives

Dualize the logic and diagrams associated to it.
Create the semantics for AND as dual to OR

So it may come as little surprise to discover that the data types for all are repeated use of pairs, sometimes called “tuples” but they can include such things as structures and arrays as well. Notations
Dependent pairs have several notations.

In mathematics (_{i:I} X(i)) is known as a “disjoint union” with terms denoted (x_i).
In logic (_{i:I} X(i)) which reads as “for some (i), a term of (X(i))”. This is a pun on the work “sum” and “some” which only works in English.
In programming X(1)+X(2) adding more terms as need is a sum of types but dependent pairs take on notation as diverse as <i,x>, i**x, but I believe in time it will converge the math notation (x_i). The only problem is that the LaTeX way to use subscripts is x_i which now clashes with the snake-case style of program names. This is easy to fix but as of today it is not yet settled.

title: Higher-order logic by Data Types (AB)
text:
Higher-order logic by Data Types (AB)
The word “data types” is synonymous with computer programs since the 1940’s when Konrad Zuse and others began to think of clever encodings of data such as “Floating Point Numbers”. But before that Types had already been envisioned in work of Bertrand Russell in 1902 and later clarified by Alonzo Church and Haskell Curry to avoid major problems in the foundations of mathematics and logic. This is generally a good sign. If an idea emerges from two or more unrelated areas then there is bound to be value in comparing the goals and resolving them into a one unified concept. Today this is known as “Type Theory” and it offers an excellent translation between the mechanical needs of computers and the fluid abstractions of human reasoning. To get start we will make our first type the first logical operator “AND”. This is a bit of a long one but it will end with actual code you can run yourself. title: Sets, Types, & Other Higher Order Logic
text:
We now have several logics in front of us and are on our way to turning this into software. One lesson we are learning is to keep concepts simple and build up complexity from small steps we can trust. So now comes the problem of mixing two context. In our first video we will encounter a new problem this brings. A paradox that forces us to add to our logic. The result is what today is known as “Higher Order Logic”, which include several sublogics with names like “Set Theory”, “Type Theory”, “Classes”, “Kinds” and “Sorts”. These are all different attempts to avoid mistakes but remain flexible.



Identify the limits of first order logic, e.g. that you cannot combine facts from two contexts without contradictions.
Be able to read set theory notation
Use set theory notation to repair problems in first order logic.







YouTube video player



The same sentence, evidence, or data can be judged differently in two contexts that need to be used together.




Your project uses 2D and 3D points. Will you need a higher order logic? - Yes *


Correct: The arithmetic storage and display of 2D points is different from 3D points and you cannot blend the two without errors. So your will need some higher order logic to separate the context. For example you might create two different types of data. - No *
Think about the point (2,1) and (1,0,1). Is there really any way that you could use these interchangeably without causing some errors?




Perhaps the simplest and most common solution to higher-order logic problems is to annotate the data. Annotations are a general term for all the symbols, superscript, subscripts, highlights, colors, etc. that we might add to text to indicate there is something special going on. Here are three of the most common forms of annotations.

(xX) Here (x) is the data and (X) the annotation. The symbol () read as “in” is meant to read as if the data (x) is in the context of (X). This is especially common in mathematics circles where might write (5) to say “5 is in the real numbers” (real numbers are just decimal numbers).
x:X or X x. Here x is the data and X the annotation. The symbol : read as “has type” is meant to read as if the data x is in the context of the data type X. This is especially common in programming circles where might write Float x or x:Float to read as “x is a floating point number.




You read the following code. Are you likely to be using higher-order logic?
def convert(file, format):
s = read(file)
return save(s,format)

Yes


Unlikely. While the names of the function and the variables give us clues that the data have special roles, there is nothing in the code that annotates this for the program and so we should assume we are operating under the conditions that any data could be coming in or out of this function. It will mean we should expect errors form confusion could occur and perhaps we should plan for this. - No *


Correct:. While the names of the function and the variables give us clues that the data have special roles, there is nothing in the code that annotates this for the program and so we should assume we are operating under the conditions that any data could be coming in or out of this function. It will mean we should expect errors form confusion could occur and perhaps we should plan for this.





Later you get a pull-request with an update to the code that reads like this. Are the modification suggestive of higher-order logic?
def convert(file:File, format:Extension):File
var s:String = read(file)
return save(s,format)

Yes




Correct: The use of annotation signals. These may help our computer program check for errors and use the data correctly according to the logic we intend. - No *
The annotations are a clue about narrowing of data and is uses.

title: Solving \(y=f(x)\) needs new types of data: subsets and partitions
text:
Suppose we have a typed function \(f:X\to Y\) and we consider the equations

Given \(y\in Y\), solve for \(x\in X\) such that \(y=f(x)\).

There are basically two things that can happen, and a third if we consider that both happen together.

a \(y\) has at most one solution \(x\) such that \(y=f(x)\), or
a \(y\) has at least one solution \(x\) such that \(y=f(x)\).

It matters to a program to plan ahead for these different situations.
For example, if \(y\) has many solutions then we need to ask what we expect a program to do when finding a solution. Does it need to find every solution? What if that is a lot of numbers, even an infinite number of solutions? We may need a strategy that considers multiple solutions equivalent so that the program can return a representative solution. Think of \(f(x)=x^2\). We can detect that for every solution \(c\) to \(y=f(x)\) then \(-c\) is also a solution. So it would be enough to give \(c\) and know how construct \(-c\) later if necessary. Meanwhile with \(f(x)=\sqrt{x}\) and \(y=2\) we have only one solution, \(x=4\), but with \(y=-2\) we have no solution and we have to prepare for this exception.
. In this case we can be sure that we have a unique solution. Finally with \(f(x)=\sin(x)\) and \(y=0\) we have infinitely many solutions, \(x=n\pi\) for any integer \(n\). In this case we need to consider if we need all of them or just one, and if just one which one do we need.
Now we can go through each \(y\) and see what happens, but who has time to consider every piece of data. However, sometimes we get a logic so powerful that it lets us get an answer
but a remarkable aspect of some of our most common reasoning gives us an overall strategy.

In the category of data types every fun






YouTube video player



A function \(f:X\to Y\) is injective when for every \(y\in Y\), \(y=f(x)\) has at most one solution.
It can be helpful to think of injective in multiple ways. For example, how can we identify that a function is injective when we do not really know its program but we see its meaning in a flow chart? We look to see if it can be cancelled as the last term.






While it is tempting to think of functions as static and unchanging, in programming it is often more accurate to think of functions as static within some possible world, or “state” as computer scientist call it. Let’s take a look at a function that can switch between being injective or not based on the world (state) we find it in.


For example, if def schedule( thread : Thread) : Time assigns a thread (a unit of computation) to a position in line for a processor to run, and def assign1( t: Task) : Thread and def assign2( t : Task) :Thread are to functions that assign threads to tasks, then what would it mean to assign that the same tasks always get run at the same time? It would mean
schedule( assign1( t ) ) == schedule( assign2( t ) )
How could this happen? Well one option is that the assignments are the same to begin with. But if that isn’t the case then for some task t, assign1(t) != assign2(t) so the only option to make them run at the same time is for schedule to to assign two tasks to run at the same time. If our computer has enough parallel computing to accommodate this then two threads running at the same time is possible and schedules are non-injective.



Do enough computing and you will soon discover it is easy to overwhelm the parallel resources of even the biggest computers. What happens to scheduling when this happens? We begin to reuse compute nodes. The schedule for a single compute node is now forced to assign threads one at a time, that is, no thread gets the same scheduled number on that compute node because there is no free unit to compute. At this stage if we ask how can
schedule( assign1( t ) ) == schedule( assign2( t ) )
it will be limited to having the exact same assigned tasks:
schedule( assign1( t ) ) == schedule( assign2( t ) )
In this possible world schedule is injective.



Some functions \(f:A\to B\) are necessarily injective,
Necessarily Injective = \(\Box \biggl(f(a)=f(a') \Rightarrow a=a'\biggr)\)
For example, def getPath( f : File ) : String is necessarily injective because a file only ever has one path. [Technical note, if you rename a file it is technically a different file.]
Other function \(f:A\to B\) are possibly injective, meaning in some worlds they are injective but perhaps not in all.
Possibly Injective = \(\diamond \biggl(f(a)=f(a') \Rightarrow a=a'\biggr)\)
For example, def schedule( t : Thread ) : Time, can be non-injective when we have enough resources for parallelism but is forced to become injective when we run out of resources.

text:
* 04-2 | Membership

 * Lesson Introduction
Now membership sounds like a simple concept: “Are you a member?” but it is in the end still proposition and it will be judged in different logics (Computation, Practical, or Theoretical). When we reason and compute these difference make different demands.


 * Learning Materials

Embedded media

 Computational Membership

“To ride the roller-coaster you must measure 4’ tall.”
“On the train you need to keep your ticket.”
I swear I have an account but I cannot remember my password.



 Why?

If membership is decided by a test then it is probably computational.
If you need to hold on to proof of membership you are probably computational.
If the benefits of membership can be withheld for lack of evidence then you are probably computational.



 Practical Memberships

“I am a member, but my ID wont scan.”
“Sometimes my membership ID does scan.”
“Looking up my membership always works.”



 Why?

Practical (xG) members ship is a mix of true/false clues.
(xG) possibly I have proved I am a member.
(xG) I can always prove I am a member.



 Theoretical Membership

“541 is in the prime numbers”
“Once you graduate you are a graduate.”
“Helium is a noble gas.”



 Why?

A strictly true or false proposition is often theoretical.
You can forget everything you learned, people may not even believe you, but you remain a graduate.
Nobel gas is a property of some atoms that is true even if you don’t know how to test it or what it means. The atom will have those qualities if it is a member.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
math156 Overview
Functions and Relations are the heart of how we transfer ideas from one context to the next. They appear in all forms of logic, form precise computation, to general logical models, to the realities of data. Often we need a special class of function to get something useful done and such special functions get names. Perhaps the simplest property we can ask of a function is to relate the possible outputs to the inputs. I mean to discuss the equation
(f(x)=b)

 *Objectives

Relations as Diagrams
Define injective, surjective, and bijective.
Recognize injective, surjective, and bijective from algebraic quality.
Describe the computational advantage of a in-/sur-/bi-jective function.
Explain all three functions diagramatically.

title: Subset \(\subset\) and Partition \(/\) Summary
text:
Subset \(\subset\) and Partition \(/\) Summary

For a function \(f:X\to Y\), all the following are equivalent:

For each \(y:Y\), \(y=f(x)\) has at most one solution \(x:X\).
\(f\) has a partial inverse on its outputs.
\(f\) is called injective.

For a function \(f:X\to Y\), all the following are equiavlent:

For each \(y:Y\), \(y=f(x)\) has at least one solution \(x:X\)
\(f\) has a partial inverse on its inputs.
\(f\) is called surjective.

For a function \(f:X\to Y\), all the following are equiavlent:

For each \(y:Y\), \(y=f(x)\) has exactly one solution \(x:X\)
\(f\) has an inverse on its inputs and outputs.
\(f\) is called bijective.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
math156 Bijective
Now lets us consider the most reversible of all functions, the bijective functions. These are when f(x)=bf(x)=b has exactly one solution. It is extremely rare, and, I will argue, comes about only when you are basically describing an alphabet for some data. Let us see what that means.

 *Objectives

Define bijective.
Identify bijective with the existence of two-sided inverse.
Understand that 2-sided inverses are unique.
Demonstrate that bijections occur when two sets have the same size “cardinality”.



 *Lectures
YouTube video player
In summary here is what we learn. A function (f:AB) is bijective precisely when one of the following is true.

For every (b:B), there is exactly one solution (x:A) to the equation (f(x)=b).
There is a function (f^{-1}:BA) such that (ff^{-1}(b)=b) and (f^{-1}f(a)=a).

Bijections line up every input with one output and vice-versa, which means that we can see the value in B as names for the inputs. If B were numbers, 1, 2,3,… it would be like we count off the value of A. But numbers often have extra properties like order and arithmetic. So a better mental model is to think of B as an alphabet, a,b,c,d,… possibly in a different language or with repeats such as (b_1,b_2,b_3,). In this way a bijection is like assigning characters from an alphabet to each of your inputs.
When we think of inputs and outputs as sets in the mathematical sense where there is a notion of size then a bijection just means |A|=|B|.


 * Quick Check
There is a bijection between the lower-case and upper-case letters of the English language.
Yes
Exactly, the forward direction is to send lower-case to upper case and inverse is to send upper-case to lower-case.
No
While the sets are not the same, a bijection can exist that relates them to each other. Think of turning lower-case into upper-case.


 * Quick Check
There is a bijection between even and odd integers.
Yes
Surprisingly yes. Take 2n to 2n-1. That will turn even to odd. And it has an inverse: send 2n-1 to 2n.
No
Think about shifting the even numbers by 1.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing

When mathematicians invent three ways to say the same things chances are it’s an important concept. We seem to lack precise language for what that concept is but by using any one of these three data types we have a tools to get work done. Translate Partitions to surjective functions.

 * Quick Check
If you are given a function from clients to phone numbers, which of the following best describes the associated equivalence relation of the function.
Two clients that are live in the same house have the same phone number.
That may be true but is not a property that this function can confirm.
Two clients with the same phone phone number are considered as equal.
Correct, the fiber equivalence of this function sends clients to a phone number. Therefore if two phone numbers are the same then with respect to this function the clients are now treated as equivalent.


 * Quick Check
What best describes the equivalence classes of the above function?
All clients who use the same phone number are in one class.

All clients with the same area code are in the same class.
No, while such a partition class could be useful it is not the one represented by this function because this function sees the entire phone number as output. You could create a new equivalence by changing the function to just output area codes.
Translation to code
As a general rule when you see software the equivalence relations are denoted with symbols or suggestive words. Here are some popular options.
a == ba.equals(b)a eq b
Most of the time software systems reserve “=” as the assignment notation.
When you need to change the equivalence relation in software you do so by what is said to “override equals”. This might look like this.
def equals(c:Client):Boolean =                   return phone_number == c.getPhoneNumber()
Partitions in software are often simply to design a new data type that is responsible for representing an entire equivalence class in the partition. Take for example the case e-mail addresses. Suppose that we know that e-mail names can have both upper and lower case letters which will be ignored, as well as periods that will also be ignored. For example mailto:James.Wilson@ColoState.Edu mailto:jameswilson@colostate.edu
James.Wilson@ColoState.Edu == jameswilson@colostate.edu

class Email(e:String) {   def makeEmail(e:String):Email = {       temp = e.toLowerCase()       head, tail = temp.splitAt( '@' )       head.remove('.')       e = new Email( head + '@' + tail )       if not (e in clients) then           clients.add(e)          return e        else           return clients.find(e).getEmail()   }}
You don’t need to truly understand this code to realize that what it is doing is modifying the input we give before finally creating an actual e-mail data type. math156 Injective
The ability to reverse a calculation is rare and powerful. Learning to spot function that have this property and exploit the condition is an essential skill. Today we look at left-reversible functions, or what are commonly called “Injective” functions.

 *Objectives

Define injective.
Recognize partial functions.
Describe left-inverses as partial functions.
Draw diagrams to demonstrate injectivity in work flows.



 *Lectures
YouTube video player


 * Quick Check
If f(x)=bf(x)=b has at most one solution for every b:Bb:B then what can you say about the function.
It is injective.
Yes, this is one of the ways we can define injective.
It is surjective
Surjective means there is at least one solution but there may be many.
So injective functions (f:AB) can be defined with any one of the following

(f(x)=b) has at most one solution.
There is a left-inverse (f:BA^?) such that for every (a:A), (ff(a)=a)
If (fh=fk) then (h=k).

A little more on partial functions. Partial functions are what you learned when you first learned of functions. Think of (f(x)=1/x). It was a partial function. When you feed it 0 you know it is undefined. It doesn’t stop you from doing that, you can ask (f(0)=1/0) as symbols, it is just that you cannot carry the algoirthm further than that and instead at this point your algorithm returns with an error. So when we type this as a function in a computer or in math we would not write simply ****
def f(x:Float):Float
Instead we should use ****
def f(x:Float):Float?
Well the syntax will be different from computer language to computer language. For example, you might see
def f(x:Float):Option[Float]
f: Float -> Maybe Float

float f(float x) throws Exception
But the idea is the same. The ? symbol is just saying, return something from B if you can, and if not treat everything else as an error.


 * Quick Check
Why is the left inverse of an injective function only a partial function?
Because there is no algorithm to reverse a computation.
This is possible but not always true. In fact it would be a big break through in mathematics and computer science to learn that in fact no such algorithm exists.
Because (f(x)=b) might not have any solution.
This is. better answer because it exposes that some (b:B) have no (x:A) to be sent to. Hence the left-inverse is only partial.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
math156 Images
Since in-/sur-/bi-jective functions carry so much computational power it is helpful to find them wherever we can. While most functions are not themselves of this special kind, there are ways that we can force functions to take on one of these flavors. Today we explore the use of an image to create an injective function from a function.

 *Objectives

Define images as a means to take a function and produce one that is injective.
Observe the universal property of images and how we can plan to migrate using this universal quality.



 *Lectures
YouTube video player

Every function (f:AB) has a decomposition into a pair of image functions (f|^{im}:A(f)) and (f|{im}:(f)B). In particular (f|{im}) must be injective, so it has a left-inverse and we often want this to exploit computation.
In computation when we speak of “an image” we really mean any data type ((f)) that we build when decomposing our function as above. So in computational settings “the” is misleading. We could have many choices. It is just that they are all universal and hence interchangeable so in this sense we don’t mind thinking of this a unique.
When we slip to classical logic we start to overlook computational difference entirely and here we really do begin to think of images as a unique set. Of course that may be realized in software by many different programs each with different qualities. But for classical reasoning we just want to observe the net behavior. For that we treat all the equivalent methods to compute the same and talk about just one set, the image. It is denoted like this.

((f) = { f(a) aA})
Recall that when we shift from computational logic to classical logic, so from types to sets, we start writing (xA) instead of (x:A). It is a good hint to pick up on what someone really means.

text: (15 mins) Solving (y=f(x))

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
section: Math 156 When (y=f(x)) always has a solution.
text:
Math 156 When (y=f(x)) always has a solution.

 The problem
At this point we know how types of data separate context, but the real goal is to have different context talk to one another. For example, suppose we have people in one context (X) and shoes in another context (Y). That is obviously not much of a story. But now suppose we link them by the function “buy” where each person in (X) buys a shoe from (Y). That relationship lets us image a cascade of computational questions.

What shoe models are selling?
Does the sold inventory should match exactly the sales receipts?
Does every client get helped by at most one employee?

These questions still have a veneer of business language. How can a computer be asked to solve things that are not about true/false and numbers?


 Making Equations
Beyond having a function (f:XY), our computers need equations they can solve.

X=Clients, Y=Shoes, and (f:XY) is shopping. Then for which (yY) does (y=f(x)) have at least one solution (xX)?
X=Shoes, Y=Receipts, and (f:XY) inventory. Does each (yY) have exactly one solution (xX) with (y=f(x))?
X=Employees, Y=Clients. Now (f:XY) assigns the employee to a client. We want to ask if (f(x)=f()) does it follow that (x=)?

From here you can begin to imagine numerous ways to express questions that can be fundamentally treated as** solutions to equations** of the form
(y=f(x))


 How do we solve equations? Algebra!
Think of how you solved equations in the past.
(x+4=2)? Add -4 to both side to get (x +4-4=2-2) so that (x=-2).
Well solving equations (y=f(x)) for an arbitrary function can be approached in somewhat the same way. Not every function is easy to use but there are broad classes of function where the behavior of (y=f(x)) is predictable. What we do is study those functions and their properties closely. Then we make strategies to write the functions we have as a composition these easier families. Let us begin with the first case.


 Surjective: (y=f(x)) always has at least 1 solution


 (y=f(x)) has at least 1 solution
YouTube video player


 * Fill-in-the-Blank
A function (f:XY) is surjective when for every (yY), (y=f(x)) has at least one solution.



Surjective property as a commutative diagram




 Surjective when Modes change
When we write functions for computations they often behave in ways that change based on the situation. And it can be frustrating to learn terms like “surjective” only to find we cannot convincingly use this term about computer programs. Yet the situation is not that bad. Often what we mean is to ask the question in “modal logic” where we consider possible worlds (also called “states”). So let’s inspect this situation.

 Assigning tasks when there are too many workers
Let def assign( t : Task ) : Thread be a function that assigns a given task to a thread (a computer unit). Threads are assigned to work on a schedule, which is a function def schedule( th : Thread ) : Time. Schedules change, so there can be several schedule functions def schedule1( th : Thread ) : Time, def schedule2( th : Thread ) : Time, and so on, for example
schedule1( thread1 ) = 1``schedule2( thread1 ) = 1
schedule1( thread2 ) = 2``schedule2( thread2 ) = 2
schedule1( thread3 ) = 3``schedule2( thread3 ) = 4
schedule1( thread4 ) = 4``schedule2( thread4 ) = 3
What happens if we only have 2 tasks and these are assigned to thread1 and thread2? In that case the schedules are functionally the same:
schedule1( assign( t ) ) == schedule2( assign( t ) )
That is, because the only differences in schedule are in thread3 and thread4 we don’t notice the difference in schedule. And yet schedule1 != schedule2. This is an illustration that for such few tasks, assign is non-surjective.
Assigning tasks with too few workers
Fast-forward to having 7 tasks and we need to use all the threads we can. Now assign includes tasks assigned to thread3 and thread4. Therefore
schedule1( assign( t ) ) != schedule2( assign( t ) )
The only pair of schedules that produces the exact same order of tasks in this case is to use the exact same schedule. Surjective assignment can be “reversed” on the right.


 Modal Surjectivity
So in practice when we compute we often benefit from considering whether functions are surjective in all worlds
Necessarily surjective = ((uv, uf = vf u=v))
For example, def getWindow( hw : WindowHandle ) : Window outputs the window labeled hw. There is a handle for every window no matter what windows we have open. So this function is surjective in all possible worlds.
Meanwhile a function like scheduling can have worlds where it is surjective but perhaps not every world.
Possibly surjective = ((uv, uf = vf u=v))

math156 The Membership Spectrum
When we say some data is a member of a set or class we can mean many different things depending on the logical assumptions we are making. If we plan to make reliable model, computations, or data sets we should be clear about the variations in membership. Let us take a closer look at three forms of logic and their implied membership. Starting with classical logic which is great for initial models and science to get started we shift to the realities of computer algorithms using intuitionistic logic before swinging over to the needs of work with big data efficiently and how we can be over zealous in our summaries of membership requiring reasoning with things like modal logic.

 *Objectives

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
section: Math 156 When (y=f(x)) has at most one solution
text:
Math 156 When (y=f(x)) has at most one solution

 Injective: (y=f(x)) always has at most 1 solution


 (y=f(x)) has at most 1 solution
YouTube video player


 * Fill-in-the-Blank
A function (f:XY) is injective when for every (yY), (y=f(x)) has at most one solution.
It can be helpful to think of injective in multiple ways. For example, how can we identify that a function is injective when we do not really know its program but we see its meaning in a flow chart? We look to see if it can be cancelled as the last term.

 



 Example of injective Modal Conditions
While it is tempting to think of functions as static and unchanging, in programming it is often more accurate to think of functions as static within some possible world, or “state” as computer scientist call it. Let’s take a look at a function that can switch between being injective or not based on the world (state) we find it in.

 A world with enough parallel computing
For example, if def schedule( thread : Thread) : Time assigns a thread (a unit of computation) to a position in line for a processor to run, and def assign1( t: Task) : Thread and def assign2( t : Task) :Thread are to functions that assign threads to tasks, then what would it mean to assign that the same tasks always get run at the same time? It would mean
schedule( assign1( t ) ) == schedule( assign2( t ) )
How could this happen? Well one option is that the assignments are the same to begin with. But if that isn’t the case then for some task t, assign1(t) != assign2(t) so the only option to make them run at the same time is for schedule to to assign two tasks to run at the same time. If our computer has enough parallel computing to accommodate this then two threads running at the same time is possible and schedules are non-injective.


 A world that runs out of parallel resources
Do enough computing and you will soon discover it is easy to overwhelm the parallel resources of even the biggest computers. What happens to scheduling when this happens? We begin to reuse compute nodes. The schedule for a single compute node is now forced to assign threads one at a time, that is, no thread gets the same scheduled number on that compute node because there is no free unit to compute. At this stage if we ask how can
schedule( assign1( t ) ) == schedule( assign2( t ) )
it will be limited to having the exact same assigned tasks:
schedule( assign1( t ) ) == schedule( assign2( t ) )
In this possible world schedule is injective.


 Modal Injectivity is common in computation
Some functions (f:AB) are necessarily injective,
Necessarily Injective = ((f(a)=f(a’) a=a’))
For example, def getPath( f : File ) : String is necessarily injective because a file only ever has one path. [Technical note, if you rename a file it is technically a different file.]
Other function (f:AB) are possibly injective, meaning in some worlds they are injective but perhaps not in all.
Possibly Injective = ((f(a)=f(a’) a=a’))
For example, def schedule( t : Thread ) : Time, can be non-injective when we have enough resources for parallelism but is forced to become injective when we run out of resources.

* 05 | Patterns and Induction Overview

 *Overview
We are now launching our second of three major units on reasoning. So far we have focussed on Deductive Logic, where we reason from the evidence provided. Now we begin our transition into the study of Inductive Logic.


 Inductive Reasoning
reasoning beyond the evidence provided.
Now it is important to hold in our minds that we are still reasoning, not imagining! The results of inductive logic can be every bit as robust and trust worthy as any deductions. Where they differ is that they often cause us to work hard to transform the conditions we have into new propositions.
How does this show up in everyday life?

Cases (Algebraic Induction): When you see a folder icon like this * , you do not know what files are contained inside. But you do know how to find out. You simply have to open the folder * . The files will then be displayed, for example: ******* . You had cases to follow that would eventually lead to answers or more cases.
Relations: When you see a number like 541 you cannot ask if it is “true” or “false”. But you can ask: Is 541 even? Is 541 < 1024? Is 541 prime? You turned data into judgments.
Default Logic: Birds can fly. Well that is until you see a photo * and now you realize this is one of those flightless birds. Your default assumptions are updated.
Probability: It is possible your will get randomly selected for Jury Duty during the final, but probably not. You should study.

We will unroll this over the next for modules take each form of inductive reasoning one at a time beginning here with cases.


 * Objectives

Recognize inductive reasoning.
Use pattern matching idioms in software.
Apply recursion.
Model the algebra of induction in both producing and consuming roles.

title: Pattern Making & its Co-operators
text:
One day Dada created a file. She named the file "Top-Secret-Read-Immediately.txt" and started typing out a story, each line adding to the story so that file grew. Almost as quick as things started, the story was over. Dada transmitted the straight to Codaydeh.
Codaydeh immediately opened the file and started to scroll, each line appearing one after other. The story was amazing! What a mystery, what would happen next? Codaydeh scrolled further but nothing happened! The file just stopped, mid sentence. There was nothing more there. This couldn’t be right? Had some of the file been cut off in transmission? Or was Dada suddenly interrupted?



The allegory of sending a file is an archetype of a form of reasoning we all face in everyday life but which presents several challenges to computation. While we would like to think of the file as one piece of data, its creation and its uses are spread apart, often separated by time and space. The separation means that the data will need a number of intermediate uses. We have already seen how we make a data type that breaks down into parts, an “Inductive Type”. This is like the letter writer Dada. There are prescribe number of ways to make the data (introduction rules)
\(\text{case }1: A^{d_1}\to A\) \(\text{case }2: A^{d_2}\to A\),…, \(\text{case }m: A^{d_m}\to A\)
We can shorten this one one function
\(\text{combined case}: A^{d_1}\sqcup A^{d_2}\sqcup \cdots\sqcup A^{d_m}\to A\)
There is only one way to use this data: match each pattern of introduction (construction) and give each of those a role.



Screenshot 2026-02-22 at 9.16.11 PM.png


There is only one elimination rule (use) for the packaged data and it is determined by identifying the uses of the individual means to package the data. Need a little more review? Go through the lab 6 slides here.



Now let’s take the perspective of the letter reader. When Codaydeh receives a transmission he knew just what to do and starts taking in line by line text. There is only once source of the data but many uses. The data could be broken into words, then characters, those could be printed in some font, shown an a screen, saved to a file, who knows. But we don’t need to know the use to know the work is to take this single source and divide it up into parts we can use. That means we can focus on the many elimination rules but need only one introduction rule. The trick is to reverse the semantics, all arrows go the opposite direction. Let us start by reversing the operators.


Suppose we expect that our algebra packaged data up using operators \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \cdots \sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_n}\to \mathbb{U}\). Then when we get a data from \(\mathbb{U}\) then we should expect it was made from one of the terms \(\mathbb{U}^{d_i}\). So we just need to reverse this. That is, we need a function \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\). How do we make it? Let make \(n=2\) to keep things easy.
Step 1. Remember that \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\) is type based on OR, and so it has 2 introduction rules, one for \(\iota_1:\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\) and \(\iota_2:\mathbb{U}^{d_2}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\).
Step 2. We need to test the incoming \(u:\mathbb{U}\) to know if it came from the left \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\) or right \(\mathbb{U}^{d_2}\). Whichever one it is we can make a function \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\) or \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\) and then compose it with \(\iota_1\) or \(\iota_2\).



Screenshot 2026-02-24 at 10.23.23 PM.png


The point is we can get form \(\mathbb{U}\) to \(\mathbb{U}^{d_1}\sqcup \mathbb{U}^{d_2}\).
Now the precise mechanics to allow this is subtle and requires the programming language called “destructors” or “unapply”. In particular there is not function \(\mathbb{U}\to \mathbb{U}^{d_1}\) because not every input comes from that side. We test to be sure but it means that this side of our program is technically not “tapeable function”. So there is a special process within the logic that lets us use this as “partial function”. You can ignore this, but it feels right to tell you that sometimes logic needs to go deeper.
Fortunately most modern programming languages include some nice notation to hide the mechanics and make it easy to use. Here’s a program that hides the work. We have a file that can have an End Of File (EOF) or we can have a character a:Char and a file tail:File and we want to add a to the file at position p. This would formally be the following function type.
\(\displaystyle \text{EOF}: \mathbb{U}^0\to \mathbb{U}\) and \(\displaystyle \text{Insert}(a,p) : \mathbb{U}^1\to \mathbb{U}\)
which means when unified as a single operator we have
\(displaystyle \text{all-ops} : \left(\mathbb{U}^0\sqcup \bigsqcup_{a:\text{Char}} \bigsqcup_{p:\text{Int}} \mathbb{U}^1\right)\longrightarrow \mathbb{U}\)
Thus the co-operators will reverse this array
\(displaystyle \text{co-ops} : \mathbb{U} \longrightarrow \left(\mathbb{U}^0\sqcup \bigsqcup_{a:\text{Char}} \bigsqcup_{p:\text{Int}} \mathbb{U}^1\right)\)
Let’s call this co-operator unpack and see how close we can get with software.

OCaml ExampleScala ExampleJava ExampleAgda Example


type file =
| EOF
| Insert of char * int * file

let unpack (f : file) : (file array, (char * int) * file array) Either.t =
match f with
| EOF -> Either.Left [||]
| Insert (c, p, rest) -> Either.Right ((c, p), [|rest|])
This approach shows the two possible returns, a File array, or a file array indexed by a character and a position. However it falls short in that it does not have the lengths of these arrays which are in fact known to us. We can achieve this by removing the array type and using the specific number.


enum File:
case EOF
case Insert(c: Char, p: Int, rest: File)

def unpack(f: File): Either[Array[File], ((Char, Int), Array[File])] =
f match
case File.EOF => Left(Array.empty[File])
case File.Insert(c, p, rest) => Right(((c, p), Array(rest)))


import java.util.Optional;

sealed interface File permits File.EOF, File.Insert {
record EOF() implements File {}
record Insert(char c, int p, File rest) implements File {}
}

class FileUnpack {
static Object unpack(File f) {
return switch (f) {
case File.EOF eof -> eof;
case File.Insert ins -> new CharFilePair(ins.c(), ins.p(), ins.rest());
};
}

record CharFilePair(char c, int p, File rest) {}
}


open import Data.Char
open import Data.Nat
open import Data.Sum using (_⊎_; inj₁; inj₂)
open import Data.Product using (_×_; _,_)

data File : Set where
EOF    : File
Insert : Char → ℕ → File → File

unpack : File → File ⊎ ((Char × ℕ) × File)
unpack EOF = inj₁ EOF
unpack (Insert c p rest) = inj₂ ((c , p), rest)







Now that we have seen how to unpack operators with co-operators we now need to link them to other co-operators. We continue to reverse the picture.



Screenshot 2026-02-24 at 7.31.42 PM.png


We can use this to convert our file into glyphs and display it on a screen. We can also use it to convert JSON into a screen image or convert to another format like HTTP or UPD to transmit it through the internet. The game keeps going.

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
Week 6 Inductive Reasoning
We are now launching our second of three major units on reasoning. So far we have focussed on
Deductive Logic: reasoning from the evidence provided.
Now we will focus on a much more realistic but nuanced form of reasoning where we have incomplete evidence and still need to make logical decisions.
Inductive Logic: reasoning beyond the evidence provided.

 Where do we use Inductive Logic?
If you read the definition “reason beyond the evidence” you might begin to worry if this is scientific, certainly it would seem dubious as mathematics which tries to be completely proof based. But what if you attempt to read a complex math formula like the following one.



LaTeX: 


For most of use this formula will be too long to absorb all at once. Instead we are very likely to begin to read it from top-to-bottom, left-to-right under the hypothesis that it will indeed reveal itself as a complete mathematical formula. When we read the numerator we don’t yet have the evidence that the denominator will be a math formula. We are reasoning beyond our evidence. And in fact it is only when we get to the very end that we find in disappointment that it was not a standard math formula because it had a stray typo, an ? that should probably have been something else. But look back, was this any less “logical” to proceed under a hypothesis that we had a formula? Probably not. We can imagine that most of the time we don’t encounter flaws and this induction—reasoning beyond the evidence—was every bit as “logical” as our examples of deductive logic.


 Where is inductive logic in computation?
Much of the data we make or use is complex which literally means it is made out of parts, like a building complex that has several smaller buildings linked together. An example of this is JSON blob that stores social network data as a mix of GPS coordinates, text messages, images, id numbers and much more. Reasoning about complex data doesn’t have to be “complex”, as in “complicated”, but it does benefit from a strategy. The strategy that logic attaches to the study of complex data is known as induction. What it means in this case is that we do not try to understand the entire JSON blob all at once. Instead we learn a series of simpler rules to reason locally under the assumption that when we see the whole data it will make sense. At any one stage we are forced to “reason beyond the evidence we have”. In retrospect the logic we have seen up to this point should be known as deductive. Induction comes from the word “induce” and the idea of induction is to study complex events as mix of smaller evidence that that induce us towards an understanding of the whole.



Screenshot 2026-02-21 at 8.10.17 PM.png




 * Objectives

Recognize inductive reasoning.
Use pattern matching idioms in software.
Apply recursion.
Model the algebra of induction in both producing and consuming roles.
