*12.1.a
** Measurements
 In a ruler the whole is the sum of its parts… or is it? Sometimes illusions deserve attention.

 *An illusion with a Lesson
There is an illusion so convincing it has earned its own Wikipedia article. It takes a triangle, cuts it into polygons, and rearranges them. Yet once re-arranged, the parts no longer cover the original area! These diagrams of curtesy of Original: CC-BY Krauss. 



The missing area puzzle.


Does the surprise you? While this is an illusion (explained below) the reason it works as a brain teaser is that we are conditioned to understand area does not get lost amongst the parts. Our mind hunts for an explanation. This should not be possible, we believe.


 Explanation of the puzzle
The main clue to offer to the illusion is to point out that the first triangle is not actually a triangle, but a pentagon. So the lower triangle has slightly different angles than the upper one. So put together they do not make one large triangle but a polygon. You can detect this better if we exaggerate the difference in angle.



Missing square puzzle


So what appears as a hypotenuse of a large triangle is in fact dented, and thus looses a small amount of area which our eyes fail to detect. When we rearrange the parts we do not see the an area disappear. In fact the opposite. By rearranging the parts we gather the missing area form the dent into one place where its far more noticeable. Area, as we think of it, truly is the sum of its parts.


 *Integral measurements: The details and Examples
So as seen in the video the world around us has dozens of natural way to glue data together. Whether that be a sum like (x+y) or a disjoint union (XY), addition of resistance, pressure, sales prices and so much more. These quite often behave in just the way the need for the whole to be the sum of its parts. And it introduces an opportunity to use common stories of length and area as metaphors for the often complicated seeming calculations we find ourselves doing. So for the next three parts we explore this technology. We begin by formally declare what is a measurement.


 Measures & Measurable sets
Let () be a set of data. A (signed)measure on () is function defined on various subsets called “measurable subsets” with the quality

Whole is the sum of its parts. Given a possibly unending list of measurable subsets (X_1,X_2,) then the union is measurable. In fact, if they are pairwise disjoint (no two have a point in common) then their measure is precisely

\[\mu(X_1 \sqcup X_2\sqcup \cdots) = \mu(X_1) + \mu(X_2)+\cdots\in [-\infty,\infty]\]%2520%253D%2520%255Cmu(X_1)%2520%252B%2520%255Cmu(X_2)%252B%255Ccdots%255Cin%2520%255B-%255Cinfty%252C%255Cinfty%255D?scale=1)

The measuring of nothing is 0. The empty subset ({}=) should be measurable with measure (()=0).
Complements are measurable. If a subset (X) is measurable then so is its complement (-X={X}).

If we want to think of () in function terms then

The domain is the power set \[\text{Prop}^{\Omega}\] (or simply \[2^{\Omega}\] in classical mathematics).
The codomain is \[[-\infty,\infty]^?=\text{decimal number}, \pm\infty,\text{ or } \text{non-measurable}\].

We may write \[\mu:\text{Prop}^{\Omega}\to [-\infty,\infty]^?\] or in software something akin to def measure( as : Collection[A] ) : Float? the precise collection may be something like List, Array, Set, Tree, HashTable etc. and the name of the function will typically depicts its role, e.g. length, weight, word_count, etc.
If negative measures are excluded (e.g. as in length or area) the we speak of a “positive measure” even though 0 is allowed.


 *Example Measurements


 Example 1**: Lebesgue’s Interval Distance measurement \[\lambda\].
The most common measurement by far is to consider a line interval \[I\] from a point \[x_0\] to a point \[x_1\]. This actually has many flavors including:
\[\begin{aligned}
(x_0,x_1) & = \{ x\mid x_0\lt x\lt x_1\} & (x_0,x_1] & = \{ x\mid x_0\lt x\leq x_1\}\\
[x_0,x_1) & = \{ x\mid x_0\leq x\lt x_1\} & [x_0,x_1] & = \{ x\mid x_0\leq x\leq x_1\}
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Clt%2520x%255Clt%2520x_1%255C%257D%2520%2526%2520(x_0%252Cx_1%255D%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Clt%2520x%255Cleq%2520x_1%255C%257D%255C%255C%250A%255Bx_0%252Cx_1)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Cleq%2520x%255Clt%2520x_1%255C%257D%2520%2526%2520%255Bx_0%252Cx_1%255D%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Cleq%2520x%255Cleq%2520x_1%255C%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Whether you include the final point at the end of an interval doesn’t mean much to the length of the interval, after all a point has negligible thickness in most context. So to each of these intervals we assign a single measurement which is so important that instead of () it gets its own special name (m) and is called the Lebesgue measure.
Each of the above interavals we assign “Lebesgue Measure”: \[\lambda(I) = | x_1-x_0 |\]%2520%253D%2520%257C%2520x_1-x_0%2520%257C?scale=1)
Now this is not yet a measure until we allow for multiple disjoint intervals \[I_1\sqcup I_2\sqcup\cdots\]
General Unsigned Distance “Lebesgue Measure”: \[\lambda(I_1\sqcup I_2\sqcup \cdots ) = \sum_i \lambda(I_i) = \lambda (I_1)+\lambda(I_2)+\cdots\]%2520%253D%2520%255Csum_i%2520%255Clambda(I_i)%2520%253D%2520%255Clambda%2520(I_1)%252B%255Clambda(I_2)%252B%255Ccdots%2520?scale=1)
So to measure the shaded regions below we first measure the disjoint parts, \[\lambda(I_1)=|(-1.5)-(-3)|=1.5\]%253D%257C(-1.5)-(-3)%257C%253D1.5?scale=1), \[\lambda(I_2)=|2-1|=1\]%253D%257C2-1%257C%253D1?scale=1), and add them together to get \[\lambda(I_1\sqcup I_2)=\lambda(I_1)+\lambda(I_2)=1.5+1=2.5\]%253D%255Clambda(I_1)%252B%255Clambda(I_2)%253D1.5%252B1%253D2.5?scale=1).



Number line with blue shading between -3 and -1.5 and red shading between 1 and 2.


Notice the close relationship to total change:
Signed Distance “Displacement”: \[\Delta x = x_1-x_0\]
Displacement is measured on a pair of numbers, not an interval. And because of this the order of the pair matters. For example 5-2=3 but 2-5=-3. Displacement offers an alternative measure which we often use along side Lebesgue measures whenever we need to consider concepts like debt, negative potential, depreciation, and related metrics.

As a weird quirk in history, the sets that can be measured as intervals are called “Borel sets” and they are “Lebesgue measurable”. Both these mathematicians made great contributions to the details of measurement. But if we are honest, this measurement was known to stone masons and carpenters and perhaps even some species of dogs long before their involvement. They merely made sure the mathematics was a precise as possible.


 Example 2**: Lebesgue’s Area Measure \[\lambda\times \lambda\]
The concept of distance generalizes to area, and then volumes. Obviously the measure of a rectangle is width times height.



2-D measure of a rectangle and an oval.


If we expect a measure then the total shaded area is the sum of the disjoint shaded areas, i.e. our square (I_1) in blue on the left and our ellipse (I_2) on the right. We will call this the Lebesque measure as well, only now in 2-D. So what is this measure? The shaded rectangle is partitioned into 9 blue sub-squares. So the whole being the sum of its parts, we should declare that measure to be 9.
\[\displaystyle (\lambda\times \lambda)\Big( (a,b)\times (c,d) \Big) = \lambda\Big((a,b)\Big) \cdot \lambda\Big( (c,d)\Big)=|b-a|\cdot |d-c|\]%255CBig(%2520(a%252Cb)%255Ctimes%2520(c%252Cd)%2520%255CBig)%2520%253D%2520%255Clambda%255CBig((a%252Cb)%255CBig)%2520%255Ccdot%2520%255Clambda%255CBig(%2520(c%252Cd)%255CBig)%253D%257Cb-a%257C%255Ccdot%2520%257Cd-c%257C?scale=1).
This is part of general strategy we can combine two measures () and () as a product.
\[\displaystyle (\mu\times \nu)( I\times J)  = \mu(I)\times \nu(J)\](%2520I%255Ctimes%2520J)%2520%2520%253D%2520%255Cmu(I)%255Ctimes%2520%255Cnu(J)?scale=1)
Now the ellipse posses a problem. So far we have only considered rectangles as having area. But this is not a rectangle. Yet we do get some clear clues about the way to make an approximation of the area. We can count rectangles that approximate the ellipse. That number here is at least 4 and at most 8. We could get a better estimate by looking at a finer grid and eventually looking for a limit.

Warning: When don’t we have a measure? Suppose instead of area we looked at the picture above and asked to measure “how tall is the shaded region?”

Option 1. Suppose we understand this sentence as asking how many boxes high is enough to fit both pictures, and we can count the blue box as 3 high and the ellipse as 2. So 3 is enough. If we did this we would be answering the question correctly but also demonstrating we do not have a measure. That is the whole has measure 3, and the parts have measures 3 and 2 but (3+2). If we really wanted to include this as a measure then we would need to revisit the idea that the two shapes are disjoint. While they are disjoint in the xy-plane they are not disjoint in the y direction alone. And so in that sense this is not a violation of measurement rules, just a misunderstanding about the meaning of disjoint for this case. An “illusion” as we have been warned about already.
Option 2. An alternative reading of this question is to ask if we stack up the shapes how tall would they be? Here we would in fact add 3 to 2 to get 5. This would be a measure as the whole would be the sum of the parts.

It is crucially important to be precise in our language of measurement. Many times a miscommunication or imprecise phrasing can lead to errors in measurement.


 Example 3:** Counting Measure \[\zeta\]
Given (E), the number of integers in (E) is the counting measure. As formula:
\[\displaystyle \zeta(E) := |E\cap \mathbb{Z}|\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%257CE%255Ccap%2520%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%257C?scale=1).
Notice this often does take different values on intervals
\[\begin{aligned}
\zeta\Big( (0,1) \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n<1\}| = |\{\}|=0 &
\zeta\Big( [0,1) \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n<1\}| = |\{ 0 \}|=1\\
\zeta\Big( (0,1] \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n<1\}| = |\{1\}|=1 &
\zeta\Big( [0,1] \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n<1\}| = |\{ 0,1 \}|=2
\end{aligned}\]%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%253Cn%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%255C%257D%257C%253D0%2520%2526%2520%250A%255Czeta%255CBig(%2520%255B0%252C1)%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%255Cleq%2520n%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%25200%2520%255C%257D%257C%253D1%255C%255C%250A%255Czeta%255CBig(%2520(0%252C1%255D%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%253Cn%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B1%255C%257D%257C%253D1%2520%2526%2520%250A%255Czeta%255CBig(%2520%255B0%252C1%255D%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%255Cleq%2520n%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%25200%252C1%2520%255C%257D%257C%253D2%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Some common places to encounter a counting measure like this include:

Counting the number of steps in a loop, e.g. for i in [a...b] Use \[\zeta([a,b])\]?scale=1).
Counting the number of steps in a loop, e.g. for i in [a...b] step 2 Use \[\zeta(\{ 2m+j \mid 0\leq m\leq b-a\})\]?scale=1).
You need to count steps of two nested loops, use \[\zeta\times \zeta\].



 Example 4:** Kolmogorov’s Probability Measures \[\kappa\], a coin flip example
Suppose you have a coin with Heads H and tails T. The simplest thing to measure is the probability of the two individual outcomes. Here space (={H,T}) and the measure is the uniform measure: \[\displaystyle \kappa=\frac{|X|}{|\Omega|}\]. That is:
\[\begin{aligned}
\kappa (\{\}) & = 0  & \kappa(\{H\}) & =\frac{1}{2} & \kappa(\{T\}) & = \frac{1}{2} & \kappa(\{H,T\})=\frac{2}{2}=1.
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%25200%2520%2520%2526%2520%255Ckappa(%255C%257BH%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%253D%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%2526%2520%255Ckappa(%255C%257BT%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%2526%2520%255Ckappa(%255C%257BH%252CT%255C%257D)%253D%255Cfrac%257B2%257D%257B2%257D%253D1.%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Now the more interesting probability is to continue coin flips and see what patterns emerge.


 First flip is heads
.The first flip is heads: ({EE_1=H}). This covers half the options and its measure is 1/2.



Probability tree of coin flips with the branches that start with heads highlighted.




 First flip is tails, second heads
The first flip is tails and second flip is heads: ({EE_1=T, E_2=H}). This covers 1/4 of the options and its measure is 1/2.



Probability tree of coin flips with the branches that start with tails and then heads highlighted.




 Every even flip is tails
Every even flip is tails: (C={EE_{2n}=T}).



Probability of coin flips with branches highlighted if every even flip is tails.


As flips continue the ones that survive a spread out and do not form a customary length. So the right measure here has to come from our understanding of probability laws instead. We can talk of this measure by considering the limit of the proportion, which decreases by 2 every time we reach an even flip (because only half of those are T). In fact, while somewhat boring to do by hand, a computer can just move the symbols around according to the formal rules to get the same answer.
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(\{E\mid \forall n.(E_{2n}=T)\}) & =\text{Prob}\left(\bigcap_{n} \{E\mid E_{2n}=T\}\right)\\
& = \prod_{n} \text{Prob}(\{E\mid E_{2n}=0\}) & \text{Conditional Probability}\\
& = \prod_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{2} = \lim_{k\to \infty}\prod_{n=1}^k \frac{1}{2}\\
& = \lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{1}{2^k}
=0
\end{aligned}\]%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%253D%255Ctext%257BProb%257D%255Cleft(%255Cbigcap_%257Bn%257D%2520%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_%257B2n%257D%253DT%255C%257D%255Cright)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cprod_%257Bn%257D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_%257B2n%257D%253D0%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257BConditional%2520Probability%257D%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cprod_%257Bn%253D0%257D%255E%255Cinfty%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%253D%2520%255Clim_%257Bk%255Cto%2520%255Cinfty%257D%255Cprod_%257Bn%253D1%257D%255Ek%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Clim_%257Bk%255Cto%2520%255Cinfty%257D%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%255Ek%257D%250A%2520%253D0%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1).


 Disjoint events
Disjoint events in probability add their probabilities. This the same rule as measures. The following illustration with coin flips demonstrates this.



Coin flips with two independent events. The blue start with heads, the red begin tails-heads.


We can turn this measurement over to computers.

(A={EE_1=H}) is the set of coin flips where the first flip lands H.
(B={EE_1=T E_{2}=H}) is the set of coin flips where the first flip is T and the second flip lands H.

Notice (AB={}) (because the first flip cannot be both heads and tails). So these two are disjoint.
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(A\sqcup B)  & = \text{Prob}(A)+\text{Prob}(B)\\
& = \text{Prob}(E_1=H) + \text{Prob}(E_{1}=T)\cdot \text{Prob}(E_2=H)\\
&= \frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} =  \frac{3}{4}
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(A)%252B%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(B)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(E_1%253DH)%2520%252B%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(E_%257B1%257D%253DT)%255Ccdot%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(E_2%253DH)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%252B%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%255Ccdot%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%253D%2520%2520%255Cfrac%257B3%257D%257B4%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D%25C2%25A0?scale=1)


 Overlapping events
Non-disjoint sets measures are not directly defined. But probabilities are not just any measure, and these have a solution directly.



Overlapping events cannot be measured as their sum because they are not disjoint.


This would be a good place to pause and notice the essential role of disjoint unions. Suppose we used (C={EE_2=T}) instead of (B). Now
(AC ={EE_1=H, E_2=T})
So now (A) and (C) are not disjoint, and this affects our probability measure
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(A\cup C)
& = \text{Prob}(\{E\mid E_1=H \text{ or }E_2=T\})\\
& = \text{Prob}(\{E\mid E_1=H\}\sqcup \{ E\mid E_1=T, E_2=T\})\\
& = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}\\
\text{Prob}(A)+\text{Prob}(C) & = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1\neq \frac{3}{4}
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2520%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_1%253DH%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520or%2520%257DE_2%253DT%255C%257D)%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_1%253DH%255C%257D%255Csqcup%2520%255C%257B%2520E%255Cmid%2520E_1%253DT%252C%2520E_2%253DT%255C%257D)%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%252B%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B4%257D%253D%255Cfrac%257B3%257D%257B4%257D%255C%255C%250A%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(A)%252B%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(C)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%252B%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%253D1%255Cneq%2520%255Cfrac%257B3%257D%257B4%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D%25C2%25A0?scale=1)
So be careful to check on the disjoint condition when using measures and if measures alone are not enough information, look at your context to see something else will help.


 Example 5**: Gaussian’s Probability Measure \[\gamma\]
Recall the second distribution for probability was useful when data had a target value but would wobble off target with some predictable variation. This was known as Gaussian distribution. See more here Probability unit. The Gaussian Measure applies to decimal numbers (x) and measures them on the “Bell curve” by the following formula.
\[\displaystyle \gamma(X) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}\]%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B%255Csigma%2520%255Csqrt%257B2%255Cpi%257D%257D%2520e%255E%257B-%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%255Cleft(%255Cfrac%257Bx-%255Cmu%257D%257B%255Csigma%257D%255Cright)%255E2%257D?scale=1)
where () is the average value “center of the bell curve” (not a measure!) and () is the standard deviation (how wide the bell is). Below we plot the curve for a bell with deviation () and mean ().



A bell curve centered at mean 0 with deviation 1.


For most people it is not important that you memorize this formula, but notice it is qualitatively different from both the distance and uniform measures.


 *Calculations & Implications
Suppose that () is a positive measure. Then all of the following are true.

Bigger subsets get bigger measures: If \[A\subset B\] and both are measurable then \[\mu(A)\leq \mu(B)\]%255Cleq%2520%255Cmu(B)?scale=1).
If you steadily approximate a measure from below you will reach the measure. If \[A_1\subset A_2\subset\cdots\] are all measurable then \[\displaystyle \mu\Big(\bigcup_i A_i\Big)=\lim_{i\to\infty} \mu(A_i)=\sup_{i} \mu(A_i)\]%253D%255Clim_%257Bi%255Cto%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Cmu(A_i)%253D%255Csup_%257Bi%257D%2520%255Cmu(A_i)?scale=1).
If you steadily approximate a finite measure from above you will reach it. If \[A_1\supset A_2\supset\cdots\] are all measurable and \[\infty\gt \mu(A_1)\]?scale=1) then \[\displaystyle \mu\Big(\bigcap_i A_i\Big)=\lim_{i\to\infty} \mu(A_i)=\inf_i \{\mu(A_i)\}\]%253D%255Clim_%257Bi%255Cto%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Cmu(A_i)%253D%255Cinf_i%2520%255C%257B%255Cmu(A_i)%255C%257D?scale=1).


 Example Calculation of Measures.

Using the Lebesgue interval measure () from above, to compute (((1,3)) and measure this as (((1,4])=4-1=3).
Using the Lebesgue interval measure () from above, to compute (({1})) first find a way to write this as an interval, e.g. ([1,1]). Then (([1,1])=|1-1|=0)
\[\mu(E)=7\]%253D7?scale=1) and \[\mu(F)=8\]%253D8?scale=1) so is \[\mu(E\cup F)\geq 8\]%255Cgeq%25208?scale=1)? Well since \[F\subset E\cup F\] then \[8=\mu(F)\leq \mu(E\cup F)\]%255Cleq%2520%255Cmu(E%255Ccup%2520F)?scale=1) so yes.
[Hard] To compute \[\displaystyle \lambda\Big(\bigcap_n \left(0,\frac{1}{n}\right)\Big)\]%255CBig)?scale=1) first notice \[\lambda((0,1))=|1-0|=1 \lt \infty\])%253D%257C1-0%257C%253D1%2520%255Clt%2520%255Cinfty?scale=1). So by the rule 3. above, \[\displaystyle \lambda\Big(\bigcap_n (0,1/n)\Big)=\lim_{n\to \infty} \lambda((0,1/n)=\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}=0\]%255CBig)%253D%255Clim_%257Bn%255Cto%2520%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Clambda((0%252C1%252Fn)%253D%255Clim_%257Bn%255Cto%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257Bn%257D%253D0?scale=1).




 *Quick Check

What is the signed measure \[\Delta (-\infty,1]\]. - It is \[\infty\] *


Correct: \[\Delta(-\infty,1)=1-(-\infty)=1+\infty=\infty\]%253D1-(-%255Cinfty)%253D1%252B%255Cinfty%253D%255Cinfty?scale=1) - It is \[-\infty\] *\[\Delta(-\infty,1)=1-(-\infty)=1+\infty=\infty\]%253D1-(-%255Cinfty)%253D1%252B%255Cinfty%253D%255Cinfty?scale=1)



 * Fill-in-the-Blank

Lebesgue’s Interval Measure \[\lambda((1,3)\sqcup (4,7])=\]%255Csqcup%2520(4%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)5 .
Lebesgue’s Interval Measure \[\lambda((1,4)\cup (3,7])=\]%255Ccup%2520(3%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)6 .
Counting Measure \[\zeta((1,3)\sqcup (4,7])=\]%255Csqcup%2520(4%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)4
Lebesgue’s Interval Measure \[\lambda((1,4)\cup (3,7])=\]%255Ccup%2520(3%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)6 .



 * Quick Check

If \[\mu(E)=0\]%253D0?scale=1) then \[E=\emptyset\] - True *
No, while \[\mu(\emptyset)=0\]%253D0?scale=1) that is on the only way, consider any one of \[\lambda(\{3\})=0\]%253D0?scale=1) or \[\zeta((0,1))=0\])%253D0?scale=1) - False *


Correct: consider any one of \[\lambda(\{3\})=0\]%253D0?scale=1) or \[\zeta((0,1))=0\])%253D0?scale=1)

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
*12.1.a
** Measurements
 In a ruler the whole is the sum of its parts… or is it? Sometimes illusions deserve attention.

 *An illusion with a Lesson
There is an illusion so convincing it has earned its own Wikipedia article. It takes a triangle, cuts it into polygons, and rearranges them. Yet once re-arranged, the parts no longer cover the original area! These diagrams of curtesy of Original: CC-BY Krauss. 



The missing area puzzle.


Does the surprise you? While this is an illusion (explained below) the reason it works as a brain teaser is that we are conditioned to understand area does not get lost amongst the parts. Our mind hunts for an explanation. This should not be possible, we believe.


 Explanation of the puzzle
The main clue to offer to the illusion is to point out that the first triangle is not actually a triangle, but a pentagon. So the lower triangle has slightly different angles than the upper one. So put together they do not make one large triangle but a polygon. You can detect this better if we exaggerate the difference in angle.



Missing square puzzle


So what appears as a hypotenuse of a large triangle is in fact dented, and thus looses a small amount of area which our eyes fail to detect. When we rearrange the parts we do not see the an area disappear. In fact the opposite. By rearranging the parts we gather the missing area form the dent into one place where its far more noticeable. Area, as we think of it, truly is the sum of its parts.


 *Integral measurements: The details and Examples
So as seen in the video the world around us has dozens of natural way to glue data together. Whether that be a sum like (x+y) or a disjoint union (XY), addition of resistance, pressure, sales prices and so much more. These quite often behave in just the way the need for the whole to be the sum of its parts. And it introduces an opportunity to use common stories of length and area as metaphors for the often complicated seeming calculations we find ourselves doing. So for the next three parts we explore this technology. We begin by formally declare what is a measurement.


 Measures & Measurable sets
Let () be a set of data. A (signed)measure on () is function defined on various subsets called “measurable subsets” with the quality

Whole is the sum of its parts. Given a possibly unending list of measurable subsets (X_1,X_2,) then the union is measurable. In fact, if they are pairwise disjoint (no two have a point in common) then their measure is precisely

\[\mu(X_1 \sqcup X_2\sqcup \cdots) = \mu(X_1) + \mu(X_2)+\cdots\in [-\infty,\infty]\]%2520%253D%2520%255Cmu(X_1)%2520%252B%2520%255Cmu(X_2)%252B%255Ccdots%255Cin%2520%255B-%255Cinfty%252C%255Cinfty%255D?scale=1)

The measuring of nothing is 0. The empty subset ({}=) should be measurable with measure (()=0).
Complements are measurable. If a subset (X) is measurable then so is its complement (-X={X}).

If we want to think of () in function terms then

The domain is the power set \[\text{Prop}^{\Omega}\] (or simply \[2^{\Omega}\] in classical mathematics).
The codomain is \[[-\infty,\infty]^?=\text{decimal number}, \pm\infty,\text{ or } \text{non-measurable}\].

We may write \[\mu:\text{Prop}^{\Omega}\to [-\infty,\infty]^?\] or in software something akin to def measure( as : Collection[A] ) : Float? the precise collection may be something like List, Array, Set, Tree, HashTable etc. and the name of the function will typically depicts its role, e.g. length, weight, word_count, etc.
If negative measures are excluded (e.g. as in length or area) the we speak of a “positive measure” even though 0 is allowed.


 *Example Measurements


 Example 1**: Lebesgue’s Interval Distance measurement \[\lambda\].
The most common measurement by far is to consider a line interval \[I\] from a point \[x_0\] to a point \[x_1\]. This actually has many flavors including:
\[\begin{aligned}
(x_0,x_1) & = \{ x\mid x_0\lt x\lt x_1\} & (x_0,x_1] & = \{ x\mid x_0\lt x\leq x_1\}\\
[x_0,x_1) & = \{ x\mid x_0\leq x\lt x_1\} & [x_0,x_1] & = \{ x\mid x_0\leq x\leq x_1\}
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Clt%2520x%255Clt%2520x_1%255C%257D%2520%2526%2520(x_0%252Cx_1%255D%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Clt%2520x%255Cleq%2520x_1%255C%257D%255C%255C%250A%255Bx_0%252Cx_1)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Cleq%2520x%255Clt%2520x_1%255C%257D%2520%2526%2520%255Bx_0%252Cx_1%255D%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255C%257B%2520x%255Cmid%2520x_0%255Cleq%2520x%255Cleq%2520x_1%255C%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Whether you include the final point at the end of an interval doesn’t mean much to the length of the interval, after all a point has negligible thickness in most context. So to each of these intervals we assign a single measurement which is so important that instead of () it gets its own special name (m) and is called the Lebesgue measure.
Each of the above interavals we assign “Lebesgue Measure”: \[\lambda(I) = | x_1-x_0 |\]%2520%253D%2520%257C%2520x_1-x_0%2520%257C?scale=1)
Now this is not yet a measure until we allow for multiple disjoint intervals \[I_1\sqcup I_2\sqcup\cdots\]
General Unsigned Distance “Lebesgue Measure”: \[\lambda(I_1\sqcup I_2\sqcup \cdots ) = \sum_i \lambda(I_i) = \lambda (I_1)+\lambda(I_2)+\cdots\]%2520%253D%2520%255Csum_i%2520%255Clambda(I_i)%2520%253D%2520%255Clambda%2520(I_1)%252B%255Clambda(I_2)%252B%255Ccdots%2520?scale=1)
So to measure the shaded regions below we first measure the disjoint parts, \[\lambda(I_1)=|(-1.5)-(-3)|=1.5\]%253D%257C(-1.5)-(-3)%257C%253D1.5?scale=1), \[\lambda(I_2)=|2-1|=1\]%253D%257C2-1%257C%253D1?scale=1), and add them together to get \[\lambda(I_1\sqcup I_2)=\lambda(I_1)+\lambda(I_2)=1.5+1=2.5\]%253D%255Clambda(I_1)%252B%255Clambda(I_2)%253D1.5%252B1%253D2.5?scale=1).



Number line with blue shading between -3 and -1.5 and red shading between 1 and 2.


Notice the close relationship to total change:
Signed Distance “Displacement”: \[\Delta x = x_1-x_0\]
Displacement is measured on a pair of numbers, not an interval. And because of this the order of the pair matters. For example 5-2=3 but 2-5=-3. Displacement offers an alternative measure which we often use along side Lebesgue measures whenever we need to consider concepts like debt, negative potential, depreciation, and related metrics.

As a weird quirk in history, the sets that can be measured as intervals are called “Borel sets” and they are “Lebesgue measurable”. Both these mathematicians made great contributions to the details of measurement. But if we are honest, this measurement was known to stone masons and carpenters and perhaps even some species of dogs long before their involvement. They merely made sure the mathematics was a precise as possible.


 Example 2**: Lebesgue’s Area Measure \[\lambda\times \lambda\]
The concept of distance generalizes to area, and then volumes. Obviously the measure of a rectangle is width times height.



2-D measure of a rectangle and an oval.


If we expect a measure then the total shaded area is the sum of the disjoint shaded areas, i.e. our square (I_1) in blue on the left and our ellipse (I_2) on the right. We will call this the Lebesque measure as well, only now in 2-D. So what is this measure? The shaded rectangle is partitioned into 9 blue sub-squares. So the whole being the sum of its parts, we should declare that measure to be 9.
\[\displaystyle (\lambda\times \lambda)\Big( (a,b)\times (c,d) \Big) = \lambda\Big((a,b)\Big) \cdot \lambda\Big( (c,d)\Big)=|b-a|\cdot |d-c|\]%255CBig(%2520(a%252Cb)%255Ctimes%2520(c%252Cd)%2520%255CBig)%2520%253D%2520%255Clambda%255CBig((a%252Cb)%255CBig)%2520%255Ccdot%2520%255Clambda%255CBig(%2520(c%252Cd)%255CBig)%253D%257Cb-a%257C%255Ccdot%2520%257Cd-c%257C?scale=1).
This is part of general strategy we can combine two measures () and () as a product.
\[\displaystyle (\mu\times \nu)( I\times J)  = \mu(I)\times \nu(J)\](%2520I%255Ctimes%2520J)%2520%2520%253D%2520%255Cmu(I)%255Ctimes%2520%255Cnu(J)?scale=1)
Now the ellipse posses a problem. So far we have only considered rectangles as having area. But this is not a rectangle. Yet we do get some clear clues about the way to make an approximation of the area. We can count rectangles that approximate the ellipse. That number here is at least 4 and at most 8. We could get a better estimate by looking at a finer grid and eventually looking for a limit.

Warning: When don’t we have a measure? Suppose instead of area we looked at the picture above and asked to measure “how tall is the shaded region?”

Option 1. Suppose we understand this sentence as asking how many boxes high is enough to fit both pictures, and we can count the blue box as 3 high and the ellipse as 2. So 3 is enough. If we did this we would be answering the question correctly but also demonstrating we do not have a measure. That is the whole has measure 3, and the parts have measures 3 and 2 but (3+2). If we really wanted to include this as a measure then we would need to revisit the idea that the two shapes are disjoint. While they are disjoint in the xy-plane they are not disjoint in the y direction alone. And so in that sense this is not a violation of measurement rules, just a misunderstanding about the meaning of disjoint for this case. An “illusion” as we have been warned about already.
Option 2. An alternative reading of this question is to ask if we stack up the shapes how tall would they be? Here we would in fact add 3 to 2 to get 5. This would be a measure as the whole would be the sum of the parts.

It is crucially important to be precise in our language of measurement. Many times a miscommunication or imprecise phrasing can lead to errors in measurement.


 Example 3:** Counting Measure \[\zeta\]
Given (E), the number of integers in (E) is the counting measure. As formula:
\[\displaystyle \zeta(E) := |E\cap \mathbb{Z}|\]%2520%253A%253D%2520%257CE%255Ccap%2520%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%257C?scale=1).
Notice this often does take different values on intervals
\[\begin{aligned}
\zeta\Big( (0,1) \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n<1\}| = |\{\}|=0 &
\zeta\Big( [0,1) \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n<1\}| = |\{ 0 \}|=1\\
\zeta\Big( (0,1] \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0<n<1\}| = |\{1\}|=1 &
\zeta\Big( [0,1] \Big) & = |\{ n\in\mathbb{Z}\mid 0\leq n<1\}| = |\{ 0,1 \}|=2
\end{aligned}\]%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%253Cn%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%255C%257D%257C%253D0%2520%2526%2520%250A%255Czeta%255CBig(%2520%255B0%252C1)%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%255Cleq%2520n%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%25200%2520%255C%257D%257C%253D1%255C%255C%250A%255Czeta%255CBig(%2520(0%252C1%255D%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%253Cn%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B1%255C%257D%257C%253D1%2520%2526%2520%250A%255Czeta%255CBig(%2520%255B0%252C1%255D%2520%255CBig)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%2520n%255Cin%255Cmathbb%257BZ%257D%255Cmid%25200%255Cleq%2520n%253C1%255C%257D%257C%2520%253D%2520%257C%255C%257B%25200%252C1%2520%255C%257D%257C%253D2%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Some common places to encounter a counting measure like this include:

Counting the number of steps in a loop, e.g. for i in [a...b] Use \[\zeta([a,b])\]?scale=1).
Counting the number of steps in a loop, e.g. for i in [a...b] step 2 Use \[\zeta(\{ 2m+j \mid 0\leq m\leq b-a\})\]?scale=1).
You need to count steps of two nested loops, use \[\zeta\times \zeta\].



 Example 4:** Kolmogorov’s Probability Measures \[\kappa\], a coin flip example
Suppose you have a coin with Heads H and tails T. The simplest thing to measure is the probability of the two individual outcomes. Here space (={H,T}) and the measure is the uniform measure: \[\displaystyle \kappa=\frac{|X|}{|\Omega|}\]. That is:
\[\begin{aligned}
\kappa (\{\}) & = 0  & \kappa(\{H\}) & =\frac{1}{2} & \kappa(\{T\}) & = \frac{1}{2} & \kappa(\{H,T\})=\frac{2}{2}=1.
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%25200%2520%2520%2526%2520%255Ckappa(%255C%257BH%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%253D%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%2526%2520%255Ckappa(%255C%257BT%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%2526%2520%255Ckappa(%255C%257BH%252CT%255C%257D)%253D%255Cfrac%257B2%257D%257B2%257D%253D1.%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
Now the more interesting probability is to continue coin flips and see what patterns emerge.


 First flip is heads
.The first flip is heads: ({EE_1=H}). This covers half the options and its measure is 1/2.



Probability tree of coin flips with the branches that start with heads highlighted.




 First flip is tails, second heads
The first flip is tails and second flip is heads: ({EE_1=T, E_2=H}). This covers 1/4 of the options and its measure is 1/2.



Probability tree of coin flips with the branches that start with tails and then heads highlighted.




 Every even flip is tails
Every even flip is tails: (C={EE_{2n}=T}).



Probability of coin flips with branches highlighted if every even flip is tails.


As flips continue the ones that survive a spread out and do not form a customary length. So the right measure here has to come from our understanding of probability laws instead. We can talk of this measure by considering the limit of the proportion, which decreases by 2 every time we reach an even flip (because only half of those are T). In fact, while somewhat boring to do by hand, a computer can just move the symbols around according to the formal rules to get the same answer.
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(\{E\mid \forall n.(E_{2n}=T)\}) & =\text{Prob}\left(\bigcap_{n} \{E\mid E_{2n}=T\}\right)\\
& = \prod_{n} \text{Prob}(\{E\mid E_{2n}=0\}) & \text{Conditional Probability}\\
& = \prod_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{2} = \lim_{k\to \infty}\prod_{n=1}^k \frac{1}{2}\\
& = \lim_{k\to \infty}\frac{1}{2^k}
=0
\end{aligned}\]%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%253D%255Ctext%257BProb%257D%255Cleft(%255Cbigcap_%257Bn%257D%2520%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_%257B2n%257D%253DT%255C%257D%255Cright)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cprod_%257Bn%257D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_%257B2n%257D%253D0%255C%257D)%2520%2526%2520%255Ctext%257BConditional%2520Probability%257D%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cprod_%257Bn%253D0%257D%255E%255Cinfty%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%253D%2520%255Clim_%257Bk%255Cto%2520%255Cinfty%257D%255Cprod_%257Bn%253D1%257D%255Ek%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Clim_%257Bk%255Cto%2520%255Cinfty%257D%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%255Ek%257D%250A%2520%253D0%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1).


 Disjoint events
Disjoint events in probability add their probabilities. This the same rule as measures. The following illustration with coin flips demonstrates this.



Coin flips with two independent events. The blue start with heads, the red begin tails-heads.


We can turn this measurement over to computers.

(A={EE_1=H}) is the set of coin flips where the first flip lands H.
(B={EE_1=T E_{2}=H}) is the set of coin flips where the first flip is T and the second flip lands H.

Notice (AB={}) (because the first flip cannot be both heads and tails). So these two are disjoint.
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(A\sqcup B)  & = \text{Prob}(A)+\text{Prob}(B)\\
& = \text{Prob}(E_1=H) + \text{Prob}(E_{1}=T)\cdot \text{Prob}(E_2=H)\\
&= \frac{1}{2} +\frac{1}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2} =  \frac{3}{4}
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(A)%252B%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(B)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(E_1%253DH)%2520%252B%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(E_%257B1%257D%253DT)%255Ccdot%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(E_2%253DH)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%252B%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%255Ccdot%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%2520%253D%2520%2520%255Cfrac%257B3%257D%257B4%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D%25C2%25A0?scale=1)


 Overlapping events
Non-disjoint sets measures are not directly defined. But probabilities are not just any measure, and these have a solution directly.



Overlapping events cannot be measured as their sum because they are not disjoint.


This would be a good place to pause and notice the essential role of disjoint unions. Suppose we used (C={EE_2=T}) instead of (B). Now
(AC ={EE_1=H, E_2=T})
So now (A) and (C) are not disjoint, and this affects our probability measure
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Prob}(A\cup C)
& = \text{Prob}(\{E\mid E_1=H \text{ or }E_2=T\})\\
& = \text{Prob}(\{E\mid E_1=H\}\sqcup \{ E\mid E_1=T, E_2=T\})\\
& = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{4}=\frac{3}{4}\\
\text{Prob}(A)+\text{Prob}(C) & = \frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2}=1\neq \frac{3}{4}
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2520%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_1%253DH%2520%255Ctext%257B%2520or%2520%257DE_2%253DT%255C%257D)%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(%255C%257BE%255Cmid%2520E_1%253DH%255C%257D%255Csqcup%2520%255C%257B%2520E%255Cmid%2520E_1%253DT%252C%2520E_2%253DT%255C%257D)%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%252B%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B4%257D%253D%255Cfrac%257B3%257D%257B4%257D%255C%255C%250A%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(A)%252B%255Ctext%257BProb%257D(C)%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%252B%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%253D1%255Cneq%2520%255Cfrac%257B3%257D%257B4%257D%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D%25C2%25A0?scale=1)
So be careful to check on the disjoint condition when using measures and if measures alone are not enough information, look at your context to see something else will help.


 Example 5**: Gaussian’s Probability Measure \[\gamma\]
Recall the second distribution for probability was useful when data had a target value but would wobble off target with some predictable variation. This was known as Gaussian distribution. See more here Probability unit. The Gaussian Measure applies to decimal numbers (x) and measures them on the “Bell curve” by the following formula.
\[\displaystyle \gamma(X) = \frac{1}{\sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^2}\]%2520%253D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B%255Csigma%2520%255Csqrt%257B2%255Cpi%257D%257D%2520e%255E%257B-%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257B2%257D%255Cleft(%255Cfrac%257Bx-%255Cmu%257D%257B%255Csigma%257D%255Cright)%255E2%257D?scale=1)
where () is the average value “center of the bell curve” (not a measure!) and () is the standard deviation (how wide the bell is). Below we plot the curve for a bell with deviation () and mean ().



A bell curve centered at mean 0 with deviation 1.


For most people it is not important that you memorize this formula, but notice it is qualitatively different from both the distance and uniform measures.


 *Calculations & Implications
Suppose that () is a positive measure. Then all of the following are true.

Bigger subsets get bigger measures: If \[A\subset B\] and both are measurable then \[\mu(A)\leq \mu(B)\]%255Cleq%2520%255Cmu(B)?scale=1).
If you steadily approximate a measure from below you will reach the measure. If \[A_1\subset A_2\subset\cdots\] are all measurable then \[\displaystyle \mu\Big(\bigcup_i A_i\Big)=\lim_{i\to\infty} \mu(A_i)=\sup_{i} \mu(A_i)\]%253D%255Clim_%257Bi%255Cto%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Cmu(A_i)%253D%255Csup_%257Bi%257D%2520%255Cmu(A_i)?scale=1).
If you steadily approximate a finite measure from above you will reach it. If \[A_1\supset A_2\supset\cdots\] are all measurable and \[\infty\gt \mu(A_1)\]?scale=1) then \[\displaystyle \mu\Big(\bigcap_i A_i\Big)=\lim_{i\to\infty} \mu(A_i)=\inf_i \{\mu(A_i)\}\]%253D%255Clim_%257Bi%255Cto%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Cmu(A_i)%253D%255Cinf_i%2520%255C%257B%255Cmu(A_i)%255C%257D?scale=1).


 Example Calculation of Measures.

Using the Lebesgue interval measure () from above, to compute (((1,3)) and measure this as (((1,4])=4-1=3).
Using the Lebesgue interval measure () from above, to compute (({1})) first find a way to write this as an interval, e.g. ([1,1]). Then (([1,1])=|1-1|=0)
\[\mu(E)=7\]%253D7?scale=1) and \[\mu(F)=8\]%253D8?scale=1) so is \[\mu(E\cup F)\geq 8\]%255Cgeq%25208?scale=1)? Well since \[F\subset E\cup F\] then \[8=\mu(F)\leq \mu(E\cup F)\]%255Cleq%2520%255Cmu(E%255Ccup%2520F)?scale=1) so yes.
[Hard] To compute \[\displaystyle \lambda\Big(\bigcap_n \left(0,\frac{1}{n}\right)\Big)\]%255CBig)?scale=1) first notice \[\lambda((0,1))=|1-0|=1 \lt \infty\])%253D%257C1-0%257C%253D1%2520%255Clt%2520%255Cinfty?scale=1). So by the rule 3. above, \[\displaystyle \lambda\Big(\bigcap_n (0,1/n)\Big)=\lim_{n\to \infty} \lambda((0,1/n)=\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n}=0\]%255CBig)%253D%255Clim_%257Bn%255Cto%2520%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Clambda((0%252C1%252Fn)%253D%255Clim_%257Bn%255Cto%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Cfrac%257B1%257D%257Bn%257D%253D0?scale=1).




 *Quick Check

What is the signed measure \[\Delta (-\infty,1]\]. - It is \[\infty\] *


Correct: \[\Delta(-\infty,1)=1-(-\infty)=1+\infty=\infty\]%253D1-(-%255Cinfty)%253D1%252B%255Cinfty%253D%255Cinfty?scale=1) - It is \[-\infty\] *\[\Delta(-\infty,1)=1-(-\infty)=1+\infty=\infty\]%253D1-(-%255Cinfty)%253D1%252B%255Cinfty%253D%255Cinfty?scale=1)



 * Fill-in-the-Blank

Lebesgue’s Interval Measure \[\lambda((1,3)\sqcup (4,7])=\]%255Csqcup%2520(4%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)5 .
Lebesgue’s Interval Measure \[\lambda((1,4)\cup (3,7])=\]%255Ccup%2520(3%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)6 .
Counting Measure \[\zeta((1,3)\sqcup (4,7])=\]%255Csqcup%2520(4%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)4
Lebesgue’s Interval Measure \[\lambda((1,4)\cup (3,7])=\]%255Ccup%2520(3%252C7%255D)%253D?scale=1)6 .



 * Quick Check

If \[\mu(E)=0\]%253D0?scale=1) then \[E=\emptyset\] - True *
No, while \[\mu(\emptyset)=0\]%253D0?scale=1) that is on the only way, consider any one of \[\lambda(\{3\})=0\]%253D0?scale=1) or \[\zeta((0,1))=0\])%253D0?scale=1) - False *


Correct: consider any one of \[\lambda(\{3\})=0\]%253D0?scale=1) or \[\zeta((0,1))=0\])%253D0?scale=1)

Module 13 what is a Feature
* The value of a stock shifts so erratically that we need to simplify the data. See is averaged over time. Plot its highs and lows. These are features. And extracting features is the name of the game in data. And calculus owns that market. So when you see our icon * of an erratic data set. You will think about taming that wave through features.

 Main Object: Features
Given a set (), a feature is a function (f:). If we have two features we might plot them as a pair ((x(),y())) as a point the xy-plane; one point for each datum (). [We saw features several times in this course, most recently in our Handwritten Digit’s lab.]. If we have 3 features we can make a list of 3, a point in 3-dimensional space, and so on. In a future course on Linear Algebra you can explore the significance of multiple features. In this module we will explore just one.


 Module Objectives

Define and recognize features and linear features.
Model integrals as linear features.
Apply the Mean Value Theorem.
Apply the knowledge that all linear features are integrals for some measure (Riesz Representation Theorem.)
Use derivatives to extract features
Increasing & decreasing rates.
Minimums, maximums, critical points.

* 11-2 | Features are integrals, now what?

 * Lesson Introduction
The integral is a powerful tool explored as far back as Archimedes, rediscovered by Newton and Leibniz and all that to say it is powerful! There is a reason it appears on chalkboards in movies about smart people. So knowing that essentially all features are integrals opens the door to compute and predict with integrals. Fortunately most of this is in calculators and computers but there are a few properties you really need to know yourself because they lead to using it properly.


 * Learning Materials

 Reading
Embedded media


 Video [mm:ss]
YouTube video player



 * Quick Check

u-substituion is just another name for … - Chaining one integral into another. *


Correct: u-substitution is a jargon phrase because so much of calculus has used the letter u to do it but the point is to compose integrals and the letter can be anything. Still use u because people will understand you. - When the variable is called u. *

title: 5000 Years of Modern Computing
text:
math156 Integrals
There are functions we create from measuring things, and the rest of our data is a calculation with those measurements. So it matters to single out the methods that measurements can be combined to calculate accurate and approximate values of the things we can’t easily measure. When a problem space satisfies the “Integral Law”—the whole is the sum of its parts—that’s when we can safely apply the integral. Part I of several things to say on this.

 *Objectives

Identify the integral law
Relate areas to areas of rectangles
Read the integral notation.



 *Lectures
YouTube video player
Much of today’s integrals are done by computer and done by methods few mathematicians even understand. Even show, there are 3 inch thick textbooks and competitions about the “doing” of integral calculus which continue to be taught as a right of passage to becoming a mathematician. None of those methods are used in modern software and what is used is so easy to access as a package and so fine tuned I consider it more important to know how to choose and use one than to know how it works. The primary lessons are the following.

 When to use an integral
Use an integral whenever you want to measure an overall quantity. Words like “area” and “volume” are good clues. Don’t be shy about it. It doesn’t have to be a math sounding problem. Think of “Sales Volume”. The thing that you want to measure should have a boundary that is easy to describe, the e.g. we know the current daily sales numbers and how many days we have been selling. Then an estimate for the sales is the current daily sales times the number of days. An even better estimate is to use the average daily sales. The actual integral is to add up all the sales of each day. That is an integral. It is also perfectly obvious to a business person and doesn’t seem like you need calculus. But this is only the first step. This is the step to get you aware there is an integral at work in an ordinary project. Over the course of this unit we will start to fill in what knowledge of an integral can do for problem solving and reasoning logically. Here are some questions we might ask and can answer with the calculus.

If I know the average daily sales and I multiply it by the number of days selling is that the same or close to the sum of all the sales?
What if some days I loose product (unsold, spoiled, etc). Can I simply call this “negative area”?
What do I need to predict future sales volume?



 Reading an integral properly
Remember the integral sign is a fancy “S” ∫and usually it is given by a command like “int” or “Integral”. Integrals are then given subscripts or superscripts based on the boundary. The boundary can be some crazy shape called a “domain” DD and we would write
(_D)
If the domain is a straight line segment we just write the end points a and b, so (_a^b). Next we write what we want to sum, and this is an area formula. Let me say this carefully, it is an area formula not a specific area. The formula must adjust to make finer and finer approximations, usually by making smaller and smaller rectangles of height (f(x)) times a width dxdx. But every now and then you need something other than rectangles so you might find a formula like (f(r)dr) where (r) is a radius or (f(x)d) where () is a much more general measure. These are not things you will need to fiddle with you will simply need to be able to read and understand what people are doing and what you are asking a computer to do. All together the integral formulas will look like this.
(_a^b f(x) dx) or (_D f(r) dr) or (_D f(x) d)

* Part 1 Why Most Features are Integrals (Riesz Representation Theorem)
In computation, information can often be minimized to a number. You might want to argue we should consider lists of numbers too, but as we are looking into the building blocks, the smallest we should go is extracting a single number as our information. The industry has given this asset the name “feature”.

 Definition of Features
A feature on a set  of data is a function  (or in computational syntax def feature( x : Data ) : Float), which assigns a decimal number or an infinity to every point.
In practice and computation we may need to get by with an approximation known as a partial feature which is a function that attempts to assign such a value but may on some inputs be undefined, i.e. , equivalently def feature( x : Data ) : Float?. (Recall  is away to assign an output of nothing to a failed evaluation.)


 Integrals as Features
Perhaps the most common feature in a collection of numbers is that average. However context is important to understand what “average” we intend. We can see the impact by looking 40 years of oil prices.


 Crude Oil in Dollars



Crude oil prices from 1986-2026.


Above we show the crude oil prices from 1986-2026 in dollars. Identified in the graphic the average, $51.02. It is a large sum scaled by the total number of daily prices.



LaTeX: (t)=_{i} (i) 


(The shaded region shows the standard deviation, roughly how much change is considered typical in a statistically noisy situation.)


 Crude Oil Adjusted for Inflation



Crude oil prices adjusted for inflation from 1986-2026


Now let’s include some subject matter expertise. The value of the dollar changes over time as well. So the meaning of these prices changes. What cost $100 in 1986 is not the same as in 2026. Below is a new graph adjusted for this effect known as “inflation”.
Here the average jumps to $73.87. And it truly is a different formula



LaTeX:


This is getting complicated. We might do better to think of this as a new kind of sum, one that uses intervals of inflation instead of days as its steps.



LaTeX:


Even familiar data like “averages” can benefit from complexities such as weighting values. In our oil prices this was done to adjust for inflation. In grades this is done to weight exams differently for homework. Both give us a clues about the meaning of the data. And both are a form of integral.

 Integrals as features.
When our data consists of numbers (f(i)) over a range of values (iI), we can attempt to create a single number adding up the values. If the list is not finite we can take an integral as a number instead. And if we want a more nuanced measure that includes how we should weight the inputs (e.g. as we did with inflation) we can simply modify how we measure (). So integrals are by design convenient features.



LaTeX: _{}(f) := _I f, d





 Multiple Measurements
While one measurement is our focus, it is worthwhile pause to acknowledge that in real life we often need multiple measurements.


 Two measures of nice objects



Measuring a shape from two different measurements.




 Two measures of awkward object



Measuring an awkward shape by measuring it in more than one way.




 Two awkward measures of awkward shapes



Measuring an awkward shape better by using awkward measurements.



 The weighted average and Expectation
Suppose our data is a list of decimal numbers (a_1,, a_n). We can take the average, which will put a number to the data, i.e. the average is a feature.



LaTeX:


Now because the average is also a sum we can write it as an integral where we weight our measure by 1/n, the total number of samples. That is how the common average works.
Yet we sometimes we want data to be weighted. Perhaps homework scores count for 35% and exams for 55%. We could still use an integral but we would need to re-weight things.



LaTeX:


A weighted average is just a new feature. It is also just a different integral. In fact this whole idea has spread to giving “average” a new name, called “Expectation”. That means an average created as an integral.


 Features in an image
Imagine you look at an image as list of numbers.
{TBD}



 Linear Features
In a phrase, a feature is linear if “it is distributed amongst summands.” But what does this actually mean? Remember we are only looking here at data (f) that are already numbers. That means we can already talk about addition. So we cannot only add data (f) to data (g), we can also add their features (F(f)+F(g)). So how different is (F(f+g)) from (F(f)+F(g))? Let us take a look at some actual data to find out.
Student (i)Homework 1 (f)Homework 2 (g)Homework 1+2 (f+g)
Brutus Buckeye7570145
Mandrake Duck8580165
Cam T. Ram9592187
Average858185+81=166
(Note all value here are accurate to one digit.)
Let’s be very careful here. We are using specifically lists of the same length 3. So we have



LaTeX: f(1)+f(2)+f(3){)}+g(1)+g(2)+g(3){)}=(f+g)(1)+(f+g)(2)+(f+g)(3))


If you had lists of different lengths you would not have such a property. However, used for data of same shape, the average truly is distributed amongst its parts. And this make it great for all sorts of reasons including that we can compute features in parallel on large server farms, or update them over time as new data becomes available.


 Linear Features
A feature (L) is called linear if  for all data (f,g).
As a flow chart:



Linear features can be applied before or after a sum creating a commutative diagram.



 Key Example
The fundamental example of linear features are integrals:



LaTeX: (f+g)d= f, d+ g, d





 Consequently (L( f)= L(f))
Ok, you need to know the heading, but it is a lovely part of algebra to walk through why. So let’s work this out together.
When we get a number of useful consequences including the following.




LaTeX:





LaTeX:


…so all together

Now that we can slide positive integers in and out, what about negatives?



LaTeX:


Ok so both positive and negative integers move in and out. What about fractions? Yep, those too…



LaTeX:


Net result: for all fractions (), (L(f)=L(f)).
Some authors may prefer to make the claim a requirement instead of a consequence. Just remember, every requirement we make is future work. Since this is a consequence we can do the work once and the use the result forever.


 Continuous Features
A final useful condition on features is the ability to use approximations. This is because data collection is often too fragile to get the same exact number over and over every time we re-measure. We realistically need to accept that our data will be approximate. But if the features of approximation are radically different then we simply cannot use those features. It will be unreliable. To avoid this the most stable features work well with approximations in the following sense.


 Continuous Features
A feature (C) is continuous if features of approximations by limits are limits of the features of those approximations, that is:



LaTeX: L(_x f_x) = _x L(f_x)


An important implicit condition is that these limits exist! If you put garbage on either side then there is no equation. As a flow chart we are saying:



Lim.png



 Key Example
The fundamental example of continuous features are integrals:



LaTeX: (_u f_u) d= _u (f_u, d)


This therefore includes

Averages of fixed length lists.
Expectation of probabilities.




 Which features are integrals?


 Riesz Representation Theorem
Every feature (L(f)) which satisfies

“Linear” . (The feature’s value is distributed amongst the data.)
“Continuous” . (Approximations of features are features of approximations.)

then there is a measure () such that



LaTeX:


… so the most useful features come from integrals!

 Implications
Let us summarize.

Integrals give use features.
All features can be seen as evaluating certain integrals.
So in a loose sense integrals are responsible for all features.

The implication is both practical and theoretical.

On the practical side we can make really good software and hardware to compute integrals. What are integral again? Giant sums. Great, make hardware that can add lots of numbers very fast. GPUs are the world leaders in this space at the moment.
On the theory side having one concrete description of features as integrals helps us give precise facts about what is possible, prove what is impossible, and link data science problems to a very long history of mathematics where new ideas have a good chance of surfacing.

If you want to know more, consider learning about Analysis and Statistical Learning. Icon Progress Bar (browser only)

* 12.2 “Area” & “Slope” Working together
 Many measurements you will encounter are accumulations of smaller measurements. If we learn to compute those measurements the rest is data collection and physical scanners.

 Simple functions
Suppose we know how to measure disjoint subsets (A_1,, A_n). Then we can measure them together because the whole is the sum of its parts:
((A_1A_n) = (A_1)++(A_n))
Now what if we discover along the way that we would like to create a new measure by simply re-weighting each individual term.

 Example: course grading
Let us suppose () represents all graded assessments in a course, each graded as a percentage. To hold on to a specific example here is a possible grade list for our fictitious student.
StudentHomework 1Lab 1Homework 2Lab 2Exam 1 Homework 3Lab 3Exam 2Raw Average \[\displaystyle \frac{\mu(A)}{8}\]%257D%257B8%257D?scale=1)Weighted Average \[\displaystyle \frac{\nu(A)}{8}\]%257D%257B8%257D?scale=1)
Ralphie T. Buffalo****75%80%72%0%74%81%85%83%69%
Cam T. Ram 92% 85%75%82%87%88%95%91%87%
The score for a subset (A) is to add up all the scores in (A) and divide them by the total number of scores, i.e. an average :
\[\displaystyle \mu(A)=\sum_{a\in A} a\]%253D%255Csum_%257Ba%255Cin%2520A%257D%2520a?scale=1)
(We included a column for the measure ((Ralphie)) in row 2 and ((Cam)) in row 3.)
Revisiting the grades. Now suppose we decide it would be better to weight scores based on categories. For example homeworks (H) should count for 40% of the grade, labs (L) for 30%, and exams (E) for 30%. Because these categories are disjoint we could adapt our existing measure to include this weighting as follows.
\[\nu(A) = 0.40\cdot \mu(A\cap H) + 0.30 \cdot  \mu(A\cap L) + 0.30\cdot \mu(A\cap E)\]%2520%253D%25200.40%255Ccdot%2520%255Cmu(A%255Ccap%2520H)%2520%252B%25200.30%2520%255Ccdot%2520%2520%255Cmu(A%255Ccap%2520L)%2520%252B%25200.30%255Ccdot%2520%255Cmu(A%255Ccap%2520E)?scale=1)
In our table above example we have to gather the homework columns to get (AH), the lab columns to get (AL) and the exam columns to get (AE) for a combined score of
\[\begin{aligned}
\nu(\text{Ralphi}) & = 0.40\mu(\{75\%, 72\%,81\%\}) + 0.30\mu(\{80\%,0\%,85\%\})+0.30\mu(\{74\%,83\%\})\\
& = 0.40\frac{0.75+0.72+0.81}{8} + 0.30\frac{0.80+0.00+0.85}{8}+0.30\frac{0.74+0.83}{8}\\
& =
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%253D%25200.40%255Cmu(%255C%257B75%255C%2525%252C%252072%255C%2525%252C81%255C%2525%255C%257D)%2520%252B%25200.30%255Cmu(%255C%257B80%255C%2525%252C0%255C%2525%252C85%255C%2525%255C%257D)%252B0.30%255Cmu(%255C%257B74%255C%2525%252C83%255C%2525%255C%257D)%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%25200.40%255Cfrac%257B0.75%252B0.72%252B0.81%257D%257B8%257D%2520%252B%25200.30%255Cfrac%257B0.80%252B0.00%252B0.85%257D%257B8%257D%252B0.30%255Cfrac%257B0.74%252B0.83%257D%257B8%257D%255C%255C%250A%2526%2520%253D%2520%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
(We included this new measure ((Cam)) for Cam
for that () takes the sum of all grades in subset (A) of graded work with () the set of all graded work for a course. For example if (A_{homework}) was homework and (A_{lab}) lab, and (A_{exam}) exam scores, perhaps we would want homework to count for 40%, quizzes and exams for 30% each. The new wait



 New Measurements from Old Ones
The following table lists a number of measurements built from existing measurements. There are many more not listed here that arise across science, industry, and business.

 Measurement


 Operator
Velocity = meters / second Ratio ()
Acceleration = velocity / hour Ratio ()
Area = square miles, meters squared, Product ()
Torque = foot-pounds Product ()
inflation = supply / demand Ratio ()
P.E. = Price / Earning Ratio ()
Market Cap. = Share Price * Volume Product ()
Work = CPUs * Hours Product ()
The unifying aspect of these measures is that they combine 2 measurements using either multiplication or division. So it matters to develop these two measurements.



 Products of measures: the integral
To explore the product of two measures let’s call them collectively as “Area”. In a rectangle this is length of the best times the length of the height. Yet concepts like length and area do not mean anything to topics like Market Capitalization, Torque or many other product related measurements. Yet it helps us often to recycle the language of shapes so we are guided towards tools that will help us work with those topics. So throughout we put quotation marks around these words that are metaphorical abstractions, e.g. “Area” and “Length”.

 An “area” from the stock market
The “Cumulative Stock Price” of a company is the sum of changing stock prices in some time window. This may not sound like an area, but we attach that vocabulary by plotting a diagram of the stock. Below is a chart from MorningStar.Com (a stock-market data broker) that charts the Cumulative Stock Price of Nvidia as a shaded area under the curve of individual daily pricing.


 Building the Integral



 A “rectangle’s area” (x) and (y)
To kick off the measurement let us put some names and symbols to the parameters.

(x) will be mean the (signed or unsigned) measurement on the x-axis of our “rectangle”. This could be a distance measure, a probability measure or some unknown measure, signed or unsigned. However, the images we plot to explain this will all be visualizations of the distance measure.
(y) will be mean the (signed or unsigned) measurement on the y-axis of our “rectangle”.
(xy) the measure of the “rectangle” with sides (y) and (x).




Area of a rectangle labeled by change measurement in the x and y axes.


Keep in mind these are metaphorical concepts. The pictures are therefore not necessary, but they are helpful to many.


 Approximating complicated “Areas” with “Rectangle areas”
It would be difficult to guess the precise area in something as complicated as the Nvidia stock prices. However we know that whatever a graphical “area” is meant to be it should 2-dimensional and have a 1-dimensional boundary. So if we are to produce that concept in other applications we need to declare upfront what is our boundary. We can do this with a combination of boundaries, (think bottom, sides, top). For example, in our Cumulative Stock Price

the bottom () was the x-axis (because stock prices cannot go negative).
The sides were the window time, say 2021 on the left and 2026 on the right.
The top is the interesting bit, it is the daily stock prices, some crazy graph (f).

Now for an approximation we can use the Stock prices at several places to set up how high our rectangle goes. And we can widen or shrink our rectangles by taking points further or closer apart. In the end we have a mix of over and under estimates of the area.



Approximate area of a curved shape make by placing rectangle near the shape of the curve.


Let us label each rectangle by the pair of intervals (X=[x_j,x_{j+1}]) and (Y=[y_j,y_{j+1}]) that define each rectangles dimensions (X) and (Y) respectively. All the rectangles collectively are (). So if (A) is the target area, our approximation by rectangles is trying to approximate () as a disjoint union.
\[\displaystyle A\approx \bigsqcup_{(X,Y)\in \mathcal{P}} (X\times Y)\]%255Cin%2520%255Cmathcal%257BP%257D%257D%2520(X%255Ctimes%2520Y)?scale=1)
Thus we can use the fact that for measures, the whole is the sum of its parts((AB)=(A)+(B)). We have finite number of parts so we distribute the measurement as sum of each rectangle measurement.
\[\begin{aligned}
\mu(A) & \approx \mu\left(\bigsqcup_{(Y,X)\in \mathcal{P}} (Y\times X)\right)\\
& \approx \sum_{(Y,X)\in \mathcal{P}} \mu(Y\times X)\\
& \approx \sum_{(Y,X)\in \mathcal{P}} \Delta Y\times \Delta X
\end{aligned}\]%2520%2526%2520%255Capprox%2520%255Cmu%255Cleft(%255Cbigsqcup_%257B(Y%252CX)%255Cin%2520%255Cmathcal%257BP%257D%257D%2520(Y%255Ctimes%2520X)%255Cright)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%255Capprox%2520%255Csum_%257B(Y%252CX)%255Cin%2520%255Cmathcal%257BP%257D%257D%2520%255Cmu(Y%255Ctimes%2520X)%255C%255C%250A%2520%2526%2520%255Capprox%2520%255Csum_%257B(Y%252CX)%255Cin%2520%255Cmathcal%257BP%257D%257D%2520%255CDelta%2520Y%255Ctimes%2520%255CDelta%2520X%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)


 The integral (_{} f d) as the best approximation. Lebesgue’s Method.
Now to make the best estimate suppose insist that our approximations are all from below the graph, written
(f) the rectangles in (mathcal{P}) are entirely below the graph of (f)
Now define the integral as the least upper bound / supremum of all approximations.
\[\displaystyle \int_{\Omega} f d\mu =\sup_{\mathcal{P}\leq f} \sum_{(X,Y)\in \mathcal{P}} \Delta Y \times \Delta X\]%255Cin%2520%255Cmathcal%257BP%257D%257D%2520%255CDelta%2520Y%2520%255Ctimes%2520%255CDelta%2520X?scale=1)
This integral was created by Lebesgue (le-bay-guh) and it is the integral that you will need in data science, probability, mathematics and science.

Technical Glitch. While this description is the right concept, sometimes no single () reaches the exact area. So there is no max. Instead there might be gradually improving max. So we should take the limit of this growing approximation.



Values steadily increasing from 2 to just above 2.5


Mathematicians have given the limit of maximum values a name. We call it a supremum instead of max.
\[\displaystyle \sup_{x} A = \lim_{B\subset A} \max B\] the limit of all subsets that have a maximum.
So the actual statement should use supremum not max.
\[\displaystyle \int_{\Omega} f d\mu =\sup_{\mathcal{P}\leq f} \sum_{(X,Y)\in \mathcal{P}} \Delta Y \times \Delta X\]%255Cin%2520%255Cmathcal%257BP%257D%257D%2520%255CDelta%2520Y%2520%255Ctimes%2520%255CDelta%2520X?scale=1)
You can probably get by confusing maximum with supremum but at least you have been warned that eventually you could need to know the difference.


 Riemann’s alternative for continuous data (Optional)
Sometimes it is nice to have more than one way to think or compute and the integral is not exception. One strategy that has had enormous success for geometry and physics problem has concerned the situations where the domain of integration is uniform (compact is the mathematician’s term). of our area are all connected by continuous lines. (Unlike our weighted stock model). more than it is not necessary to have more than one way to compute integrals, the integral we have defined works for all measurements, there is a popular alternative designed specifically for geometry. If you have seen calculus then chances are the this is the integral you were taught.
We should think of the change in the x-axis as striding between (a) and (b), so it is sequence (a=x_0<x_1<< x_n=b).



Approximate area of a curved shape make by placing rectangle near the shape of the curve.


Each change in x is the measure of that stride:
(x_j = x_{j+1}-x_j)
Since we measure the height from the x-axis, a height of 0, and we stop when we reach the curve (f), the change in y is
(y_j=f(x_j)-0)
Take as a sum we have the formula at any one approximation. Taking all the approximations together we can ask for the limit (if it exists) and give that a similar name. The giant S () to invoke the growing size of the sums over increasing numbers of boxes, and the lower case d (dx) to invoke the shrinking measure of each stride in the x axis.
\[\begin{aligned}
\int_a^b f\, dx & =\lim_{n\to \infty} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \Delta y_j \Delta x_j,
& \Delta y_j & = f(x_j)-0 & \Delta x_j & = x_{j+1}-x_j\\
& =\lim_{n\to \infty} \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} f(x_j) (x_{j+1}-x_j).
\end{aligned}\]-0%2520%2526%2520%255CDelta%2520x_j%2520%2526%2520%253D%2520x_%257Bj%252B1%257D-x_j%255C%255C%250A%2520%2520%2526%2520%253D%255Clim_%257Bn%255Cto%2520%255Cinfty%257D%2520%255Csum_%257Bj%253D0%257D%255E%257Bn-1%257D%2520f(x_j)%2520(x_%257Bj%252B1%257D-x_j).%250A%255Cend%257Baligned%257D?scale=1)
This integral is credited to Riemann though it appeared in various forms in earlier work. While some people find this model easier to learn, it does not work with many of the important applications of measurement, including probability and data science applications. So it is best to invest in our first integral.


 Run an interactive Demo
The best way to gain intuition is to try this with your own shapes and boxes. The GeoGebra project offers some incredible demonstrations. Below are two, but you should poke around and find more that answer your questions. Book mark this website. It will be a go-to tool in much of your scientific training.

Geometry offered our first measures as line segments. Probability took us further letting use measure points that might spread out but still have a clear notion of measurement. * 12.2.b Combing Integral and Derivative thinking
 The power of measurement is strongest when we can go forward with integrals and backwards with derivatives.

 Video
y=(y*x)/x and therefore Calculus

 A bit of history and context
Historically derivatives were defined as the slope of tangents to a curve or instantaneous rates of change. These concepts are not immediately logical—how do you define a unique tangent to a graph without already having the slope, i.e. it makes for a circular definition. An instant in time is also not a precise concept. But its ability to solve questions made Newton (1660’s) a hero of science. Between the 1800-1900’s Cauchy, Weirestrass, and Riemann each contributed ideas to make the concept precise. Still issued persisted not least of which was the difficulty in stacking integrals measurements. While geometry suggested we can remeasure as many times as we like, the formulas of the Cauchy-Riemann method had gaps and oddities that did not match the graphical intuition.
To solve these problem Lebesgue’s integral (1900) threw the subject on its head. Instead of beginning with the concept of smaller and smaller approximations, Lebesgue classified what a measurement under the basic concept that: the whole is the sum of its parts. Once created integrals stand out as accumulation of measurements under any grouping into parts – be those small approximations or large chunks. The concept now being sound later authors such as Radon-Nikodym (1915) explored how to convert the calculus of the previous generation into this formalism. This new integral has proved compelling flexible and useful so it has dominated the sciences. For data sciences and probability it is the main tool. Icon Progress Bar (browser only)
